Yet grid investment is increasingly becoming a critical constraint on electrification, renewable deployment and energy-system resilience. The treatment of electricity networks highlights the complexity of sustainable finance classifications. In practice, not all green bond frameworks require network investments to be dedicated solely to renewable energy projects. Convenience yields represent the income investors are willing to forego to hold n sovereign bonds compared to other forms of duration. Our preferred measure of convenience is the difference between sovereign bond yields and swap rates, corrected by the market compensation for default risk from credit default swaps. Meanwhile, clean energy investment has surged, reaching a record $2.3 trillion in 2025, more than double the $1 trillion flowing into fossil fuels. This is a remarkable achievement. But it has not been sufficient to displace the fossil fuel system it was intended to replace. The arithmetic is unforgiving: global energy demand grew 1.3% in 2025, and while low-emissions sources contributed nearly 60% of that, the remaining 40% still required more oil, more gas, and more coal. The world added clean energy at an impressive pace. It just was not fast enough to allow the old system to shrink. The result is a system that is underinvested on both sides. Traditional energy has been starved of the capital needed to maintain supply. Clean energy, while attracting record investment, remains geographically concentrated – roughly 75% of global clean energy investment flows to a small number of markets – and has not yet built the grid infrastructure, storage capacity, or baseload reliability needed to serve as a full replacement. The capital gap exists everywhere one looks. M BluePaper 12 Productivity and Convergence: 1961-81 Canada’s strongest growth regime combined rapid expansion in inputs with substantial productivity gains. Between 1961 and 1981, business-sector output grew by approximately 4.8% annually. Hours worked contributed around 2.0 percentage points (pp), while labor productivity added a further 2.8pp. In other words, nearly 60% of output growth came from producing more in each hour worked rather than simply adding hours. The productivity contribution was also relatively balanced. Capital intensity added approximately 1.3pp annually, labor composition contributed 0.5pp, and MFP contributed close to 1pp. Workers were receiving more capital, the quality of the labor force was improving, and the economy was also generating gains beyond what could be attributed to measured inputs. This was the latter part of Canada’s postwar convergence phase. Canadian business-sector productivity growth exceeded that of the United States during much of the early postwar period, and Canada’s relative productivity level moved above 90% of the US level in the early 1980s. That convergence reflected both capital accumulation and the adoption of technologies and production practices already in use at the global productivity frontier. records.text: ysical AI is effectively creating a new category of energy consumer: machines capable of performing physical labour. Robots are a new category of energy consumer Physical AI is still a small market today, but our research suggests it could evolve into a $1trn ecosystem by 2035, spanning humanoids, autonomous vehicles, industrial automation and drones. As deployment accelerates, investors may need to think about robotics as not only a technology theme, but also an energy theme. Unlike traditional software, physical AI creates a two-layer energy demand: cloud compute to train increasingly complex models and local power to run robots performing tasks in the physical world. Training physical AI models is particularly energy intensive because they must learn not only reasoning, but also physics, motion, balance, navigation and manipulation, much of it through large-scale simulations and digital twins. Advanced AI model training currently consumes energy at a rate of 100-154MW, with projections exceeding 4GW by 2030. While data on physical AI models remain limited, we expect their energy requirements to be even greater, given the added complexity of learning and executing tasks in the physical world. 3 September 2026 130 Barclays | The global energy race

Macro momentum has weakened, delaying the earnings recovery: Following a disappointing 2Q and a cut in Morgan Stanley's GDP growth forecast, China's macro data since July have kept worsening. The policy response remains incremental rather than a broad-based demand stimulus, suggesting that a meaningful reflation impulse is unlikely in the near term. Consensus EPS estimates remain well below prior peaks – YTD, MSCI China EPS forecasts have been trimmed 3.7% for 2026 and 3.9% for 2027. MSCI China's ERB is still the worst among major global peers, making it difficult to allocate capital to the market, amid macro uncertainty. The liquidity backdrop has become less supportive: A series of measures YTD tightening oversight of offshore listings, cross-border brokerage, outbound investment, and offshore wealth flows has increased near-term investor concerns, particularly around Hong Kong as a wealth and investment hub. records.text: M Japan Insight Morgan Stanley MUFG 35 Importance of valuation-based stock selection We thus apply these findings to selection of stocks. Among the determinants of conversion to wholly owned status, we focus on valuation, a metric that fluctuates monthly and is thought to reflect market expectations most directly. We divided listed subsidiaries into quintiles based on their P/B and compare their respective stock price performances. We find that the group with the lowest valuations (Q1) demonstrated the best performance, while the results tended to decline as valuations rose ( Exhibit 44 ). This may be due to the weaker economic rationale for full conversion as valuations become higher, or the risk that if expectations for an unwinding of the parent-subsidiary structure were already discounted, the share price could sink if that unwinding failed to materialize. Note that this relationship was observed from the late 2010s through 2021, a period when the value factor struggled in the markets as a whole. That suggests that the results in Exhibit 44 cannot be explained solely by broader market value cycle trends. Therefore, as parent-subsidiary listings approach their conclusion as an investment theme, it is important not only to identify stocks likely to become wholly owned subsidiaries but also to avoid stocks with high valuations. Most are now between 1-1.3%. That shouldn’t be a surprise: previous forecasts dated back to the spring, ie the beginning of the energy crisis. Data has held up better since then. Our own forecasts have moved back to 1% for this year, which is where we expected growth to be before the energy crisis hit. Two observations strike us about forecast changes elsewhere. First, we note that 2027/28 have moved much less than 2026 ones. if at all. It seems to be consensus that 2026 revisions are “one-offs”, rather than a permanent shift higher in the growth trajectory. That’s a view we would agree with. Our own forecasts stay at 1.0% for 2027 and 0.9% for 2028. Our other observation is that the forecasts don’t seem to reflect otherwise abundant headlines on Rhine water level disruptions over the summer. We think 3Q26 GDP could be relatively weak (close to 0% qoq), not so much because of the Rhine itself, but more because the purchasing power recovery to consumers gets delayed, private capex looked very weak in 2Q, and we struggle to see foreign demand improving (hence question a sustained net export recovery). From Sector Signals to Macro Growth Levers We use our sector analysis from above to identify where the gains for further active capital depending and sustained MFP increases could originate. The sector evidence allows us to distinguish between scenarios in which the current capital build remains concentrated and scenarios in which it broadens and begins to generate productivity gains elsewhere in the economy. Our analysis indicates that the sectors attracting the largest tangible-capex pipelines are not the sectors with the strongest observable technology adoption. The capital build is concentrated in infrastructure, networks, and resources. The current technology-adoption impulse is concentrated in large service industries. The swing sectors sit between the two. Their capex pipeline is smaller, but their spending is much more machinery-intensive. They also have lower AI adoption and larger measured MFP shortfalls relative to the pre- pandemic period. The announcement of capital spending leads to a waterfall effect. Once there is an announced investment in a sector, the next step is the actual installation of productive capital. As that leads to further private sector crowd-in, there is broader technology adoption, and this could be a channel for a further increase in MFP. Passive Normalization or Active Capital Deepening? We distinguish between two forms of capital deepening. Passive capital deepening occurs when hours growth falls faster than capital growth. Capital per hour rises, but the economy is not necessarily undertaking more investment. This raises measured productivity while leaving aggregate potential growth relatively subdued. Active capital deepening occurs when the productive capital stock itself accelerates. Firms and governments add machinery, equipment, software, intellectual property, infrastructure, and other productive assets quickly enough to raise capital per worker, even while labor input stabilizes or expands. The Bank’s baseline contains elements of both. Slower population growth produces passive capital deepening, while stronger projected business and government investment provides an active component. The open question is which channel will dominate. The current investment evidence remains mixed. Machinery and equipment — the category most directly associated with productive capital deepening — has remained soft. Business fixed investment weakened after trade-policy uncertainty intensified, while recent strength in aggregate investment has been disproportionately government-led and concentrated in a relatively narrow set of categories. records.text: M Japan Insight 32 Broad investment in listed subsidiaries is an obsolete strategy Let us consider now how to approach the fading investment theme of parent-subsidiary listings. First, we examine the stock price performance of listed subsidiaries. Exhibit 41 illustrates the excess returns relative to TOPIX under a strategy of investing in all listed subsidiaries using an equal-weighted monthly rebalancing approach. This produced robust results until around 2020, but the performance since then has been sluggish. We attribute the lackluster performance since 2021 to the fact that parent-subsidiary listings have become overcrowded and obsolete as an investment theme. The unwinding of parent-subsidiary listings has continued throughout this period, so the catalyst itself has not vanished. Nonetheless, the excess returns generated from holding listed subsidiaries across the board have fallen. This suggests that expectations regarding the unwinding of these listings are now being priced into stock values more rapidly and widely than before. Generally, the more widely recognized an investment strategy becomes, the more likely its subsequent effectiveness will diminish. Parent-subsidiary listings have long been a popular investment theme, with trades often executed in anticipation of subsidiaries becoming wholly owned. To incur this level of demand destruction, prices likely need to move significantly higher than current levels, with prices up to €100/ MWh or above possible. If Qatari constraints continue past Q1 27 and Europe exits winter with inventories ~15% full, this could sets up a more similar backdrop to 2022. The 2021/22 European gas price crisis was preceded by a sustained tightening of gas markets throughout 2021. A key contributing factor was Gazprom’s unusually limited injection into its European storage facilities in summer 2021, leaving regional inventories at only 76% heading into winter. This helped drive gas prices from its prior stable €15-30/MWh range in Q1 21 to over €100/MWh by December 2021 ( Exhibit 42 ). The current set-up into winter shares parallels with the 2021 scenario, with low inventories and supply constraint themes once again. A continuation of the current status quo could set the gas market up for a very tight summer next year.

JGB: This Week in Review, The Week Ahead A 3% 10y, the first-every 30y auction – and three straight sessions of flattening, sell-off or rally September opened with a noticeable curve-flattening twist, as a short-end sell-off associated with the pull-forward of a September BoJ hike was accompanied by a rally in the long end. Over the first three sessions, the curve flattened through bear- parallel, bear-twist, and bull-flattening moves, with 5s20s moving below its August range to close at 153bp. Recent auctions suggest that this dynamic may partly reflect different buyer behavior across the curve: the 10-year sale was relatively well absorbed around the 3% level, while today's 30-year auction was somewhat soft, clearing at a historic 4-handle before buying interest returned after the sale. With a September hike now close to fully priced, the scope for a further move driven solely by timing may be more limited; a sustained rise in yields from here would likely require the market to price a higher terminal rate. This backdrop remains supportive of our curve-trade view. We continue to hold the 5s20s flattener with a 125bp target, alongside the receive-1y1y versus pay-3y1y steepener, and would consider any temporary steepening ahead of the meeting as a potential opportunity to add. Population growth returns to a moderate positive pace in the 2030s. The post-pandemic immigration boom is therefore better viewed as an overshoot followed by normalization than as the start of demographic stagnation. Slower Labor Growth Creates a Capital-Deepening Window Immigration did not cause Canada’s investment weakness. Capital formation per worker had already deteriorated materially after the mid-2010s; the post-pandemic population surge amplified the problem by expanding the workforce much faster than the productive capital stock. The international comparison is striking. Taking 2014 as the base, total investment per employee has risen strongly in the United States and more modestly in several European and developed-market peers, while Canada has fallen materially below its 2014 level. Canada therefore entered the population surge with unusually weak capital formation and then added workers at an unusually rapid pace. At the same time, European gas storage inventories are trending at precariously low levels ahead of winter 2026-27, setting the stage for increased competition between Europe and Asia for available cargoes. We wait to see how these dynamics impact longer-term LNG adoption rates across Asia, which has generally been perceived as the engine of global demand growth once gas prices are low enough to catalyze more elastic demand. On the refined products front, US refined products have emerged as a key source of global supply since the outset of the conflict between the US and Iran. With significant Middle Eastern and Russian refining capacity down, coupled with limited access to Middle Eastern feedstocks among Asian and European refiners, all our covered refiners have observed robust export demand. For example, as we have written about previously, MPC has seen new markets open up, reporting it exported ULSD from LAR to Australia. It also observed particularly strong demand from Latam and Europe. With the Strait again mostly closed and infrastructure abroad still under threat, we expect US refined product exports will continue to be a crucial source of supply for global markets as US refiners remain both unencumbered by the risk of bombardment and able to access feedstocks. Generally, this favors the clean energy space as opposed to more traditional gas powered solutions, as emission levels are smaller and power generation is often quieter. The need for speedier power solutions is also the driving force behind the growing level of investment in behind-the-meter solutions, whereby companies forego grid interconnection (for the time being) in order to get needed power generation faster. It is crucial for some data centre operations that they have a constant stream of power (many data centres express a desire for "5 9s" availability, meaning products that can provide 99.999% guaranteed uptime). Neither the grid, nor any individual power source, can promise these uptimes, so this has created a large market for backup power, specifically for battery energy storage solutions (BESS), such as those offered by FLNC, or backup generators, like those assembled by GNRC and EROC. The electrical work in and around data centres also provides some of our coverage with an opportunity to take some meaningful share, either through new or existing products. A material policy gap may therefore remain between product-specific trade defence and the EU’s most powerful economic-security instruments A European instrument inspired by US Section 301 could potentially bridge this divide. French President Macron has already called for such a tool to help protect strategic industries (Politico,22 May). Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 empowers US authorities to investigate unfair or discriminatory trade practices and to impose remedial measures, including tariffs, where appropriate. Importantly, its scope extends beyond areas explicitly covered by WTO rules, allowing policymakers to address a broader range of market distortions. Recent US investigations into semiconductors, shipping and structural excess manufacturing capacity illustrate how Section 301 can target systemic distortions rather than focusing solely on individual products. records.text: M Idea 12 Exhibit 17: Cash withdrawals from the DHS - CBP , as a proxy for tariff refunds 0 20 40 60 80 100 120 140 Cash Withdrawals from DHS, CBP (Fiscal YTD, Bil $; 4-wk avg) Source: US Treasury, Haver Analytics, Morgan Stanley Research Tariff refunds represent cash returned to importers when customs duties were previously overpaid or later determined to be refundable, for different reasons, including a tariff exclusion or court-ordered refund or a drawback claim tied to goods that are exported or destroyed. The process generally runs through CBP, where importers or brokers submit the relevant claim and supporting documentation; CBP then reviews eligibility, confirms the entry and status, and certifies approved refunds for payment. In Treasury cash-flow data, we monitor these payments at high frequency through CBP-related withdrawals in the Daily Treasury Statement. We interpret this as a tariff-refund proxy.

records.text: M Japan Insight Morgan Stanley MUFG 3 Overview of the Reform Landscape—Key Frameworks Relevant to This Report Japan’s corporate governance reform has advanced not through a single measure, but through the layered interaction of laws and regulations, principles-based codes, TSE listing rules, index methodologies, and guidelines issued by relevant ministries and agencies. Below are the frameworks most closely related to this report’s investment themes.. The Corporate Governance Code sets out principles for listed companies and is jointly formulated and revised by the Financial Services Agency and the Tokyo Stock Exchange. It took effect in June 2015, was revised in 2018 and 2021, and its third revision was finalized in July 2026. The 2026 revision emphasizes growth investment for medium- to long-term corporate value and on strengthening board effectiveness. It calls on companies to explain specific measures and continuously review the allocation of management resources, including investment in capital equipment, R&D, human capital and intellectual property, as well as their business portfolios. The Stewardship Code sets out principles for institutional investors and is developed primarily under the leadership of the Financial Services Agency. It calls on investors to promote medium- to long-term corporate value through constructive dialogue with investee companies. First introduced in 2014, it was revised in 2017, 2020 and 2025. records.text: What drives convenience yields? Our prior analysis on swap spreads and academic research point to a range of relevant inputs: Liquidity. Government bonds are generally deemed more liquid than other debt n securities bearing similar credit risk. This liquidity benefit can itself fluctuate with time. In periods of heightened uncertainty investors can value the ease of entering/exiting positions more strongly than in quieter macro-economic environment. Regulation. Post-GFC financial regulation has improved the relative attractiveness n of government securities for banks for regulatory compliance. Most prominently, under the Basel framework, government bonds contribute to bolster banks’ liquidity coverage ratios2 and carry zero risk-weights in capital ratios. Similarly, sovereign bonds generally benefit from a favorable regulatory treatment for insurers. Collateral value / short-term funding cost. Government bonds can be pledged as n collateral with small or no haircuts to obtain central bank or market funding through repos. Funding costs can also influence the economics of investors’ decision to get interest rate exposure through bonds or derivatives, given long bond positions often need to be financed. On this point, CME reports and ECB research point to increasing repo funding through EGBs. Government debt supply. records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 7 summer. The EU + UK region has been absorbing ~1.3 Mt of LNG supply loss every month from Apr-Aug, equivalent to ~1.8 bcm/month of lost supply YoY. Our European perimeter was responsible for ~1.5 bcm/month of this supply loss, with a net supply impact of 7.5 bcm so far. Combined with 5.2 bcm less gas in inventory at the start of this summer, this largely explains why inventories in our European perimeter are ~12 bcm lower than this time last year. The end of summer is now here and European gas storage is only 64% full in our European perimeter. This is the lowest level for early September in the 15 years of high frequency data we have on the European gas market. On a full EU level the number is only marginally higher at 65%. Current storage levels are 14pp lower YoY and 20pp lower than the 10Y seasonal average. If we compare to 2023 and 2024, in the immediate aftermath of the 2022 gas price spike, gas inventories were over 80% full at this time of year. Current inventory levels are lower even than September 2021, when Gazprom failed to fill their European storage ahead of winter 2021/22. Major storage holders Germany and the Netherlands remain laggards, at only 53% and 47% storage fill respectively. Southern Europe has the healthiest inventory levels, with gas fill >70% across Italy and Spain. The average interest rate on outstanding marketable Treasury debt remains well below prevailing market yields, at roughly 3.4%. Looking specifically at coupon-bearing securities, current market rates imply that debt rolled over in coming years will be refinanced at interest rates approximately 1.4 percentage points higher, on average, than those on the securities being retired (Exhibit 2). Nearly $7 trillion of Treasury bills are currently outstanding, the vast majority of which mature within one year (Exhibit 3). The quantity and quality of capital are diverging. The sectors with the largest investment pipelines are not those with the most machinery-intensive spending. Manufacturing intentions are approximately flat relative to 2025, but machinery and equipment accounts for 61% of planned expenditure. Construction intentions increase by around 3%, with machinery and equipment representing 86% of the total. Wholesale intentions rise by around 6%, and machinery accounts for roughly 65%. Across the four swing sectors — agriculture, construction, manufacturing, and wholesale — machinery and equipment represents almost 69% of intended capex. But these sectors account for only 24% of selected-sector spending, compared with 61% for the capital builders. This creates a second conversion gap. Canada’s largest capital projects are concentrated in structures and engineering, while the more machinery-intensive investment that could directly transform firm production is smaller and less broadly accelerating. Structures and engineering assets can still be highly productive. Their larger contribution is often indirect: they remove constraints that otherwise prevent firms from investing, expanding and reorganizing production. The relevant test is therefore not whether Canada builds more infrastructure. It is whether that infrastructure changes private investment

records.text: M BluePaper 14 The Growth Handoff Canada’s historical growth experience therefore has two layers. The first is the long- running disappearance of MFP growth after 2000. The second is the more recent reliance on rapid labor-input expansion while capital and productivity failed to keep pace. Those two problems require different solutions. Slower labor growth can mechanically reverse some of the recent pressure on capital per hour. It cannot, by itself, restore a durable MFP contribution or raise Canada’s long-run growth rate. The next phase of Canadian growth will consequently look very different from the last. Population and labor-force growth are slowing sharply, and the contribution from hours will be much smaller. A larger share of output growth must come from capital deepening and productivity. The key question is not whether measured productivity will improve. Some rebound is likely as the recent labor-supply surge fades. The more important question is whether that rebound represents a passive reversal of capital dilution or the start of a genuine investment and productivity cycle. USMCA: The Unspoken Risk The principal near-term risk to the productivity-and-investment-driven transition at the center of this Blue Paper is trade. Canada’s existing growth model remains exposed to the US; at the same time, preferential trade access has become less predictable. M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 5 Executive Summary Overview In this report, we offer an alternative to the current Canada narrative and a framework for a new growth path. The prevailing view of Canada's economy is well established: weak productivity, falling GDP per capita, excessive reliance on immigration and labor supply, and chronic underinvestment, compounded by growing uncertainty around access to the US market. We argue that Canada is entering a new growth phase. Bolstered by supportive government policy, it is moving beyond the post-commodity boom adjustment and a post-pandemic expansion that was driven by rapid labor-force expansion. We chart a course to sustained acceleration in potential growth, anchored in higher productivity, capital deepening, and efficiency gains. Our model suggests that the current investment pipeline can raise productive capacity and plausibly move potential growth from around 1.5% toward 1.7%. Reaching 2% requires the capital build to spread into private machinery and intangible investment and to produce sustained multifactor- productivity (MFP) gains in the industries that build, move, and manufacture across the economy. We envision a two-stage process. In the late 2020s, the growth comes from capital deepening and multifactor productivity (MFP), not labor input (from K and A, not L). BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH A compounding problem In addition to higher refinancing costs on the horizon, a more fundamental concern is the feedback loop between interest rates and debt. Ultimately, debt sustainability depends not only on the level of interest rates, but also on how those rates compare with nominal GDP growth. When nominal growth exceed borrowing costs, debt-to-GDP ratios can stabilize over time. However, as the gap between interest rates and nominal growth narrows, higher debt levels become increasingly difficult to sustain. The risk is that the self-reinforcing dynamic between interest costs and deficits can further narrow that gap over time. Meanwhile, there is a feedback loop between higher interest costs and deficits that we must account for. Higher interest costs increase deficits and Treasury borrowing needs. Increased Treasury issuance can put upward pressure on term premiums as investors demand greater compensation to absorb a larger supply of duration. Higher term premiums raise borrowing costs, which further increase interest expense and deficit

Canada’s constraint is capital conversion, not capital scarcity. Canada is financially capital-rich. Pension assets were equivalent to roughly 158% of GDP at the end of 2024, while banks, insurers, investment funds and other financial institutions hold assets equal to several multiples of annual output. Canadian institutions also have extensive expertise in infrastructure, private equity, real estate, and other long-duration assets. The problem has been whether domestic projects offer sufficiently attractive risk-adjusted returns to compete for that capital. The emerging policy regime seeks to make investments more attractive through four channels: (1) lowering the after-tax cost of investment, (2) shortening approval and construction timelines, (3) absorbing project-specific risks that private investors cannot efficiently hold, and (4) investing alongside private capital. This has resulted in a smaller and more episodic CMBS market, but has also reinforced conservative underwriting, stronger lender- borrower relationships, and historically stronger credit performance. Canadian Securitized CRE Market Despite the size of Canada’s commercial mortgage market, securitization has historically played a more limited funding role. According to Intellifi’s 2023 Canadian Commercial Mortgage Survey, the Canadian commercial mortgage market totaled approximately C$449 billion, while nonagency CMBS represented only ~1% of outstanding commercial mortgage debt as of 2022. Despite the size of the underlying CRE debt market, cumulative Canadian CMBS issuance has totaled only C$37.8 billion since the market emerged in the late 1990s, as we noted in our publication titled A Primer on the Canadian CMBS Market from last November. Historical issuance has been concentrated across a handful of major property types, led by retail at C$12.3 billion (32.4%), office at C $7.6 billion (20.0%), and industrial at C$7.3 billion (19.4%), which together account for more than 70% of issuance. Multifamily and lodging account for an additional 12.4% and 5.5%, respectively.

Capital intensity contributed approximately 0.8pp annually over 2000-19 and only around 0.3pp over 2019-23. The post-2000 period was already highly dependent on capital deepening, while MFP made almost no positive contribution. The stronger medium-term contribution reflects two different mechanisms. First, some capital deepening is passive. With labor-input growth falling toward zero, the existing capital stock is spread across fewer incremental hours. records.text: Back to the future: An argument that can be made is that AI and energy security accelerate a transition in energy that was already underway, taking it back to where it came from. For a significant period of time, the energy market was based on building the biggest, most efficient processing unit on a coastline, then taking supply from the global market. As a result, countries had refineries and petrochemical plants, and took feedstock from around the world. This arguably changed in the 2000s when the Middle East launched a series of major world scale processing facilities, dis-intermediating the refineries in regions like Europe, but the model was very much a hub-and-spoke approach to energy, with the Middle East firmly at the hub. Transition changed this, with the sources of energy becoming much more distributed. The UK, for example, in 2000 had ca 70 thermal power plants, which has fallen to ca 50. In the same period, the number of wind turbines (individual generators) has grown to over 12,000 from ca 1,000. As such, the number of generating sites has exploded, with distance to market key and the system becoming distributed. For other transition fuels, such as biofuels, this is even more the case. Distance to feedstock and market are key determinants of economic viability. Transition systems are very much, in our view, a distributed nodal system. The recent composition of greenfield foreign direct investment suggests that this is already happening selectively in the sectors most closely aligned with Canada’s emerging strategic advantages. Announced inbound greenfield investment totalled roughly US$309 billion over 2015-26, but the composition has shifted materially. The clearest comparison is between 2015-17 and 2023-25. Investment associated with energy transition rose from US$4.6 billion to US$28.6 billion, while investments liked to trade diversification and critical minerals security in a multipolar world, as well as AI-linked investments increased from US$6.0 billion to US$28.2 billion. At the sector level, critical-minerals investment increased from less than US$1 billion to roughly US$15 billion, battery investment went from effectively zero to US$11.5 billion, and AI and data-center investment rose from approximately US$3 billion to US$8.3 billion. records.text: Global installed data centre IT capacity reached ~70GW in 2025. We estimate that capacity additions could increase by about 25GW in 2026 and >30GW in 2027, with the US accounting for the largest share of incremental capacity, contributing ~15GW and >21GW, respectively. Beyond 2027, we expect the pace of additions to plateau, with the US adding a further 20GW+ per annum, reflecting a transition from the acceleration phase to a more sustained growth trajectory as indicated above. We expect hyperscalers to account for the largest share of new capacity additions, representing c60% of total additions over our forecast period (excluding China). After analysing close to 500 projects, we conclude that a significant proportion of those announced by non-hyperscalers could face clear execution bottlenecks and might not be realised at all. As a result, we believe realised capacity additions are likely to be more heavily skewed towards hyperscalers than announced project pipelines alone would suggest. Upside risk While current forecasts already imply substantial growth in AI infrastructure, we believe the debate is increasingly shifting from whether demand will emerge to how large and durable that demand ultimately becomes. Several factors could drive data centre demand materially above expectations, including broader enterprise AI adoption, continued AI scaling, increasing inference intensity, ongoing cloud growth, and the emergence of sovereign AI as a strategic priority. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 29 The Capital Build Can Raise Capacity; Conversion Determines the Speed Limit Canada’s current investment pipeline can raise the level of potential output even if it does not produce a permanent productivity acceleration. New power, transport, resource and digital infrastructure would expand productive capacity and leave the economy with a permanently larger capital stock. But a one-time build does not permanently raise the growth rate. Once the investment surge matures, the contribution from capital accumulation falls unless private investment remains persistently stronger. A lasting growth acceleration requires the capital build to generate one of two outcomes: 1. Persistent active capital deepening: Capital services continue growing faster than labor input after the initial projects are completed. 2. Sustained MFP diffusion: Infrastructure, technology, and market integration produce continuing efficiency gains in manufacturing, construction, transportation, wholesale, and other swing sectors. Our sector analysis suggests that neither outcome follows automatically from the current capex pipeline. The pipeline is large, but concentrated in structures — and engineering- heavy sectors with historically weak direct MFP conversion. Observable technology adoption is strongest in service sectors with smaller tangible-capital requirements. The opportunity lies in connecting the two. records.text: son Hole speech was so forceful. Warsh's main objective at Jackson Hole was to remedy the poor impact that his communication strategy at the July press conference had on markets. Back then, he communicated that markets themselves had done much of the tightening and therefore the Fed could afford to wait. A mild correction at Jackson Hole would not have been enough to restore credibility. He needed to be bolder. In July, he hinted he was on the Bernanke trail. At Jackson Hole, Warsh had to convince markets that a switch to the Kohn trail was still a real possibility. Despite insisting that he wants less forward guidance and more learning from markets, the need to repair July’s credibility damage pushed Warsh into a communication trap. Because he had more reputational capital tied to reversing the July message, he could not simply describe a neutral reaction function. He had to lean in the only direction that could restore credibility. records.text: Europe Multi-Asset 03 September 2026 Citi Research 52 Appendix: The Limits of the EU’s Trade-Defence Toolbox and case for an EU-style Section 301 The EU already possesses a broad and increasingly assertive trade-defence toolbox. Traditional instruments include anti-dumping and anti-subsidy duties and safeguards, while newer autonomous tools include the Foreign Subsidies Regulation and the Anti-Coercion Instrument. However, most existing instruments are calibrated either to product-specific injury, distortions within the single market or clearly defined instances of economic coercion. This leaves a potential gap in addressing persistent, economy-wide distortions on the scale of China’s state- supported industrial expansion and growing external surplus. Traditional anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations are generally reactive, evidence-intensive and product-specific. They require the Commission to demonstrate dumping or subsidisation, injury to EU producers and a causal relationship between the two. This can make the framework relatively slow and vulnerable to circumvention or product substitution. Duties imposed on Chinese battery electric vehicles, for example, may redirect exports towards hybrid models, while measures covering one chemical intermediate may encourage producers to shift capacity towards an unprotected downstream derivative. The new European framework combines tariff-rate quotas, a 50% out-of-quota duty, CBAM and greater flexibility over the pace of carbon-cost adjustment. The detailed earnings and valuation implications are discussed in the Steel chapter. Four cross-sector lessons stand out. First, protection can support regional pricing power. Once quotas are exhausted, the out-of-quota duty raises the marginal cost of imported steel. Our preference is for USD/JPY calls vs. LY G10 / JPY calls, for two reasons. First, they satisfy a general requirement of owning options in the higher beta of the two underlyings, which in this instance also offers a useful long USD vol vs. short cross-vol orientation that is useful going into a busy September of US-centric events. Second, with current spot / forwards / vol levels, zero-cost long / short option spreads allow ~1.2x weight on the USD/JPY leg on top of its higher beta stature for equivalent tenor/moneyness strikes, and amplifies participation in any Yen weakness. A European version could allow the Commission to assess broader structural distortions, including state-directed capital allocation, restricted market access, forced technology transfer, persistent currency undervaluation or policies that suppress domestic consumption while supporting export-led industrial expansion. Rather than requiring a separate subsidy calculation for every producer and product, the framework could permit remedies across selected products, sectors or strategically connected value chains where the Commission demonstrated a material burden on European commerce. Such an instrument would not necessarily imply blanket tariffs on Chinese imports. It could target sectors in which Europe retains meaningful productive capacity and strategic interest, including autos, chemicals, machinery, batteries, clean technologies and semiconductors. Its principal value would be to reduce the opportunity for exporters to evade narrow measures through product substitution, while giving the EU a more credible negotiating lever in discussions over market access and economic rebalancing. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 Normalization from Extreme Underweights and Lukewarm Southbound Flows Suggest Limited Flow Upside In 1H26, investor positioning in China remained extremely light: Foreign active managers maintained sizable underweights as global portfolios stayed heavily tilted toward the AI trade and other outperforming markets. Positioning became particularly extreme in May-June: EM equity fund managers were around 5-6ppt underweight China, leaving substantial room for a positioning-led catch-up should sentiment improve. July marked a notable inflection: The global AI correction triggered some reversal of previously crowded positioning and contributed to a relative improvement in allocations to China. Based on the latest disclosed positions: • Global Equity funds are now around 1.0ppt underweight China, • EM funds around 1.8ppt underweight, and • Asia ex-Japan funds have moved to around 2.5ppt overweight. Compared with the much more extreme underweights seen earlier in the year, current positioning suggests that a meaningful portion of the previous positioning gap has already been closed, leaving less room for further inflows purely from underweight normalization. The flow picture is broadly consistent with this partial normalization, although the improvement remains uneven. However, there could be gaps: a large investment announcement can fail to raise potential growth if the project is delayed, if spending largely replaces depreciated capital, or if new infrastructure does not change investment decisions elsewhere. Similarly, the installation of software, servers or machinery raises capital, but does not automatically raise MFP. The MFP payoff depends on whether firms reorganize production, develop complementary skills, operate at greater scale and diffuse the technology beyond a narrow set of adopters. In the sector analysis, we organize the sector-to-macro transmission around four channels: Channel 1: Capital realization. The first question is how much of the spending pipeline becomes operating capital. The 2026 intentions data are a leading indicator, not an installed-capital forecast. They are nominal, gross of depreciation and subject to execution risk. Permitting, procurement, labor availability, cost overruns. and financing conditions determine how quickly spending turns into productive assets. This is particularly important for utilities, transportation, and resources, where projects tend to be large, construction-heavy, and slow to complete. records.text: M BluePaper 10 Canada Economics: The Next Acceleration Arunima Sinha and Mayank Phadke Canada is entering a new phase of growth. The economy is moving away from a model driven by rapid labor-force expansion and toward one where productivity, capital deepening, and efficiency gains must do the heavy lifting. In our view, a productivity rebound is likely; the more important question is whether that rebound evolves into a sustained acceleration in potential growth. Our analysis proceeds in four stages. First, we trace how Canada generated growth historically and identify where that model began to break down. Second, we assess whether the coming productivity rebound represents a genuine improvement in the economy’s productive capacity or is largely the arithmetic consequence of slower labor- input growth. Third, we use our sector framework to identify where a durable acceleration would need to originate — and whether investment in Canada’s capital-building sectors can translate into broader private investment and efficiency gains across the wider economy. Finally, we calibrate the combinations of capital deepening and multifactor- productivity growth that could lift potential growth from roughly 1.5% toward 2.0%, and assess what would be required for that improvement to persist. More Workers, Less Productivity — How Canada Generated Growth Canada’s growth model has changed substantially over the past six decades. records.text: M Japan Insight 12 Introduction: Reform progress brings shift in alpha Japanese corporate governance reform remains a crucial theme in assessing Japanese equities. Management practices are steadily evolving through initiatives like the TSE’s call for “management conscious of capital cost and stock price,” an increase in shareholder returns, reductions in strategic shareholdings, business portfolio reviews, the dissolution of parent-subsidiary listings, and an increase in management buyouts (MBO). Improvements in corporate capital efficiency are also evident. ROE at Japanese companies has grown to levels approaching those of European firms, though a significant gap remains with the US ( Exhibit 17 ). The recent rise in ROE is driven primarily by improvements in net profit margins rather than increased financial leverage (Exhibit 18 ), but little improvement has been seen in total asset turnover (Exhibit 19 ). Therefore, companies must achieve further gains in profit margins and asset efficiency by reviewing less profitable businesses and realizing returns on growth investments in order to narrow the gap with US companies in a sustainable manner. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro issued an executive order ending the state’s fast-track permitting program and mandating that data center projects must first be approved by local officials. It also prevents NDAs from being used, introduces new environmental standards, and requirements to bring your own capacity. See more here. We expect this conversation to spread as it gains relevance with voters ahead of the midterms — the majority of community pushback is concentrated around 3 issues: (1) affordability and the concern that data center power consumption will raise consumer power bills, (2) environmental issues especially water use and air pollution, and (3) quality of life concerns including noise, dust, and traffic. A Different Growth Model for the 2030s The remainder of the 2020s is a transition period: Population growth falls sharply, labor contributes little to potential output, and productivity has to carry more of the expansion. On our normalization path, that leaves potential growth around 1½% for a time. The 2030s can look different because labor input becomes supportive again. If total hours show strong growth in the 2030s, labor-productivity growth closer to 2% would move growth toward 2.5%, representing a materially stronger upside case rather than our central assumption. In either case, productivity — not labor input — would remain the dominant source of growth. The sequencing is favorable. Slower labor growth in the late 2020s creates a window to install infrastructure, machinery, software and compute while the workforce expands slowly. As population growth normalizes in the 2030s, workers would enter an economy with more productive capital available to them. Canada’s demographic advantage is therefore not another immigration boom. It is the ability, under current long-run demographic assumptions, to retain positive labor-force growth while aging subtracts less from labor supply than in many developed-market peers. There has been much discussion over how low current European gas inventories sit vs usual levels for this time of year, however there are varying degrees of concern across some market stakeholders as to how critical these low inventory levels are. Withdrawals from gas storage is a key source of supply across Europe over the winter. In particular, it acts as a smoothing source of supply, being able to meet intraday swings in demand e.g. from the power sector better than imports are able to. On average across winter, storage withdrawals comprise ~30% of European gas supply. Storage is most crucial in January when withdrawals provide 44% of supply on average across our European perimeter, but up to 60% for a heavily reliant country like the Netherlands. However, some argue that lower gas demand post-2022 reduces Europe's gas storage requirements and that on a demand-adjusted basis, current storage levels no longer look too concerning. On first look, even once adjusted for demand, current inventory levels are still in the bottom quarter of the historical range. LatAm credit Unlike other regions, Latin America's energy-security challenge is less about securing fuel imports and more about maintaining reliability. Renewables account for roughly 60% of the region's power mix, among the highest shares globally, leaving most countries relatively well positioned from a resource perspective. Instead, energy security is shifting towards the ability to move electricity from resource-rich regions to demand centres and maintain system reliability during climate-related disruptions. Mexico remains a key exception given its reliance on US natural-gas imports. We view the next decade of investment as directed less toward new generation capacity and more toward transmission expansion, storage deployment, and grid resilience. Across several countries, the principal constraint is the ability to deliver electricity rather than generate it. Transmission bottlenecks, renewable curtailment, and climate volatility are becoming the key drivers of investment needs. The challenges vary by market. Mexico remains exposed to natural-gas imports from the US and faces growing transmission constraints in industrial regions. Chile has abundant renewable resources but requires additional storage and grid infrastructure to reduce curtailment and support reliability. records.text: ies can materially affect global LNG flows, driving competition with Asia for volumes and pushing up international gas prices. European gas inventories are set to enter winter at the lowest level in the 15 years of European gas market data, following a collapse in LNG imports over summer. We now forecast pre-winter storage fill in our European perimeter of 71%, 5pp below the previous end-Oct low in 2021 and 20pp below the 10Y average. In a normal to cold European winter, it would be normal to draw inventories by 60 to 70pp, raising the possibility of Europe reaching critical low storage levels. Entering winter with low storage significantly reduces Europe's buffer to cold weather over the winter, increases reliance on procuring spot LNG cargos to avoid inventory depletion and raises upside risk to gas prices. Europe's one trump card this winter may be a mild to warm winter, influenced by a strong El Niño phase. Consensus expectations in the gas market are for milder than average winter temperatures in Europe due to El Niño. Gas for heating accounts for 50% of European gas demand over winter, so milder temperatures can incur significant demand savings. We model milder winter weather reduces gas demand in our perimeter by 4% vs winter 2025/26 levels (a 'normal' winter gas demand in a post-2022 market). We model this demand outlook would still require Europe to import more LNG YoY over winter but avoid drastic inventory depletion by winter end (MSe end-March storage fill of 26%)

records.text: Refreshing our estimates We raise our estimates materially, reflecting a more constructive outlook for middle distillates. We increase our diesel and jet crack assumptions for 2H26 and 2027 to $65/$40/bbl, from $50/$25/bbl previously, while also modestly increasing gasoline assumptions. As a result, our EBITDA estimates rise by an average 35% in 2026 and 45% in 2027 across Helleniq, Motor Oil and Neste. Since our latest post-results updates, EBITDA estimates increase by 11%/42% for Helleniq in 2026/27, 79%/56% for Motor Oil and 12%/37% for Neste. The larger revision for Motor Oil reflects the fact that the company reported 2Q26 results last week and therefore had not yet benefited from our updated refining assumptions, whereas HELLENiQ’s forecasts were partially refreshed following its August 2Q26 results. Our updated forecasts now place us c.56%/54% above Bloomberg consensus EBITDA in 2026/27 on average across coverage. Importantly, despite these higher estimates, our forecasts remain conservative relative to current forward pricing, as our diesel, jet and gasoline crack assumptions for 2H26-28 remain below the levels implied by the forward curve, suggesting further upside risk should current market conditions persist. Higher earnings also translate into higher shareholder distributions. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 2 September 2026 1 Insights Classification: General, Complimentary Material DM FX Weekly : Uncertainty and contrarian JPY convictions KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Policy uncertainty remains the defining feature of FX markets. Opacity is the Fed’s new modus operandi, while softer US activity, renewed inflation pressure and persistent USD selling by asset managers argue for retaining our USD underweight despite higher September hike odds. By contrast, our models agree on one contrarian conviction: long JPY. Valuation, investor holdings and relative equity performance all support the currency, while a hawkish BoJ move could finally challenge the market’s dovish narrative. We retain EURUSD, EURGBP, AUDCAD and CHFJPY positions, and add short AUDJPY, the most contrarian trade relative to existing positions, which expresses the clearest divergence between a mature RBA cycle and emerging BoJ tightening. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 04 Sep 2026 08:54:14 ET │ 14 pages US Economics CPI Preview – Three months make a trend CITI'S TAKE In the last crucial data release before the September FOMC meeting, we expect another month of subdued core inflation that will likely have officials leaving policy rates unchanged. We expect a 0.184%MoM increase in August core CPI, with the year-on-year reading falling to 2.3%, the lowest annual reading since before core CPI jumped above 2% in April 2021. Details of our forecast include modest goods prices with limited sign of pass through from higher energy costs, slowing shelter inflation, and a slight decline in airfares. PPI data released before CPI could give some insight into risks around certain CPI components. Uncertainty around core PCE in August is elevated given methodology changes highlighted by Governor Waller this week. But for now, we expect a moderate 0.19%MoM increase and for revisions to lower the annual reading by over 30bp to 3.0% in August. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 43 If the full 50bp acceleration persists for five years, potential output would be approximately 2.5% higher than in the baseline. If it persists for 10 years, the level difference approaches 5%. The durability of the scenario depends on its composition. The extra capital contribution may fade after the build phase. For potential growth to remain near 2%, either capital formation must stay persistently stronger or MFP must continue to rise after the initial diffusion period. This is why construction and the other swing sectors are central. A one-time efficiency improvement raises the level of output. Continued adoption, organizational change, and innovation raise its growth rate. Which Scenario Does the Current Evidence Point To? The current data do not yet support the broad-reset scenario as the baseline. The capital pipeline is large but concentrated. The sectors receiving the most tangible investment have historically generated weak direct MFP, while the current AI impulse remains concentrated in services. Manufacturing intentions are broadly flat. Construction has substantial productivity shortfall but low adoption. Transportation combines a major capital pipeline with a large recent MFP shortfall, making it the clearest early test of whether the capital build can become a productivity cycle. This understanding of the labor market is already widely held across the committee, meaning focus should remain squarely on upcoming inflation data in determining whether or not to adjust policy rates. Yesterday, Governor Waller guided that it would take a “hot” inflation report for him to support a rate hike, and in our base case core CPI rounds to 0.2% MoM and the Fed stays on hold. It’s a closer call on a 0.3% MoM CPI reading, and anything rounding to 0.4% MoM would likely provoke a hike. We had expected a residual seasonal pattern to repeat in this year’s data, with the unemployment rate rising over the summer months and creating an urgency to cut rates. This did not materialize, meaning there should be no urgency among Fed officials to cut rates. We still think the next policy move is likely to be a cut, and in our base case we have 25bp cuts penciled in June, September, and December of next year based on slowing inflation. The sectors receiving the largest capital inflows are therefore not the sectors currently showing the greatest technology adoption. records.text: M Idea 6 below. Software and accessories PCE The most consequential methodological change relates to computer software and accessories. The BEA will replace the current deflator, which is based exclusively on the CPI for software, with a composite index incorporating both CPI and PPI measures, including PPIs for game software publishing and for hosting and IT infrastructure services. These changes may partially address the measurement issues highlighted by Federal Reserve Board staff in Barbarino et al. (2026). As Exhibit 6 shows, both PPI software measures have run considerably below the CPI index so far this year, making the direction of the revision relatively clear: it should be downward. The main unknown is the weighting of the new PCE index. As highlighted by Barbarino et al. (2026), personal consumption of software and accessories is split between software publishers, which account for 84%, and data processing, hosting, and related services, which account for 16%. We therefore assign a 16% weight to PPI hosting and IT infrastructure services. We split the remaining 84% between PPI game software at 56% and CPI software and accessories at 28%. We assume the BEA will assign a relatively lower weight to the CPI because that index is affected by price changes in flash drives and blank media, components that are excluded from the BEA’s nominal consumption measure for software. Satellite data continue to show some baseline thermal activity at the Ras Laffan facility which is taken as evidence of train activity. Over March-August, Qatar has shipped 49 cargos (3.9 Mt of LNG) to Kuwait. The quantity and quality of capital are diverging. The sectors with the largest investment pipelines are not those with the most machinery-intensive spending. Manufacturing intentions are approximately flat relative to 2025, but machinery and equipment accounts for 61% of planned expenditure. Construction intentions increase by around 3%, with machinery and equipment representing 86% of the total. Wholesale intentions rise by around 6%, and machinery accounts for roughly 65%. Across the four swing sectors — agriculture, construction, manufacturing, and wholesale — machinery and equipment represents almost 69% of intended capex. But these sectors account for only 24% of selected-sector spending, compared with 61% for the capital builders. This creates a second conversion gap. Canada’s largest capital projects are concentrated in structures and engineering, while the more machinery-intensive investment that could directly transform firm production is smaller and less broadly accelerating. Structures and engineering assets can still be highly productive. Their larger contribution is often indirect: they remove constraints that otherwise prevent firms from investing, expanding and reorganizing production. The relevant test is therefore not whether Canada builds more infrastructure. It is whether that infrastructure changes private investment

The relatively small size of the Canadian CMBS market results in greater concentration by sponsor, property type, and geography. The outstanding market totals $5.0 billion, including $2.3 billion (45%) of conduit and $2.7 billion (55%) of SASB transactions, compared with roughly $654 billion outstanding in the US nonagency CMBS market, excluding CRE CLOs. Industrial makes up nearly 56% of outstanding balances, followed by retail at 19.3%. Blackstone has emerged as a programmatic industrial SASB issuer, completing four transactions since 2024 and accounting for roughly 43% of the current outstanding market. Geographic exposure is similarly concentrated, with Ontario representing 63% of outstanding balances, followed by Quebec and British Columbia at 15.7% and 10.2%, respectively; together, Canada’s three most populous provinces account for roughly 89% of outstanding CMBS exposure.

records.text: ECB Preview—Another Hike Without Guidance The incoming data in recent months have been broadly in line with the ECB staff’s June projections. Growth has again been firmer than expected. GDP surprised to the upside in Q2, printing at around 0.30%qoq (non-annualised) excluding Ireland (Exhibit 1, left). The activity data for Q3 has so far been more mixed as soft data continued to recover from Q2 lows, but hard data showed some sign of softening in July, most notably in Germany (Exhibit 1, right). Our nowcast model currently points to ex-Ireland growth of 0.19% for Q3. Several ECB officials acknowledged the economy’s recent resilience, and both Executive Board member Schnabel and Bank of Ireland Governor Makhlouf hinted at a small upgrade in the projections for growth. We therefore look for the staff to lift Q3 by 0.1pp to 0.3%, which will likely raise the annual averages by 0.1pp each to 0.9% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027 (Exhibit 2). We look for the 2028 figure to remain unchanged at 1.5%, although we see a low bar for it to fall back to 1.4%. records.text: d on its historical explanatory power relative to the CSI 300 Index. Weights are determined by the R-squared values from a single-factor regression between the metric (relative to its 100-day moving min max) and the CSI 300 (relative to 100MA) performance. This weighting method gives greater emphasis to indicators that have historically demonstrated stronger correlations with market movements, ensuring that the overall index reflects sentiment components most relevant to A-share performance. Step 3: Constructing the MSASI (Weighted) Using the weighted sentiment indicator derived in Step 2, we construct the MSASI (Weighted) as the composite measure of overall market sentiment. This index is then re-scaled to a 0-100 range, based on its distance from historical high and low values since January 2024. This scaling allows the indicator to reflect relative sentiment strength over time – where higher readings indicate stronger investor enthusiasm, and lower readings reflect weaker sentiment or risk aversion. Step 4: Constructing the MSASI (Weighted 1MMA) To highlight underlying trends and reduce short-term volatility, we apply a one-month moving average to the MSASI (Weighted). The resulting MSASI (Weighted 1MMA) smooths out high-frequency fluctuations, providing a clearer picture of medium-term sentiment dynamics and improving interpretability for tactical or strategic analysis.

records.text: M BluePaper 80 With respect to natural gas, persistent oversupply has caused Western Canadian (AECO) natural gas prices to trade at stubbornly weak levels. Low producer break-even economics, long resource inventory, and a fragmented upstream industry in the Montney and Duvernay basins have all contributed to supply imbalances. Additionally, Canada’s structural condensate deficit presents another challenge: increasing NGL-rich regional production to supply condensate for oil sands blending also generates associated dry gas, Given that traditional domestic demand growth (residential, commercial, and industrial consumption) is likely to be relatively modest, new LNG export capacity and/or gas-fired power demand associated with data centers are likely necessary to drive higher AECO prices. Beyond 2026, LNG developments remain the primary mechanism for structurally tightening Western Canadian gas fundamentals. Woodfibre LNG is expected in 2027 and Cedar LNG in late 2028, together adding nearly 800 MMcf/d of export capacity. Including LNG Canada Phase 1, Canadian LNG export capacity could reach approximately 2.5 Bcf/d by 2030. Further tightening would depend on LNG Canada Phase 2 and Ksi Lisims reaching FID. Rystad views LNG Canada Phase 2 as technically more advantaged because it is a brownfield development backed by Shell and existing partners, but a weakening global LNG outlook and SHEL’s cautious stance toward additional LNG exposure could delay FID until around 2030. records.text: t inventory levels are still in the bottom quarter of the historical range. We would also highlight that all else equal, Europe needs higher levels of gas storage now than it did prior to 2022 due to longer supply chains. When Europe's key supplier was Russian pipeline gas, this gave a much high degree of flexibility in import supply over winter. Buyers were able to nominate Russian gas on a day-ahead basis, enabling quicker response of supply to demand fluctuations. However, now Europe's major source of swing gas supply is US LNG, which sits 2-3 weeks sailing time away. Consequently, the ability of Europe's imports to flex over winter has been significantly reduced, making storage all the more important. In this context, we would still see current inventory levels as concerning. Additionally, Germany, which has the EU’s largest gas storage capacity, still has very low inventories even on a demand-adjusted basis. This matters for the broader European balance. Lower German storage increases its winter import requirement, likely supporting a premium in German gas prices relative to neighbouring markets as Germany competes for incremental pipeline supply. Higher German prices would, in turn, attract additional cross-border flows from markets such as Italy, increasing withdrawals and putting downward pressure on storage inventories elsewhere in Europe.

records.text: Note: the estimates are in terms of the percentage point annual contribution. Why the 2% case is not simply an infrastructure scenario. The capital-build scenario can succeed without producing a broad productivity reset. New utility and transport capacity can raise the level of potential output, improve resilience and support strategic projects. Resource investment can raise exports, profits, fiscal revenue and national income. But Canada's historical experience shows that large capital accumulation in network and resource sectors does not automatically produce positive MFP. From 2000 to 2019, capital intensity was a strong positive contributor in mining, utilities, and transportation, while MFP was negative across all three. The larger macro payoff arises when capital generates effects outside the industry in which it is installed. Power and transport capacity → lower constraints → private investment → scale and technology diffusion → MFP. This is also why trade access is not a separate additive growth contribution. Market access affects the expected return on capital, scale, technology transfer and the allocation of resources. Canada's existing industrial structure remains concentrated in resources and lower-complexity manufacturing, with less capacity in machinery, electronics, and AI-linked production. A benign trade outcome removes a headwind, but stronger capital formation and productive capacity are still required to capture the fastest-growing areas of external demand

An industry long defined by drilling and pressure pumping has pivoted hard toward power generation, leveraging its heritage of providing on-site electricity to remote oil and gas operations. A growing number of service companies now run power businesses, ordering gigawatts of turbines and reciprocating engines to serve data centres, while capital has rotated out of the hyperscalers themselves and into the hard assets that power them. This also reshapes the energy and credit picture: more gas demand, more midstream and power-linked infrastructure investment, and growing competition for capital between energy and digital infrastructure. The discriminator for investors is contract quality, distinguishing operators with long-term hyperscaler agreements and operating megawatts from those still marketing order books. Distributed power has graduated from bridge to baseline. In roughly a year, medium-sized turbines and reciprocating engines have gone from oilfield niche to a critical speed-to-power solution, validated by hyperscalers signing contracts of ten years and longer for off-grid supply. US utility uranium purchases declined 16% YoY to 46.9Mlb U3O8 in 2025 from 55.9Mlb in 2024. We do not view this inventory accumulation as evidence of an oversupplied market. Rather, it suggests utilities are increasingly concerned about future availability of uranium and fuel-cycle services, and are willing to carry larger strategic inventories than at any point in recent years to protect against future disruptions. The more important story, however, is not inventories but the transformation of procurement portfolios. Across both regions, Canada has emerged as the clear beneficiary of diversification efforts, while Kazakhstan remains an indispensable pillar of global uranium supply. In the US, Canadian-origin uranium purchases increased from 11.0Mlb U3O8 in 2020 to 18.6Mlb in 2024, making Canada the largest source of supply for US utilities. Europe has experienced a similar shift, with Canadian deliveries rising from just 1.5ktU in 2019 to 5.4ktU in 2025, while Uzbekistan's contribution expanded from 0.6ktU to 1.5ktU over the same period. Although the first periodic rebalancing will be in October this year (using the last business day of August as the reference date), we conducted monthly estimates assuming the end of each month as the reference date. Stock price returns (relative to TOPIX) per group for the following month based on our estimates are shown in Exhibit 28 . Here, “add” represents stocks newly adopted in TOPIX, “del” is those removed, “stay_in” is those retained, and “stay_out” is those that remain excluded. The respective counts for each group as of the end of July 2026 were 40, 700, 950, and 2,000 stocks. The “add” group outperformed markedly from late 2025 through March 2026. We attribute this to anticipatory buying of stocks projected to join TOPIX, driven by expectations of capital inflows. Subsequently, the group declined in June and July due to a drop in space-related stocks and lower risk appetite following the correction from the AI rally. We have since seen signs of a recovery after the unwinding of the momentum in the final week of July. The distinction matters particularly for autos, metals, machinery, transportation equipment and wood products, where US trade and industrial policy has become more interventionist. Canada and the US also have genuinely different strategic interests. The US increasingly wants domestic production and greater control over strategic supply chains; Canada wants predictable access that allows investment north of the border to serve the broader North American market. The Canadian objective therefore cannot simply be to preserve existing exports or tariff levels. An agreement that protects current trade but steadily redirects marginal capex into the US through other forms of industrial policy would be less favorable than the headline tariff outcome suggests. Nor would USMCA necessarily evolve symmetrically: a more favorable outcome for Mexico could allow its lower costs and deeper manufacturing ecosystem to attract incremental investment at Canada’s expense. Canada therefore needs to strengthen its own value proposition and productive capacity, not simply preserve market access. Nevertheless, our base case remains that Canada and the US ultimately find sufficient common ground. The strategic complementarities are substantial: Canada supplies energy, uranium, critical minerals, agricultural products and industrial inputs that become more valuable as the US seeks secure North American supply chains. records.text: Impacts (18 Jun 2026) While the status quo outcome avoids an immediate break in the agreement, we see three distinct risks from here: • Escalation risk is the most acute near-term concern throughout the negotiations. We see three avenues through which the US could escalate if negotiations stall over the next 6-9 months: (1) tightening the existing tariff regime to reduce the exemption for USMCA-compliant goods outside of the USMCA framework, (2) raising Section 232 tariffs on sectors such as steel and aluminum, or (3) instructing trade negotiators to formally initiate the six-month exit process, which remains an available option to the president at any time. The escalation has already begun to materialize: The president signed three proclamations imposing 50% Section 338 duties on Canadian motor vehicles, alcohol, and dairy 30 days ahead of the scheduled implementation. records.text: M BluePaper 10 Canada Economics: The Next Acceleration Arunima Sinha and Mayank Phadke Canada is entering a new phase of growth. The economy is moving away from a model driven by rapid labor-force expansion and toward one where productivity, capital deepening, and efficiency gains must do the heavy lifting. In our view, a productivity rebound is likely; the more important question is whether that rebound evolves into a sustained acceleration in potential growth. Our analysis proceeds in four stages. First, we trace how Canada generated growth historically and identify where that model began to break down. Second, we assess whether the coming productivity rebound represents a genuine improvement in the economy’s productive capacity or is largely the arithmetic consequence of slower labor- input growth. Third, we use our sector framework to identify where a durable acceleration would need to originate — and whether investment in Canada’s capital-building sectors can translate into broader private investment and efficiency gains across the wider economy. Finally, we calibrate the combinations of capital deepening and multifactor- productivity growth that could lift potential growth from roughly 1.5% toward 2.0%, and assess what would be required for that improvement to persist. More Workers, Less Productivity — How Canada Generated Growth Canada’s growth model has changed substantially over the past six decades. In the earlier part of the period, growth reflected a combination o

pital build and MFP, it should not be added as a separate source of potential growth. A benign USMCA outcome lowers uncertainty and prevents further capital scrapping or reallocation losses. It can support private investment, scale and technology transfer. But preserving market access does not solve Canada’s product-composition and productive- capacity problems. We have previously written about how Canada remains underrepresented in machinery, electronics, and AI-linked production, while its industrial capital stock remains concentrated in resources and legacy manufacturing. Greater certainty around trade policy therefore raises the probability that the economy moves beyond the arithmetic-rebound scenario. It does not, on its own, produce the broad-reset scenario. The same applies to interprovincial integration. Reducing internal barriers can raise the level of MFP through scale, specialization and better allocation. The growth effect persists only if the larger effective market generates continuing investment, innovation and firm entry. Scenario Analysis: From Arithmetic Rebound to Productivity Reset We construct four scenarios around our baseline. Trend labor input remains close to 0.1pp, and labor composition contributes 0.2pp. The scenarios differ in the strength and form of capital deepening and MFP. our central calibration is capital-led normalization. 1. Scenario 1: Arithmetic rebound. This is closest to the medium-term baseline. Labor input growth falls close to zero.

Fuel-switching boost to Indian LNG imports to fade CITI'S TAKE The market’s view that Asia strongly competes against Europe for LNG is just that, a perception. Demand from China and Japan is weak. India's recent LNG import rebound, another emerging key LNG buyer, also looks misleading, driven largely by temporary fuel switching rather than broad structural demand. The tailwind from industrial users switching from propane to LNG has already peaked and is now reversing as propane prices decline. A similar reversal is underway in the refining sector, where a switch back to naphtha is expected as LNG's price advantage erodes. Structural demand growth remains confined to the City Gas Distribution (CGD) sector, with consumption in the fertilizer and power sectors flat to weaker year-on- year. We therefore expect these fuel-switching reversals to cap near-term LNG import growth, offsetting resilient demand from the CGD segment. This report examines various fuel switching mechanisms in India, including propane and naphtha to natural gas switching, as well as growth prospects of CGD going forward. While acknowledging greater uncertainty, officials deemphasized growth risks from new tariffs and highlighted upside risks to inflation from higher-for-longer energy prices, despite core inflation measures having fallen below 2% in recent months. Our base case remains that sluggish ~1% growth will keep the economy in excess supply until policy rates become more accommodative. While energy security concerns could ultimately support higher commodity prices, the pathway remains uncertain. In that environment, management teams are understandably reluctant to make large, long-duration capital commitments. The result is an industry that remains biased toward flexibility, balance- sheet strength, and shareholder returns rather than broad-based production growth. This stands in stark contrast to prior cycles, where higher commodity prices often translated almost mechanically into accelerating capital spending.
