records.text: the physical limitations of transition hit home. We have long argued that transition is a multi- faceted beast, with the simple premise being "electrify all that can be electrified and generate the rest as cleanly as possible" . This is not new, the hydrocarbon industry has consistently improved over time, removing lead from fuels, then sulphur, and over recent years the focus has been the carbon embedded in the molecules themselves. In that context, our message has mirrored that from the major national producers – there is an “All of the Above” requirement for energy with the overriding message of “And not Or “ (See On the Road in the Middle East – licence to drill 8 Nov 22). Transition, in our view, has always been a journey not an end point, as we put it – a verb, not a noun or a dial, not a switch (see Middle East trip - what we learned on the ground 22 Nov 21) (see A dial not a switch 30 Oct 23). AI and Energy Security have arguably just crystallised a physical reality. Energy remains, by definition, the ability to do work and GDP is arguably the sum of the output of all work. The Energy Service sector makes the infrastructure that produces energy and facilitates GDP growth. 2. records.text: sage through the Strait. LNG on-the-water has risen again from the July lows, now surpassing the previous April peak of ~1.6 Mt. Currently, ~2.2 Mt of LNG sits on 16 tankers in the Gulf. There are also no ballast LNG vessels currently left in the Gulf to load. These trapped volumes represent a bearish risk to TTF prices under a Strait flow recovery scenario, but still only represent ~10 days of usual daily Qatari exports ex-Gulf (0.21 Mt/day). We assume consistent safe shipping through the Strait needs to be possible again before the Ras Laffan facility will fully ramp up again. The slow cycling of the trains should help compress the restart timeline, but even so we assume a month for the facility to normalise flows on the 12 operable trains. Currently force majeure notices issued by Qatar cover volumes until early November for European buyers (announced last week) and early-October for Asian buyers. We now assume Qatari deliveries to Asia only normalise into year-end and for Europe in January.

records.text: Business spending: Full steam ahead Business spending should maintain its two-speed story over the forecast horizon. We expect nonresidential business fixed investment to grow by 7.7% in 2026 and accelerate to 8% in 2027. AI-related capex should continue to drive overall growth, supported by sustained hyperscaler spending – which should exceed $1tn in 2027 – and the ongoing buildout of compute and power capacity. In contrast, non-AI investment has been weaker but is beginning to show early signs of stabilization. As cyclical conditions improve in 2027, we expect a gradual broadening of the investment cycle, though AI- related spending will remain the dominant driver.

records.text: M Japan Insight Morgan Stanley MUFG 15 Nevertheless, that does not imply that corporate governance reform has been negative for Japanese investors. The truth is quite the opposite. The TSE market reforms make the changes within Japanese companies more visible. This has heightened the interest of market participants, including overseas investors, and brought about a significant reassessment of Japanese equity markets as a whole. The reforms took a portion of the alpha that had been locked within individual companies and broadened it to a market-wide reassessment. In other words, we could argue that a share of the alpha that was once easily captured has been transformed to market-wide returns, i.e., beta. This is in a sense the flip side of the success of the reforms. When overall market valuations were low and expectations for reform were not yet discounted, investors could generate considerable alpha by selectively targeting stocks with the potential for improved governance. Subsequently, as reform become a theme affecting Japanese companies across the board, that same information began to be reflected in the valuation of the entire Japanese equity market rather than just individual stocks. As a result, while alpha has not completely disappeared, previously effective strategies cannot be expected to yield the same results. Industrial policy fits the same framework where strategic returns exceed private returns or common infrastructure creates coordination failures. Canada has the financial and fiscal capacity to support a larger productive economy; the test is whether that capacity converts into realized projects, broader private investment and ultimately higher capital per worker. From Financial Capital to Productive Capital Canada does not appear constrained by aggregate financial savings or institutional balance-sheet capacity. Yet business investment per worker has deteriorated for much of the past decade despite one of the deepest pools of institutional capital in the developed world. The disconnect points to a different constraint: the risk-adjusted investability of domestic projects rather than the availability of savings itself. Canadian pension funds and institutional investors already command substantial balance- sheet capacity, but that capital is allocated against a global opportunity set. A Canadian infrastructure asset competes with comparable investments in the US, Europe, Australia and elsewhere on expected risk-adjusted returns. The policy objective should therefore not be to force Canadian capital home; it should be to create more Canadian projects capable of clearing commercial hurdle rates. Phase 1, completed in January 2025, introduced criteria such as a minimum free-float cap of ¥10bn and the exclusion of strategic shareholdings from the free-float calculation. Stocks must have a minimum annual trading value turnover ratio of 0.14 for continuing inclusion and 0.20 for new inclusion. Furthermore, stocks meeting the turnover ratio criteria are ranked by free-float market cap in descending order. To qualify, a stock must fall within the top 97% of the cumulative ratio for continuing inclusion or top 96% for new inclusion. By setting a higher hurdle for new inclusion than a continuing presence, the design aims to minimize frequent reshuffles of index constituents. We consider free-float market cap a more important criterion than annual trading volume turnover. A European Section 301-style instrument would face significant legal and political hurdles, though. The EU has long presented itself as a defender of the rules-based multilateral trading system. A framework authorising unilateral remedies without first using applicable WTO procedures would therefore represent a meaningful policy shift and could itself face legal challenge. Also, preserving a decision-making structure that avoids unanimity would be important if the instrument is to provide credible and timely leverage. Ultimately, a Section 301-style instrument would function as an intermediate option. It could be broad enough to address systemic non-market distortions, while remaining more targeted than an indiscriminate tariff regime or activation of the Anti-Coercion Instrument. records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 37 Review of supply, demand and inventories for August Gas demand across our European perimeter strengthened again on a YoY basis in August, with total demand up 5% YoY. Residential-commercial demand fell 9% YoY, running 10% below its 3-year average, while industrial gas demand also stayed soft. Strong growth in gas demand for power generation more than offset this softness, pulling total demand back into positive YoY territory for August. Industrial gas demand extended its recent softness into a second consecutive month of YoY contraction in August, down 2% YoY. Italy (-15% YoY) and Belgium (-14% YoY) showed the most weakness, while France (-2%) and the Netherlands (-5%) also lagged. Germany was a rare bright spot, posting a marginal 1% YoY gain. This is broadly consistent with the July Euro Area manufacturing PMI, which rose to a three-month high of 51.9, with Germany posting its strongest reading in over four years even as France remained a laggard. The pickup in Dutch factory activity captured in the same survey has not yet shown up in Dutch gas demand. Gas demand for power generation remained a key source of demand strength in August, rising 28% YoY and running 14% above the 3-year average. High temperatures across NW Europe boosted overall power demand (+11% YoY) while weighing on hydro and nuclear generation, increasing the call on gas for power. records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 23 Exhibit 36: How the market has balanced over the last five months from an EU + UK perspective Exhibit 37: How the market has balanced over the last five months from our European perimeter's perspective Base case for winter In our base case for the next six months, we see the global gas market tightening further and prices moving higher. In this scenario, TTF averages €85/MWh over winter, as higher prices are required to induce additional demand reduction outside Europe but mild winter weather prevents the market from moving into a more severe stress scenario. We also assume Qatar LNG flows to Europe normalise in January 2027. Under this scenario, we see Europe competing more aggressively for LNG cargos over winter due to concerns over the security of supply situation given historically low inventory levels. To achieve our modelled 6% YoY increase in LNG imports, ex-perimeter demand destruction would need to accelerate from 1 Mt/month over the summer to ~1.6 Mt/month. We see prices needing to move higher to stimulate this additional demand destruction across Asia and Latin America. In this scenario, end-winter inventory levels reach 23% fill, avoiding critically low levels but still the second lowest end-winter level in the 15 years of gas market data.

Indeed, business investment has grown by 2.6% so far this year. And the information and communications sector is running at a pace of over 4% over the same period . Signs of AI capex a re everywhere in the national accounts data. While it is difficult to isolate the share of spending directly attributable to AI, a significant portion of the recent uplift across these sectors likely reflects the UK's broader AI -driven growth story. And more l ikely with time , AI spending will become an even more significant part of the UK’s GDP story, with the UK boasting the second most data centres in the world (only behind the US). What have we heard on AI investment in the UK? You won’t have to look very far to find headlines on AI investment. records.text: M Japan Insight Morgan Stanley MUFG 31 Subsidiary privatization announcements generate high returns The fundamental approach when looking at parent-subsidiary listings as an investment strategy is to buy listed subsidiary stocks in anticipation of their privatization. Announcements regarding privatization, particularly those involving a takeover bid (TOB) to make the subsidiary wholly owned, tend to generate impressively high returns (Exhibit 39 ). The problem is that investment opportunities naturally decline as the number of eligible listed subsidiaries lessens. That said, the stock market reactions associated with the unwinding of parent-subsidiary listings are not uniform. Considerable positive reactions have been observed in cases of TOB-led conversion to wholly owned subsidiaries or delisting and sale to a third party, while the reaction is relatively muted when conversion to a wholly owned subsidiary takes place via a stock-for-stock exchange. Also, the subsidiary’s shares are often negatively impacted when a parent firm sells a portion of its stake while the subsidiary remains listed, though the number of such cases is limited. Fundamentally, the unwinding of a parent-subsidiary listing is a booster event for the subsidiary’s shares. records.text: M BluePaper 22 Our new sector-level work suggests that these two improvements are unlikely to originate in the same parts of the economy. The sectors with the largest forward capital- spending pipelines are utilities, transportation and resources. The sectors with the strongest observable technology adoption and recent multifactor-productivity performance are information, finance, and other knowledge-intensive services. This creates what we call Canada’s conversion gap: Capital is building where direct TFP performance has historically been weak, while digital adoption is strongest in sectors with comparatively modest tangible-capital pipelines. The macro payoff therefore depends on what happens between those two groups. Power, transportation, resource, and digital infrastructure can raise the stock of productive capital. But they generate a broader productivity reset only if they lower economy-wide costs, crowd in private machinery and intangible investment, expand market scale, and allow technology to diffuse into larger, lower-readiness industries. What Is New in Our Framework? We construct a framework to map different sectoral dimensions into a conversion gap framework. We use historical capital-intensity contributions, historical and recent MFP, 2026 capex intentions, construction versus machinery-and-equipment spending, sector economic weights, and current AI adoption. Moreover, like June, it may be presented as a hike that is ‘robust’ across two-sided scenarios for energy. Electrification, AI-related power demand and security-of-supply objectives all require a materially larger, more resilient and more flexible grid. Networks, however, are only part of the solution. Rising power demand, growing system- balancing requirements and declining dispatchable capacity are reinforcing the need for baseload generation alongside grid investment. While Europe has added significant renewable capacity over the past decade, current market-price signals remain insufficient to support large- scale investment in new generation without regulatory support or risk-sharing mechanisms. As a result, network expansion, storage, flexibility assets and derisked baseload investments are increasingly moving to the forefront of utility capex plans. From a credit perspective, the shift is constructive but capital-intensive. Regulated networks and regulated/derisked generation offer stronger earnings visibility, lower commodity exposure and better cash-flow predictability than merchant generation, but they also require sustained upfront investment. While Europe knows what needs to be built, the key question is whether supportive regulation, robust risk-sharing schemes and efficient market design can be implemented so that the sector can finance and deliver this investment cycle in a well balanced manner. 3 September 2026 107 Barclays | The global energy race

Gas- price shocks typically reach consumer prices with a long and uncertain lag, often around 6-12 months, while the scale of pass-through differs materially across countries. Retail tariffs reflect previous and planned procurement, while hedging and fixed-term contracts initially protect part of the customer base. Suppliers may also treat a winter price spike as temporary rather than pass the full spot-price increase to households. Regulation, price caps and tax measures can further delay or limit the CPI effect. Czechia has the greatest exposure to wholesale prices, followed by Poland, while administered prices largely insulate CPI in Hungary and Romania. But we argue that the headwinds to bond convenience are reaching their peaks. An Inconvenient Time for EGBs? European core yields are reaching new highs in the context of the global bond sell-off. Duration risk premium is elevated amidst a higher level and skew of inflation risks, and significant bond supply in key markets like Germany and France. And while still tight, sovereign credit spreads have started to move wider as political risks come into focus. But how much of this repricing of duration risk is bond-specific vs broader macro risks to duration or credit? One way to answer this is to look at “convenience yields” in European government bonds (EGBs). Convenience yields represent the income investors are willing to forego to hold sovereign bonds compared to other forms of duration. Benefits to holding government bonds can include safety, liquidity, collateral usage, and improving regulatory compliance. The lower convenience yields are, the more valuable bonds are against other securities / derivatives with similar cash flows. It would require the kind of developments that lead to very persistent moves in energy prices, similar to the severe scenarios the ECB outlined in the March and June forecasts. Crucially, we still expect cuts in 2027, but rather than starting in March, we moved them recently to June after taking on board energy price moves that delay the drop in inflation. Our bigger conviction remains that cuts will follow in 2027, bringing the ECB deposit rate to, or below, 2% by end-27 again. The first phase of the cycle is likely to be concentrated in structures — transmission lines, ports, mines, LNG facilities, transportation corridors, and other large infrastructure assets. Those projects directly raise the capital stock and can alleviate important constraints, but the productivity implications become considerably larger if they also change investment incentives elsewhere in the private sector. This is where the distinction between a project cycle and a capital cycle becomes important. A transmission line such as the North Coast Transmission Line adds productive infrastructure directly, but its larger economic value comes if additional electricity capacity raises expected returns on mines, mineral processing, LNG facilities, data centers, and other industrial investments. A new port adds capacity, but its broader payoff comes if lower congestion and improved access to export markets induce manufacturers, logistics firms, and wholesalers to invest themselves. The same principle applies across the MPO pipeline: enabling infrastructure can create a second round of investment considerably larger than the initial asset when it removes a binding constraint on complementary private capital. records.text: M BluePaper 44 The three sector groups perform separate roles. The capital builders dominate the forward tangible-capex pipeline. Utilities, mining and oil & gas, and transportation account for more than 60% of intended 2026 spending. Their investment is predominantly structures and engineering. That supports power generation and transmission, mines, pipelines, ports, rail, roads, and other network assets. The initial macro effect is therefore strongest through K, productive capacity and bottleneck relief. The higher-adoption sectors have much smaller tangible-capex pipelines, but considerably higher AI use and stronger observable digital readiness. Their productive investment is also understated by the tangible-capex data because software, data, intellectual property and organizational capital play a larger role. The swing sectors sit between the two. They account for approximately one-quarter of GVA and one-quarter of intended capex in the screen, but nearly 70% of their spending is machinery and equipment. They also combine relatively low AI adoption with meaningful MFP gaps. The sectors receiving the largest capital inflows are therefore not the sectors currently showing the greatest technology adoption. The macro outcome depends on whether infrastructure and resource capital change investment and productivity behavior in the swing sectors. Calibrating the incremental K. A net MFP contribution of 0.7pp would therefore be well above the 1981-2000 rate, below the early postwar regime, and almost 0.8pp above the post-2000 experience. This route would require broad gains from technology, scale, competition, organizational change, and resource allocation. AI adoption would need to extend materially beyond the current leaders in information, finance, and professional services. It would also require stronger productivity in industries where recent performance has been weakest: construction, manufacturing, transportation, wholesale trade, and parts of the resource economy. The Bank of Canada's AI baseline provides only part of the required impulse. Its central estimate is that AI adds ~0.2pp annually to MFP for 10 years. The upside scenario adds another 0.2pp, bringing the potential AI contribution to around 0.4pp annually. records.text: e capital and productivity cycles to become mutually reinforcing. The three routes are accounting illustrations, but K and A are not independent in practice. Higher MFP raises the expected return on investment. Firms are more likely to add capital when technology, market access, scale, or organizational change allow them to use it more profitably. Likewise, new capital can enable MFP. AI adoption requires compute, software, data infrastructure, and skills. Advanced manufacturing requires machinery, power, and logistics. Internal trade reform raises productivity more effectively when firms have the capital to expand and serve a larger market. The 2% scenario is therefore less likely to emerge from a simple addition of separate capital and TFP shocks. It is more likely to emerge from a conversion cycle: Infrastructure and resource capital→lower bottlenecks→private crowd-in→technology and organizational diffusion→higher TFP→higher returns to further capital. That feedback loop is what distinguishes a temporary capital build from a lasting productivity reset.

records.text: To assess these drivers formally we run a range of specifications of two panels, one across Germany/France and the other across Italy/Spain. We regress convenience yields on: net bond supply (capturing both net issuance dynamics and ECB QE/QT), the bond free-float as a share of GDP , the KFW-Bund spread to capture the liquidity dimension, and repo spreads to reflect funding costs. We control for the macro-economic environment (via consensus economics 12 months ahead growth and inflation). In contrast to our prior studies on the effect of QE on outright yields, because our independent variable is a spread of 10y rates, we think the signaling channel of QE through policy rate expectations is unlikely to be active here. Our main takeaways from this analysis are: Net bond supply flows are the most compelling driver of convenience yields (Exhibit n 7), statistically and economically significant across a range of different specifications. We find that 1ppt increase in net supply over 6 months (expressed as a share of GDP) is worth about 8.5bp in yields in the core and 6bp in the periphery. The total amount of debt outstanding is a significant driver too, but only when net n supply flows are omitted. This suggests that the total free-float matters to set the market environment (and credit risk / term premium) but is less impactful in predicting shift in convenience yields. August Beige Book: Resilient growth meets sticky inflation We have previously leveraged our proprietary LLM tools to analyze the Fed’s Beige Book, assessing economic sentiment across key macroeconomic variables: growth, the labor market, inflation, and perceived recession probabilities (see From qualitative to quantitative: decoding Beige Book with AI ). The derived sentiment scores were able to capture economic dynamics over the past decade. In this piece we continued this exercise and update our analysis for the latest Beige Book from August 2026. As a reminder, the score is based on a scale of 0 to 10, a score of 0 is associated with a lower assessment of conditions, and a score of 10 is associated with higher assessment. A score of 5 is neutral (see Appendix for full prompts). Note that for the last topic on recession, a score of 0 would suggest that the recession is not expected in next 12 months, while a score of 10 would suggest that the recession is nearly certain in next 12 months. records.text: 2 UK Viewpoint | 02 September 2026 Back to School: Waiting out the energy shock Sonali Punhani MLI (UK) sonali.punhani@bofa.com Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com Forecast update: A better start, a slower finish? We expect growth at 1.2% (+10bps) in 2026, 1.2% (-10bps) in 2027 and 1.5% (unch.) in 2028 to reflect better-than-expected H1 growth and marginal lowering of sequential growth due to higher energy prices and domestic policy uncertainty ahead of the Budget. But risks are tilted to the upside due to potential fiscal loosening in the Autumn Budget. We raise our inflation forecast in Q4 2026 to 3.4% (20bps), with 2026 average unchanged at 3.1% and to 2.6% (+30bps) in 2027, to reflect higher oil and gas prices than our post-peace deal assumptions. We expect core at 2.8% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. Our 2028 forecast remains unchanged at 2.1% for headline and 2.1% for core. Headline inflation is expected to pick up from here, with the peak now expected at 3.5% in Nov. vs 3.3% in Sept/Nov 2026 before. Inflation is expected to stay above 3% until Q2 2027 and reach close to target later in Q4 2027, but there are risks that the return to target sustainably is delayed. We expect the passthrough of the energy shock to domestic inflation and second round effects to remain contained but also think there are risks that the disinflation to 2% next year is stalled. We keep our BoE call unchanged with BoE on hold in 2026, followed by a single 25bp cut

A capital-heavy baseline is more dependent on maintaining a high rate of investment and may produce a larger transitional level effect. A TFP-heavier baseline is more durable and has stronger implications for real incomes, returns to capital and the economy’s longer- run speed limit. Our baseline calibration is already a more productive economy than the one Canada experienced in the immediate post-pandemic period. It assumes capital per worker recovers, investment strengthens, and AI begins to contribute to efficiency. To meaningfully move the needle on potential growth by another 50bps per year, we need to look to other upside sources. The following aspects are not a part of our baseline: 1. a broad private machinery and intangible-investment boom; 2. large private-sector crowd-in; 3. rapid AI diffusion into the swing sectors; 4. a material easing of internal trade and permitting constraints. records.text: M BluePaper 56 Mobilizing Canada's Balance Sheet Canada’s investment problem is not primarily a shortage of financial capacity. Business investment per worker has weakened for much of the past decade despite deep pools of pension and institutional capital. The more binding constraint is project economics: whether domestic opportunities offer sufficiently attractive risk-adjusted returns to compete for capital against a global opportunity set. The policy regime is increasingly targeting that constraint. Faster capital-cost deductions raise after-tax returns; permitting reform reduces the cost of delay; guarantees and co-investment can reallocate specific risks; and enabling infrastructure raises returns to complementary private capital. The objective is not for government to finance the investment cycle, but to improve project economics enough to crowd in substantially more private investment. Execution is now the key test. The Major Projects Office matters less for the headline value of projects referred than for whether approvals become faster and more predictable, projects reach final investment decision and construction, and private capex broadens beyond the initial infrastructure build. Canada’s public balance sheet is most valuable when used at the margin to remove binding constraints rather than substitute for commercially viable private capital. In terms of overseas demand, the temporary increase in R&D services that lifted exports in Q2 is likely to drop out, while crude oil import volumes recover, reducing the contribution to growth in Q3. records.text: decline in the labor force participation rate since December 2025 (Exhibit 5). We expect a few of these factors to be less of a drag on participation going forward. We expect residual seasonality in the 16-24 year-old group to turn from a drag on participation again in August to a boost to participation over the rest of the year. And the sampling bias that has weighed on participation among the 25-34 year-old group in recent months should fade as those groups move out of the household survey sample over the next few months. How concerned should we be about the decline in the labor force participation rate this year? Most of the increase in the number of people not in the labor force since January reflects college graduates over the age of 55 retiring from work (Exhibit 6, left). We see this concentration among older and likely higher-income workers as consistent with positive wealth effects on retirement decisions, possibly reflecting AI-related equity gains. While it appears that some of the decline in the labor force participation rate this year is genuine, the fact that it mainly reflects retirement of workers who are potentially well-positioned to do so rather than an increase in discouraged or other marginally attached workers makes the decline somewhat less concerning from a cyclical perspective. records.text: January 2025, the UK Government launched its AI Opportunities Action Plan, which included plans for a 20x expansion in public compute capacity – including the introduction of AI Growth Zones. As part of its announcement, it also included GBP 14bn in private-sector commitments including from Vantage Data Centres, and Kyndryl linked to AI and digital infrastructure. In September 2025, Microsoft ( and others) announced plans for what was described as the UK’s largest AI supercomputer in Essex – this came as part of Microsoft’s broader USD 30bn UK commitment. Investment plans didn’t stop there. OpenAI and NVIDIA launched Stargate UK - designed to build sovereign AI compute capacity in Britain as part of a wider investment package. Google too joined the fray, making its own announcement spanning AI infrastructure, DeepMind research and healthcare initiatives. Taken together, there have been more than GBP 50bn of AI -related private-sector investment announcements in littler more than a year (roughly 1.5% of GDP). But headlines can be deceiving – both in terms of the timing of investment and how it actually feeds through into the economy. In this weekly, we present the key trackers to watch when looking at broader AI spending in the UK. This, in our view, will give us as close to a real-time gauge on the contribution of AI spending in the UK. This legislation has forced EU OEMs to manufacture and launch much more expensive BEV /PHEV models into a European market that did not demand EVs in the numbers required. In its current format, even at 90%, the 2035 legislation essentially bans all ICE, HEV, and PHEV models altogether in the EU. Whilst this anyway has interesting connotations for the eventual growth of Chinese OEMs (ie the BEV tariffs become more and more helpful as we approach 2035), it also means more expensive cars for EU consumers, and likely profit margin pressure for EU OEMs to try to persuade EU consumers to buy these more expensive models; to maintain multiple sets of drivetrain technologies and increased model complexity – all weighing on EU profitability. Interestingly, since April 26, EU BEV demand has picked up sharply as energy prices rose (and new EU incentives started), reducing the pressure on OEMs to meet the new 2025-2027 CO2 emission averaging standard, and potentially even allowing OEMs to meet the much tighter 55% fleet CO2 emissions reductions required by 2030. Beijing may target politically sensitive products, companies and member states in ways that maximise pressure on the EU coalition while limiting the economic cost to China. China has already signalled that it would respond firmly to new European trade restrictions and has demonstrated a willingness to use targeted trade and supply-chain measures (Bloomberg, 29 May). The most exposed sectors include Autos, Luxury, Agriculture, Aerospace and selected Chemicals companies. Potential measures include anti-dumping or anti- subsidy investigations, tariffs, public-procurement restrictions, customs and licensing delays, administrative pressure on European companies operating in China and informal measures affecting consumer demand. Companies with significant Chinese revenues, assets or local partnerships may therefore receive less benefit from stronger European protection than their European production exposure initially suggests. Controls on critical inputs could be more disruptive than tariffs on European exports. China holds strong positions in rare-earth processing, permanent magnets, batteries, selected semiconductor-related inputs and dual-use goods. Restrictions on these products could interrupt European production even for companies with relatively limited Chinese revenue. Exports not only improve their low Chinese capacity utilization (providing very low marginal costs of production), but with less competition and very competitive products, Chinese OEMs can price their products at much higher levels in Europe than in China. This means that China exports to Europe and RoW can drive much higher EBIT margins (despite logistics and homologation costs). Chinese exports to EU reach 10% market share - Obviously, a number of the larger China OEMs have now been pursuing this strategy aggressively and have pushed China OEM market share in Europe (incl UK) to over 10% in recent months (from 8.8% in FY25). Two Small Parties, One Large Stake Against a backdrop of cyclical resilience but persistent structural challenges, Italy is scheduled to hold a general election in 2027. The exact date has not yet been decided, but the two most likely options are April or September, with consensus prediction markets leaning towards the former. PM Giorgia Meloni now leads the longest-serving Italian government since WWII. Italy has benefited from four years of political stability, which, combined with cautious fiscal guidance, has been reflected in favourable financial conditions and relatively tight sovereign spreads. That stability is now more uncertain because it is unclear whether the election will deliver a clear parliamentary majority. We think investors should focus on two key elements in the run-up to the vote: the electoral reform and whether two smaller parties, Futuro Nazionale (FN) and Azione (Az), are included in the main coalitions. The current pipeline includes large investments in electricity, transportation, resource infrastructure and selected digital assets. Slower labor growth also makes it easier for capital per worker to rise. So the capital-only route could be plausible. But this would require more than execution of a limited set of major projects. It would require capital accumulation to broaden into private machinery, equipment, software and intellectual property, and to remain elevated after the initial infrastructure build has matured. The durability issue is central. If the capital-deepening contribution rises to 1.5pps for several years and subsequently returns to 1.0, Canada would retain a permanently larger capital stock and a higher level of potential output. But its growth rate would fall back toward 1.5%. The capital-only route can build a larger economy. It is less likely, on its own, to create a permanently faster-growing economy. records.text: What’s Driving the Decline in the Labor Force Participation Rate? The labor force participation rate has declined 1.0pp since December 2025 (Exhibit 1). The January 2026 labor force participation rate was revised down by 0.4pp following the implementation of updated population controls to the household survey in February which re-anchored the survey’s population estimate to the Census population estimate, resulting in one-time adjustments to the levels of the labor force, employment, and other series (Exhibit 2). The benchmarking incorporated data from 2020 with a long lag and resulted in the January labor force participation rate—which had increased by 0.1pp relative to the December level in the initial print—being revised down by 0.4pp, or 0.3pp below the December level. This was partially driven by large increases in the estimates of the population aged 65 and over, which has a below-average participation rate. Because the annual revisions are not carried backward, their incorporation results in a statistical break which makes the decline in the official labor force participation rate appear 0.4pp sharper than it would otherwise be. In today’s Daily, we investigate what has caused the 0.7pp decline in the labor force participation rate since January. While there are always many factors that could add up to a gross decline in participation that is well in excess of the net decline, we highlight factors that we think are most important. records.text: Energy addition, not substitution, is the present – and the future The data support a clear conclusion: the world is in an era of energy addition, not substitution. All major energy sources are growing. The IEA's own Global Energy Review 2026 confirms that oil, natural gas, and coal each reached record consumption levels in 2025. Renewables are growing faster – solar PV contributed the largest single share of demand growth for the first time – but they are growing in addition to fossil fuels, not instead of them. This is likely to persist for several years. Non-OECD energy demand is being driven by industrialisation, urbanisation, and rising living standards, forces that are not discretionary and that require energy in all its forms. India's electricity demand is growing at 6-7% per year. Southeast Asia is building coal plants alongside solar farms. The Middle East is investing in renewable capacity and upstream oil production simultaneously. The assumption that the world would transition linearly from fossil fuels to renewables was always an abstraction. The reality is a system that needs more of everything, for longer, than the models assumed. This is not an argument against the energy transition. It is an argument for realism about its pace and its capital requirements. The transition is happening: renewable capacity additions, EV adoption rates, and clean energy investment are all at record levels. records.text: M BluePaper 12 Productivity and Convergence: 1961-81 Canada’s strongest growth regime combined rapid expansion in inputs with substantial productivity gains. Between 1961 and 1981, business-sector output grew by approximately 4.8% annually. Hours worked contributed around 2.0 percentage points (pp), while labor productivity added a further 2.8pp. In other words, nearly 60% of output growth came from producing more in each hour worked rather than simply adding hours. The productivity contribution was also relatively balanced. Capital intensity added approximately 1.3pp annually, labor composition contributed 0.5pp, and MFP contributed close to 1pp. Workers were receiving more capital, the quality of the labor force was improving, and the economy was also generating gains beyond what could be attributed to measured inputs. This was the latter part of Canada’s postwar convergence phase. Canadian business-sector productivity growth exceeded that of the United States during much of the early postwar period, and Canada’s relative productivity level moved above 90% of the US level in the early 1980s. That convergence reflected both capital accumulation and the adoption of technologies and production practices already in use at the global productivity frontier. The First Slowdown: 1981-2000 Growth slowed materially after 1981, but productivity remained an important part of the model. The distinction matters particularly for autos, metals, machinery, transportation equipment and wood products, where US trade and industrial policy has become more interventionist. Canada and the US also have genuinely different strategic interests. The US increasingly wants domestic production and greater control over strategic supply chains; Canada wants predictable access that allows investment north of the border to serve the broader North American market. The Canadian objective therefore cannot simply be to preserve existing exports or tariff levels. An agreement that protects current trade but steadily redirects marginal capex into the US through other forms of industrial policy would be less favorable than the headline tariff outcome suggests. Nor would USMCA necessarily evolve symmetrically: a more favorable outcome for Mexico could allow its lower costs and deeper manufacturing ecosystem to attract incremental investment at Canada’s expense. Canada therefore needs to strengthen its own value proposition and productive capacity, not simply preserve market access. Nevertheless, our base case remains that Canada and the US ultimately find sufficient common ground. The strategic complementarities are substantial: Canada supplies energy, uranium, critical minerals, agricultural products and industrial inputs that become more valuable as the US seeks secure North American supply chains. Majors & E&Ps have structurally changed their capital allocation priorities Source: Barclays Research Energy security & capital allocation shifts From return of capital to securing molecules The return of history and concurrent geopolitical upheavals has thrust energy security and resource access back into the limelight. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the U.S. Integrated Oil & E&P landscape’s capital allocation priorities shifted to prioritize capital returns over growth, with corporates racing to strengthen balance sheets and adopt robust, formulaic shareholder return frameworks to the tune of 50-100% of FCF. Return of capital over return on capital had become the name of the game. Investors swiftly punished companies perceived as swaying from capital discipline and rewarded those that channelled marginal dollars into capital returns. While capital discipline priorities remain intact, the emerging energy security dilemma is redefining respective corporate strategies. Growing call on US molecules and companies is introducing some diversification in upstream spending. The market is once more beginning to reward molecule optionality and resource access for Integrated Majors such as CVX and XOM, while inventory depth becomes an even greater focal point across the U.S. shale landscape. But in our view, this reads more as a normalization than a break. The negative print lands against an otherwise firmer backdrop: second-quarter GDP rose a broad-based 3.3% (q/q saar), and the Bank of Canada held at 2.25% this week with a more hawkish tone. That said, the Bank's tone on the labor market was more balanced – emphasizing subdued demand for labor against a broader backdrop of excess supply. The drop in employment was within the survey's margin of error, the unemployment rate held at its two-year low of 6.4%, and employment is still up 217k (+1.0%) from a year ago. The composition is softer than the flat headline rate suggests — the rate held only because the labor force contracted alongside employment, the losses were concentrated in services and full-time work, and wage growth slowed for a second straight month to a multi-year low. We read the data as a pause in the firming over the summer, rather than a reversal. The existing project portfolio explicitly contains several such enabling assets. The clearest evidence of regime change would therefore be a broadening in the composition of private capex. An initial rise in structures investment should eventually be followed by stronger spending on machinery and equipment, software, intellectual property, and other assets that raise productivity throughout the business sector. At the same time, new infrastructure should make additional projects commercially viable without requiring the same degree of public support. The investment cycle then becomes increasingly self-reinforcing: infrastructure relieves bottlenecks → expected private returns rise → complementary investment is crowded in → capital per worker increases → technology and organizational improvements diffuse → productivity strengthens. That progression provides a practical framework for assessing the thesis over the next several years. First, conversion: More projects should move from announcement and referral to FID and construction, ideally on shorter and more predictable timelines. Second, breadth: Investment should spread beyond megaproject structures into machinery, software and intellectual property. records.text: critical minerals, energy security, semiconductors, defense, and other advanced or dual-use manufacturing. Industrial policy is most defensible where strategic returns exceed private returns and the underlying externality or coordination failure can be identified. Critical minerals, defense, and enabling energy infrastructure can meet that test: projects are often capital intensive, slow to mature and dependent on common infrastructure, procurement scale or supply-chain security whose benefits extend beyond the cash flows of an individual investor. Canada can use fiscal capacity selectively through enabling infrastructure, guarantees, procurement and co-investment. The potential payoff is highest when public support raises returns across several complementary private projects rather than financing a stand-alone asset that the private sector would have built anyway. Discipline is therefore central. Support should not protect incumbents, replace commercially viable private capital or sustain projects that remain uneconomic without permanent subsidy. The objective is to close identifiable gaps between private and strategic returns while preserving commercial discipline.

How Our Results Compare with the Literature Sharpe and Sargent show that capital intensity remained the principal positive contributor to Canadian labor-productivity growth after 2000, while MFP largely disappeared. They also find that most aggregate productivity growth occurred within industries, with labor reallocation making only a small contribution. records.text: Foreword Ajay Rajadhyaksha(i) BCI, US The global energy race AI's speed with which it spreads through the world economy, the use cases it generates in industry after industry, its effect on the labor market, the societal implication, etc: this will be the defining macro theme for the next decade. The global energy race, we believe, will be a close second. In 2025, every major energy source – oil, natural gas, coal, solar, wind, nuclear – notched new highs. All of them. Oil consumption rose to a record. Natural gas hit a record. Coal hit a record. And renewable capacity additions were the largest in history, with solar photovoltaic systems (PV) alone meeting more than a quarter of global demand growth for the first time. This is not what the consensus predicted. A decade ago, the prevailing narrative was sequential. Renewables would rise, but fossil fuels were supposed to decline. The energy system would transition from one to the other, in an orderly fashion. The reality has been messier, more expensive, and hence more consequential for capital markets. The world is not substituting one energy system for another. It is running both simultaneously, and it does not have enough capital deployed in either. That is the central argument of this report. Energy demand is rising at the same time as geopolitical fragmentation is increasing the premium on energy security. records.text: Europe Multi-Asset 03 September 2026 Citi Research 7 Carbon taxes are Europe’s tool to drive its Energy Transition ambitions and current policy (e.g. Affordable Energy Action Plan) continues to map a pathway to a lower cost future as coming from this Transition. Put another way, we would argue the Transition used to be positioned by policymakers as a ‘save the planet’ narrative, now it appears to be positioned as a ‘security and competitiveness imperative’ . Yet the energy price outcome of European policy, we think, is likely to be inflationary, rather than deflationary, as policymakers perhaps hope. Yes, it is certainly true that the marginal short-run cost of renewables is low, even close to zero, but long-run marginal costs are much higher, especially in northern Europe which needs to rely more on offshore wind than solar. Added to that, we are building an energy system that is inherently less efficient than the one we have today with significant system redundancy needed to cope with seasonal swings in power demand and renewables generation capability. Consider that in Germany winter demand is typically 3x higher than in summer. Batteries, pumped storage and other chemical and mechanical storage facilities will be important for short-term power market balance, but it is only gas that can provide the energy density to meet such a big seasonal demand increase. records.text: Europe Multi-Asset 03 September 2026 Citi Research 15 Industrials contain both threatened producers and potential beneficiaries of European investment. Machine tools, electrical equipment and selected machinery face increasing Chinese competition. Other companies should benefit from factory localisation, automation, grids, defence production and critical- material investment. The sector is therefore unlikely to receive one uniform policy treatment. The strongest beneficiaries should be companies with strategic technology, significant European production and limited dependence on Chinese revenues or inputs. Energy and Utilities should see substantial investment in grids, renewable and flexible generation, system optimisation and integrated power and LNG. records.text: M BluePaper 34 additional change would be required to add another 50 basis points to potential growth, and can that improvement persist once the initial catch-up in capital intensity and labor composition has run its course? Canada’s 1.5% baseline is already productivity-led, but most of the improvement comes from capital deepening and normalization. Moving toward 2% requires the productivity rebound to broaden from a recovery in capital per worker into sustained active investment and MFP growth. What Would It Take to Reach 2%? The medium-term baseline leaves Canada with potential growth of around 1.5%. The next question is whether that speed limit can move closer to 2%. More important, what kind of growth model would generate the additional 50 basis points? As labor input already contributes very little in the baseline, and the assumed productivity recovery is itself relatively optimistic, this is not a small hurdle. Moving from 1.5% to 2% requires either capital deepening to rise well above its recent and post-2000 rates, MFP to shift into a materially stronger regime, or both. We hold trend labor input and labor composition broadly unchanged in the central exercise. Demographic policy could generate upside to labor supply, while better integration of newcomers could raise labor quality. Colombia's hydro-dominant system is increasingly exposed to drought risk, while Brazil's rapid renewable buildout is creating transmission and congestion challenges that require significant network investment. Chile Chile is simultaneously one of the world’s most renewable-heavy markets, though curtailment remains a key issue. Chile’s power system is well advanced in the transition from fossil fuels generation to renewables: renewables account for close to 70% of generation and the country has committed to retire all coal by 2040. However, this decarbonization is colliding with grid geography. Chile's main investment need is increasingly storage and transmission rather than additional renewable generation. Solar and wind are concentrated in resource-rich zones away from central demand, and new solar projects face curtailment during times of peak supply. BESS is therefore becoming the nearer-term monetization tool for the utilities. records.text: M BluePaper 16 A Productivity Rebound Is Likely — but Is It a New Growth Cycle? Canada is likely to experience a meaningful improvement in measured labor-productivity growth over the next several years. But the source of that improvement matters. Productivity can rebound because the capital stock grows faster, whether because firms use capital and labor more efficiently, or simply because labor-input growth slows and the existing capital stock is spread across fewer incremental hours. Those outcomes produce very different implications for aggregate growth. A productivity rebound driven mainly by a slower denominator can coexist with weak potential-output growth. An active investment cycle, by contrast, can raise capital per worker while also expanding the economy’s productive capacity. A Productivity Rebound Is Already in the Baseline The Bank of Canada’s 2026 potential-output assessment provides a useful external benchmark. One possible reason is the value effect. That is, historically the value factor has been effective on Japanese stock markets, and as noted above companies with a high likelihood of MBO tend to be value stocks, which may be contributing. That said, there is no marked underperformance even around 2020, when value factor returns were particularly muted, suggesting the general value effect is also an insufficient explanation. Another possibility is the management effect. That is, as we noted in our 2025 report, the greater the effective ownership of management (including through asset management companies), the higher the likelihood of MBO; and consequently, the higher the management ownership ratio, the higher the MBO Score. Transmission is becoming as important as generation The most acute shortfall is not necessarily in clean generation itself, but in the infrastructure required to make that generation usable. Cheap generation does not necessarily imply reliable power. Its value depends increasingly on route-to-grid, storage, demand flexibility, interconnection and the ability of the power system to manage changing patterns of supply and demand. The Iberian blackout illustrates the challenge. As we wrote in our Network Security series, the Spanish government’s investigation identified insufficient voltage-control capacity as a principal contributor, rather than high renewable penetration or a simple lack of system inertia. Renewable generation was not inherently the problem, but its rapid growth had exposed weaknesses in a power system that had not been modernised sufficiently quickly. The investment is also needed for large renewable adopters such as China and India, evidenced by their latest capex budgets. Bringing network investment closer to generation could define the next phase of the transition. Global investment into grids amounted to roughly $400bn globally in 2024, compared with about $1trn in generation assets, highlighting the potential scale of the investment opportunity as this ratio moves closer to parity

He added that financial conditions remained accommodative and reiterated the BoJ’s intention to continue adjusting the degree of accommodation through rate hikes. Ueda also said that data released since the July meeting have been broadly in line with the BoJ's outlook and that rate hikes would be thoroughly discussed at every meeting, including the next one. On the other hand, he noted that “we have raised rates about five times, and the effects are always emerging gradually and cumulatively, so the BoJ intends to carefully look at those. ” These comments suggest that while he is laying the groundwork for a September hike, he remains cautious about the pace thereafter. With a September hike already almost fully priced by the market and effectively becoming a “done deal, ” attention is shifting to the pace of rate hikes thereafter. We expect the BoJ to accelerate for a time from its previous pace of roughly one hike every six months, raising rates in September and January before a further hike in July next year. At the same time, a September hike would take the policy rate to 1.25%, clearly above the lower bound of the BoJ’s estimated nominal neutral-rate range (1.07%-2.53%) for the first time, bringing the median (1.64%) into view. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS EM yield curve flattening? While flows into 2y EM sovereign bonds have continued to decline, flows into 10y bonds appear to have bottomed out and have increased since mid-August (Figure 2). We believe these flows dynamics point to flattening pressure driven mainly by domestic hawkishness, as both EM fuel and food inflation have continuously risen amid prolonged geopolitical tension and the impact of El-Niño (Figure 3). India is a good example. The INR 2s10s swap spread has narrowed by -7bp since August 19 (Figure 4). Both early dollar deposit window (FCNR(B)) closure and hawkish August RBI MPC minutes have raised short-term yields. In addition, India real GDP growth marked 7.8%yoy in 1QFY27 (2Q26), well above the market consensus. Following the GDP release, market is now fully pricing in a 25bp rate hike at the October RBI MPC meeting. The PLN swap curve is also bear-flattening, as both July PPI and August CPI (3.4%yoy) exceeded consensus and market has started to question the prospect of further NBP rate cuts . By contrast, the PHP swap curve is bull-flattening: although BSP hiked its overnight borrowing rate to 5% on August 28, the hike had already been fully anticipated. The market is now putting more weight on weakening growth momentum (see page 3) after 2Q26 GDP miss, pushing long-term yields lower. We believe FX implications of EM yield curve flattening may be different depending on the underlying driver

records.text: of capital discipline, most U.S. Integrateds and E&Ps now operate with sub-1x leverage, substantial free cash flow generation, and shareholder return frameworks that often distribute 50-100% of FCF through dividends and buybacks. Yet despite stronger business models, increasing calls on U.S. molecules, and growing competition for resource access, sector valuations remain relatively compressed. In our view, the market continues to underestimate both the scarcity value of future U.S. production growth and the sector's strategic importance in an increasingly security-focused energy landscape. The irony is that shale may be more valuable as it matures than it was during its peak growth phase. Investors are being offered exposure to a sector with improving scarcity, stronger capital discipline, increasing strategic relevance, and some of the strongest balance sheets in the market. That combination makes the investment case for U.S. Upstream more compelling than it has been in years. 3 September 2026 62 Barclays | The global energy race

This shift is visible in Europe’s (not only Germany’s) greater willingness to use fiscal policy to (1) foster its defence capabilities, (2) modernise its infrastructures, (3) diversify energy supplies, and (4) reduce technological dependencies. The big spending announcements from Germany shaped market expectations in 2025, but 2026 is the year when actual spending is hitting the ground (see Fig 1). This in our view explains part of the remarkable resilience of the European economy since the start of the year. Moreover, higher German public investment is adding to a trend already in place across other European countries, where public investment is accelerating financed still through the 2020 NextGenEU fund (see Fig 2). This shift towards domestic demand is also visible in notably robust private business investment over the last few years. This strength is somewhat counterintuitive given the several negative shocks that have hit Europe since the pandemic. Industrial policy is most defensible where strategic returns exceed private returns and the underlying externality or coordination failure can be identified. Critical minerals, defense, and enabling energy infrastructure can meet that test: projects are often capital intensive, slow to mature and dependent on common infrastructure, procurement scale or supply-chain security whose benefits extend beyond the cash flows of an individual investor. Canada can use fiscal capacity selectively through enabling infrastructure, guarantees, procurement and co-investment. The potential payoff is highest when public support raises returns across several complementary private projects rather than financing a stand-alone asset that the private sector would have built anyway. Discipline is therefore central. Support should not protect incumbents, replace commercially viable private capital or sustain projects that remain uneconomic without permanent subsidy. The objective is to close identifiable gaps between private and strategic returns while preserving commercial discipline.

First, some capital deepening is passive. With labor-input growth falling toward zero, the existing capital stock is spread across fewer incremental hours. The Bank of Israel delivered on our out-of-con- sensus 25bp cut to 3.25% this week and retained a dovish tone. Below-target inflation, slower wage growth, moderate domestic demand, and a stronger shekel argue for further eas- ing, but higher commodity prices and global rates may con- strain the cycle. We expect the BoI to pause in October before delivering a final cut in November. In Türkiye, August inflation eased to 31.5%oya and annual- ized core momentum fell to around 28%, while 2Q GDP con- firmed that weak domestic demand is being offset by stronger net exports. The September CBRT meeting is therefore live, but the recent 300bp easing in funding conditions, the rise in oil prices, and uncertainty around services repricing argue for patience. We retain our call for 100bp cuts in October and December, but risks are tilted towards rates remaining higher for longer. records.text: US Economics 04 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Data – The US economy added 162k jobs in August, well above consensus for 55k and Citi at 20k. Jobs gains were broad-based across categories, with notable rebounds in leisure and hospitality +62k and local government +50k—categories that had run aberrantly weak in recent months. Private payrolls registered 127k with a three-month moving average now at a solid 74k. Manufacturing hiring appears to have persistently picked up, with the sector adding 16k jobs in August and averaging 15k over the last three months. Health care sector hiring has slowed, still adding 28k jobs in August but substantially fewer than the above 50k pace that prevailed in prior years. The unemployment rate increased only slightly from 4.09% to 4.141%, leaving the rounded 4.1% unchanged. The stability in the unemployment rate is notable given that the participation rate rebounded from 61.4% to 61.6% after falling 1pp since December of last year. The rise in participation was matched by a very strong 569k increase in household employment. Wage growth was expectedly subdued, with average hourly earnings at 0.3% MoM and 3.1% YoY. Citi’s take – Fed officials will likely read this morning’s jobs report as showing a labor market that is “stable” but not creating inflationary pressure. In growth rates: g_Y = g_H + g_(Y/H). And we use a quality augmented production function for the framing: Y = A(K^alpha)*(QH^(1-alpha)), where K is capital, Q is composition or labor quality, A is the MFP. Then putting in growth rates: g_(Y/H) = alpha*(g_K/H) + (1-alpha)*(g_Q)+g_A. And just to make explicit: The growth in labor productivity is equal to the alpha*(g_K - g_H) + (1-alpha)*(g_Q)+g_A. In the decomposition, the first term is capital intensity, the second is labor composition, and A is the MFP term. records.text: M BluePaper 16 A Productivity Rebound Is Likely — but Is It a New Growth Cycle? Canada is likely to experience a meaningful improvement in measured labor-productivity growth over the next several years. But the source of that improvement matters. Productivity can rebound because the capital stock grows faster, whether because firms use capital and labor more efficiently, or simply because labor-input growth slows and the existing capital stock is spread across fewer incremental hours. Those outcomes produce very different implications for aggregate growth. A productivity rebound driven mainly by a slower denominator can coexist with weak potential-output growth. An active investment cycle, by contrast, can raise capital per worker while also expanding the economy’s productive capacity. A Productivity Rebound Is Already in the Baseline The Bank of Canada’s 2026 potential-output assessment provides a useful external benchmark. Bank staff estimate potential-output growth of 2.3% in 2025, falling to 1.2% in 2026, before recovering to 1.3% in 2027, 1.5% in 2028, and 1.8% in 2029. The underlying composition changes more dramatically than the headline path. The contribution from trend labor input falls from 1.3pp in 2025 to -0.3pp in 2026, and then recovers only gradually to 0.3ppby 2029. Demand-side debates have largely disappeared; the binding constraint is supply, with OEM manufacturing capacity the industry’s biggest bottleneck. Geothermal is emerging as the clean firm-power answer to the medium-term gap. While gas-fired distributed power fills the near-term void, geothermal offers dispatchable, zero-fuel baseload with round-the-clock capacity factors that solar and wind can’t match, and it retains rare bipartisan tax support. The step change is enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), which apply the horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing playbook that unlocked shale to engineer reservoirs almost anywhere with hot rock, removing the geographic constraint that kept the technology niche. Fervo is the standard-bearer: leaning on the existing oilfield services supply chain rather than a constrained OEM order book, it has binding PPAs and a multi-gigawatt hyperscaler framework agreement in hand, with a cost trajectory from roughly $7,000/kW today toward $3,000/kW at scale, competitive with new-build gas and well below nuclear. Although shareholder engagement has long been a crucial topic for corporate governance, it was not always under the market spotlight to the same extent as at present. We think this is because the piggybacking strategy is becoming less effective as a wide range of investors (including retail investors) have started using activist investors’ ownership reports as investment reference data, spurred by TSE market reforms and a greater market focus on shareholder engagement. In addition, the TSE market reforms have turned concepts such as cost of capital, P/B, surplus capital, and shareholder returns, once largely associated with activist investors, into a common language across the entire market. As a result, listed companies as a whole have increased shareholder returns ( Exhibit 56 ), narrowing the efficacy of demanding that companies simply raise dividends or buy back shares as a means to further release value. As noted by Suzuki (2025), “activist demands are shifting away from simply asking for higher shareholder returns and towards focusing on board-level governance and management that can generate longer-term improvements in earnings.” For this reason, share price returns are becoming less immediate. The market is now pricing in approximately three rate hikes by the April 2027 meeting, a level that aligns with our forecast. It appears that market expectations have now caught up to our outlook. However, the driving force behind this shift was not an improvement in economic fundamentals or communication from the BoJ, as we had anticipated, but rather external pressure from the US. During the drafting process for this fiscal year's "Basic Policies for Economic and Fiscal Management," language that could have been interpreted as government interference in the BoJ's monetary policy drew criticism and had to be amended. Industrial policy fits the same framework where strategic returns exceed private returns or common infrastructure creates coordination failures. Canada has the financial and fiscal capacity to support a larger productive economy; the test is whether that capacity converts into realized projects, broader private investment and ultimately higher capital per worker. From Financial Capital to Productive Capital Canada does not appear constrained by aggregate financial savings or institutional balance-sheet capacity. Yet business investment per worker has deteriorated for much of the past decade despite one of the deepest pools of institutional capital in the developed world. The disconnect points to a different constraint: the risk-adjusted investability of domestic projects rather than the availability of savings itself. Canadian pension funds and institutional investors already command substantial balance- sheet capacity, but that capital is allocated against a global opportunity set. A Canadian infrastructure asset competes with comparable investments in the US, Europe, Australia and elsewhere on expected risk-adjusted returns. The policy objective should therefore not be to force Canadian capital home; it should be to create more Canadian projects capable of clearing commercial hurdle rates. Energy security and the return of capital One of the defining characteristics of the current power regime has been the shift of attention to behind-the-meter (BTM) investments and applications. BTM refers to generation that happens "behind" the grid, meaning it bypasses grid interconnection to provide power directly to one or multiple sources. As the wait for interconnection has ballooned to several years (depending on location), and hyperscalers in particular are time sensitive with regards to power access, there has been a lot of recent discussion about the prospects for BTM power solutions. In some cases, these could be permanent, "islanded" power plants, never connected to the grid. In others, they could be temporary measures before formal grid interconnection could be secured. Either way, BTM optionality has opened up a new source of build and investment. How energy security is changing capital allocation As hyperscaler demand strains utilities, the US power grid has become, and will continue to be, increasingly less stable. Hyperscalers' AI training data centre locations in particular are very sensitive to power outages or fluctuations, and can even cause problems for the grid themselves (AI compute's inherent volatility can create issues for the more stable grid load). To combat these issues, data centres need grid stabilizers and backup solutions.

records.text: .100% marked the first 4-handles since 30y auctions began in 1999. Even so, the details were not uniformly bearish. A 3.79x cover remained comfortably above the year's softer sales (3.66x in March, 3.12x in April, and 2.94x in June), suggesting that the underlying demand base remained intact. The weakness was concentrated in the tail, where price discovery at untested 4% levels coincided with caution ahead of a policy meeting two weeks later. The comparison was also demanding, given July's 4.55x cover with a 4-sen tail and August's 3.86x with 21 sen. Demand therefore appears to have moderated rather than disappeared. One possible reason is that the yield level at which life insurers add super-long exposure has moved higher by roughly 40bp with each stage of this cycle; with a potential 25bp hike approaching, there may be limited incentive to add aggressively. Banks and carry-oriented investors appear more responsive to levels in the belly, while super-long real money may prefer to wait for greater stability. This distinction may help explain the current flattening. The subsequent close was also consistent with that interpretation: buying returned to super-longs after the sale, and #91 finished at 98.99—six sen above the auction average of 98.93—at a 4.06% compound yield. An investor allocated at the lowest price of 98.65 ended the session with a 34-sen gain. Overall, the first 4-handle appears to have been absorbed without prompting a broader deterioration in demand. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 03 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Clarifying the Warsh inputs Don’t call it forward guidance. Going into the Jackson Hole meeting, we had not expected much to come out of the Warsh speech, given his strong guidance to expect no guidance. In the event, Chair Warsh repeated his decision to give no guidance and also explained why he prefers not to lay out his reaction function. However, he then proceeded to lay out a list of indicators he focuses on, as well as a (shorter) list of indicators he does not deem overly relevant. While this information may not be enough to construct a fully-fledged reaction function, it certainly gives more detail where there was previously none. The inputs into Chair Warsh’s reaction function are hawkish. The market reacted to the Warsh speech largely because most of the indicators listed as important are red hot, while most of the ones listed as less relevant are much less hot. We illustrate this in Figure 1 and Figure 2. For ease of comparison, we use post-Covid z- scores, i.e., rolling three-year z-scores. As can be seen, the z-scores for the inflation components are nearly all green (as in displaying a high z-score, resulting in a hawkish bias), with the exception of core CPI, and, interestingly, PCE components > 3%, which has been sideways recently. But the emerging pattern is more constructive than a simple story of dependence on US financing. Canada is increasingly attracting global capital because specific domestic assets are becoming strategically valuable. The next test is whether announced greenfield investment converts into operating productive capacity and a broader private capital cycle. Canada Is Investment-Starved, Not Capital-Starved Canada’s capital-intensity problem predates the post-pandemic immigration boom. Investment per worker began weakening after the commodity investment cycle turned in the mid-2010s. Rapid employment growth after the pandemic subsequently amplified that weakness by expanding the workforce faster than productive investment, but it did not create the underlying investment shortfall. The international divergence is material. Canadian investment per worker remains below its mid-2010s level, while the US and several developed-market peers have continued to invest more around their workforces. The economists view that conversion from infrastructure into private capital and MFP as the key hurdle for a genuine productivity reset. That would matter disproportionately for CAD because it would change the quality of Canadian growth. CAD would become less dependent on commodity prices and more sensitive to stronger relative productivity, investment returns and capital inflows. We do not see enough evidence of that yet. Bottom Line We think the macro mix supports USD/CAD toward 1.36. The economy is moving away from the weakest phase of the post-pandemic growth model. Capital per worker should improve. Resource investment is rising. Oil export capacity is expanding. The current account should receive support from stronger resource exports. But this remains a capital-heavy Canadian recovery, not yet an MFP-led one. Trade uncertainty remains elevated. The investment pipeline is concentrated. And the oil-CAD relationship is much weaker than it was during earlier commodity cycles. That combination argues for CAD appreciation from current levels, rather than a return to the old commodity-currency regime. In our view, 1.36 captures that distinction well.

records.text: 12 Global Economic Weekly | 04 September 2026 Inflation moves higher due to energy prices We raise our inflation forecast in Q4 2026 to 3.4% (+20bps), with 2026 avg. unchanged at 3.1%. We raise inflation more meaningfully in 2027 to 2.6% (+30bps), as oil and gas prices are higher than our post-peace deal assumptions. We incorporate the announced 4% rise in the October price cap (which takes into account the VAT cut on electricity bills). Moreover, our forecast of higher gas prices in the winter is likely to imply a larger rise in January and April price cap vs. before. The change in our core inflation forecasts is more muted at 2.8% (unch.) in 2026 and 2.3% (+10bps) in 2027. Our 2028 forecast remains unchanged at 2.1% for headline and 2.1% for core with upside risks. Headline inflation is expected to pick up from here, with the peak now expected at 3.5% in Nov. vs 3.3% in Sept/Nov 2026 before. Inflation is expected to stay above 3% until Q2 2027 and reach close to target later in Q4 2027. But there are risks that the return to target sustainably is delayed, given BoE’s tolerance for above target inflation allowing it to potentially run policy a little loose. Core inflation is expected to be hover in the 2.5-3.0% range in the next few months from here and reach close to target in Q4 2027. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 13 than in earlier decades. The principal change was that the economy stopped generating meaningful productivity gains beyond those directly attributable to greater capital intensity and improvements in labor composition. Around 70% of the decline in labor-productivity growth in 1981-2000 and 2000-19 can be traced to the deterioration in MFP. The remainder was divided broadly evenly between slower capital-intensity and labor-composition contributions. Prior studies similarly found that falling MFP accounted for roughly 72% of the post-2000 slowdown. This was also the period in which Canada’s productivity performance began to diverge materially from that of the United States. Canadian business-sector productivity advanced at less than 1% annually after 2000, while US productivity continued to grow considerably faster. Canada’s productivity level, which had approached the US level in the early 1980s, had fallen to an estimated 70% of the US level by 2022. The weakness was not primarily the result of workers moving into less productive industries. Most Canadian productivity growth after 2000 continued to occur within industries, while net labor reallocation made only a small positive contribution. The challenge was therefore not simply to move workers from one sector to another. Firms and industries themselves were generating less productivity growth. Despite elevated gross and net supply, EUR covered bond spreads have remained remarkably resilient, highlighting the market's ability to absorb issuance and the benefits of a broader and more diversified investor base. Looking ahead, a supportive redemption profile and lower expected issuance should continue to underpin market technicals. That said, we remain cautious on longer maturities. The significant flattening of the covered bond spread curve has reduced compensation for extending duration, while investor demand remains heavily concentrated in the front end. As a result, we continue to favour the sub-5 year segment, where relative value and technicals remain most supportive. At the jurisdiction level, we see increasing value in Italian covered bonds relative to French peers. While French covereds have been among the strongest performers in 2026 and continue to benefit from strong liquidity and defensive characteristics, their outperformance has left valuations looking increasingly rich. Italian covereds, by contrast, continue to offer one of the largest spread pick-ups among major covered bond jurisdictions while benefiting from supportive technicals and improving sovereign fundamentals.
