records.text: M Japan Insight Morgan Stanley MUFG 59 Conclusion In the analysis in this section, we confirmed that names with higher MBO Scores have more MBO announcements in fact, and generate strong share-price performance. Meanwhile, the number of MBO announcements is limited, and it is difficult to explain excess returns for the leading names by Score using MBO events alone. MBO Score may be capturing characteristics of companies that are motivated to realize corporate value, owing to low valuations or incentives for management and major shareholders. Such companies could see share price gains, even without actually undergoing an MBO, through measures such as share buybacks and management reform. It follows that the significance of MBO investment is not only in identifying future take- private moves. What matters is selecting companies with shareholder compositions that make privatization a viable option and possess a strong incentive to improve the share price, but where that value has not yet been sufficiently priced in. MBO Score is best viewed as a signal that captures both the option to take the company private and the incentives for management or major shareholders. records.text: Conceptually, measuring the convenience yield in risk-free sovereign bonds requires controlling for interest risk. However, in the Euro area we also need to control for credit risk given the non-zero pricing of credit risk across sovereign markets. Based on Jiang, Lustig, Van Nieuwerburgh, Xiaolan (2026), we use as a measure of convenience 10y sovereign yields against swaps, corrected by the respective CDS premium to account for credit risk compensation. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 show our measure of convenience for the EMU-4 at the 10y point of the curve, both in outright terms and as a spread to Germany1. Since 2009, the convenience yield on EMU-4 government bonds has generally been low (negative) only moving broadly into positive territory in 2025. During the Euro area crisis convenience yields diverged between Germany and France on the one hand, and Southern Europe on the other. Since 2015, co-movements generally appear strong across the EMU-4 although the post-COVID period is associated with German outperformance vs peers. Since we observe market prices for credit risk through CDS for each country, we can break down sovereign spreads vs Germany into a credit risk component and a convenience spread component. This analysis suggests that while convenience spreads have at times been relatively small, they can represent a large share of the variance in spreads. records.text: a global LNG market, and provided the feedstock foundation for a renaissance in U.S. petrochemicals and manufacturing. Investors, however, experienced the opposite outcome. An industry fueled by abundant resources and cheap post-GFC capital pursued growth at all costs, destroying value even as it transformed the global energy system. As a result, markets became conditioned to view U.S. Upstream as an industry capable of delivering seemingly unlimited growth whenever prices rose. The problem is that this assumption increasingly no longer holds. The same shale resource base that delivered an unprecedented growth cycle is maturing. Inventory quality is becoming more heterogeneous, resource replacement has re-emerged as a strategic concern, and the sector's ability to rapidly deliver multi-million-barrel-per-day production growth is materially lower than it was a decade ago. In many respects, the largest change facing global energy markets is not what the U.S. will do next, but what it is unlikely to repeat: another decade of unconstrained supply growth that consistently bailed out the rest of the world. The implications are profound. A mature U.S. shale sector does not imply declining production, but it does imply greater scarcity value for future growth, higher strategic importance for secure molecules, and increasing competition for access to long-duration resources. We believe investors continue to underappreciate this shift. 3 September 2026 60 Barclays | The global energy

Historically, purchasers of clean energy products (such as solar, wind, and storage) had been eligible to receive a 30% investment tax credit (ITC) of the purchase price, as well as some "adders" , such as an additional 10% for domestically manufactured products (domestic content). However, the OBBBA tied the foreign entity of control (FEOC) requirements to the ITC. Essentially, any clean energy product made substantially of products from China or China-related entities will not be eligible to receive the ITC or domestic content adder. This creates a 30%+ moat from just a tax credit perspective. On top of that, many tariffs have been levied against Chinese and other foreign clean energy imports. In addition to the ~10% rate currently applied to all Chinese imports through Section 301, there are numerous more specific taxes that apply to the clean tech space. records.text: M BluePaper 56 Mobilizing Canada's Balance Sheet Canada’s investment problem is not primarily a shortage of financial capacity. Business investment per worker has weakened for much of the past decade despite deep pools of pension and institutional capital. The more binding constraint is project economics: whether domestic opportunities offer sufficiently attractive risk-adjusted returns to compete for capital against a global opportunity set. The policy regime is increasingly targeting that constraint. Faster capital-cost deductions raise after-tax returns; permitting reform reduces the cost of delay; guarantees and co-investment can reallocate specific risks; and enabling infrastructure raises returns to complementary private capital. The objective is not for government to finance the investment cycle, but to improve project economics enough to crowd in substantially more private investment. Execution is now the key test. The Major Projects Office matters less for the headline value of projects referred than for whether approvals become faster and more predictable, projects reach final investment decision and construction, and private capex broadens beyond the initial infrastructure build. Canada’s public balance sheet is most valuable when used at the margin to remove binding constraints rather than substitute for commercially viable private capital. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 73 Exhibit 114: ~85% of Canada's oil production is in Alberta, which has long transport distances to get to market. As a result, Western Canadian Select (WCS) crude tends to trade at a large discount to other global price benchmarks like WTI (West Texas Intermediate). Source: RBN Energy. Pipeline capacity has historically been a key constraint on growth. Over 80% of Canadian oil production and 97% of reserves are in Alberta. Much of this is tied to the oil sands, which produce bitumen (heavy oil). While there is some local refining capacity, most of this oil is either upgraded to a lighter crude or blended with condensate for pipeline transportation to other regions. Since Canadian oil production far exceeds domestic refinery demand, the sector is structurally export-oriented. Pipeline capacity to move this oil to demand centers has been a key limiter of growth over the past decade. In 2024, the Trans Mountain pipeline improved the egress situation and opened a new end market — the Pacific Coast. With more pipe expansions on the horizon, Western Canada is well positioned for further growth.

And they also suggest a lower vote share for the federal governing parties CDU and SPD compared with the previous state elections. In our deep dive published this week (here), we discuss potential implications. There are three potential debates, raised by the press - a change in SPD party leadership (here), a replacement of Chancellor Friedrich Merz (here) or a coalition break-up (here). Our bottom line, though, is that there are likely limited near-term economic and policy risks and a coalition break-up remains a tail risk in our view. This overview leads to an evident conclusion: European macro in the next months will be characterized by a lot of idiosyncratic uncertainty at the level of Member States. Even successful conversion, however, will not produce an immediate improvement in every macro indicator. The early stages of a capital build are resource intensive, while much of the resulting output arrives only after projects become operational. Canada also imports a significant share of sophisticated machinery, electrical equipment and technology capital, meaning stronger domestic investment can initially raise imports and weaken the contribution from net trade. Large infrastructure projects can similarly absorb labor and intermediate inputs during construction without immediately increasing the flow of output from the completed asset. The likely sequence is therefore FID → construction → capital-goods imports → installed capital → utilization → productivity. This creates an investment J-curve that will be important when interpreting Canadian data over the next several years. A widening trade deficit driven by imported capital equipment is fundamentally different from one caused by weak exports or stronger consumption imports; similarly, soft measured productivity during a period of intensive construction need not signal that the investment thesis is failing. records.text: ve of the source. Since the days of the first oil well drilled in the late 1800s, the services industry has been an integral part of the energy complex. Whether in exploration, evaluation, drilling, completing or producing, energy services plays a critical role in the lifecycle of the oil well. It provides the technology to interpret the subsurface, locate the hydrocarbons, and plan the wells for maximum recovery; the drilling tools to efficiently and effectively reach the target; the completion techniques to maximize flow; and equipment needed to control pressure and optimize production rates. Furthermore, the industry provides the assets needed to facilitate the activity – the offshore and onshore rigs, vessels, workover equipment, and testing facilities. In other words, oil cannot be produced without a fully capable, technically forward, and robust global Energy Services industry. But it’s more than just oil, Energy Services encompasses all energy sources. This is a sector that has proven to have a transferrable set of skills well beyond the oil markets. Natural gas markets are directly related as much of the equipment, technology, and infrastructure in oil is also needed for natural gas production. However, one major difference is the transportation of natural gas, which requires pipelines to move regionally in a gaseous form or must be liquefied in a complex process to be exported as LNG, supported by equipment from service companies. MFP can generate a level or a growth effect. A one-time improvement in A — for example, the removal of an internal trade barrier — raises the amount of output that can be generated from the existing capital and labor stock. Potential growth rises while the economy moves to the more efficient level of production. Once that adjustment has occurred, growth returns toward its earlier rate, leaving a permanently higher level of potential output. A sustained increase in the growth rate of A is different. If TFP continues to grow more quickly each year, potential- output growth also remains persistently higher. The gap between the new path and the old path widens over time rather than stabilizing at a fixed level. AI illustrates the point particularly well. The Bank of Canada assumes that AI contributes about 0.2 percentage points annually to TFP for 10 years, producing a cumulative TFP-level gain of approximately 2%. If that contribution ends once diffusion matures, growth returns toward baseline after 10 years while the 2% level gain remains. If AI capabilities and adoption continue advancing, the growth contribution can persist for longer. The distinction can be illustrated using the capital-intensity benchmarks discussed above. Over the summer, global pressures have broadened from the front-end and question marks about the Fed reaction function, to the long-end, where renewed concerns over fiscal excess and AI issuance have prompted a sell-off in US duration. We think that the fiscal drivers of higher US term premia will remain persistent, so this should put a floor under how much and how broadly EM local rates could further compress, especially given tight spreads. AI services as an 'energy export' In a manufacturing-dominated world, cheap labour has typically been a crucial factor in the allocation of production, but as value creation shifts towards digital and AI-enabled services, it becomes less important, while energy abundance becomes more important. The electricity required to power data centres means that energy-rich regions may increasingly export computing capacity and AI services in much the same way that manufacturing exporters effectively exported cheap labour in previous decades. Trends for the next ten years • Energy abundance will gain importance as a determinant of economic activity and international trade, while abundant cheap labour becomes less significant. • Electricity generation is key, which widens the energy sources to renewable (wind, solar, geothermal, etc.) and brings a refocus on nuclear. This redraws the global map of where power can be generated cheaply. • Electrification and renewable energy shifts vulnerabilities ‘upstream’ (grid infrastructure, green tech access), while also creating new downstream dependencies for critical minerals, which have a different geography than the traditional fossil fuel dependence. This requires large investments, favouring regions that are capital rich and have abundance of potential energy sources (eg, US, China). records.text: strial production Japan's industrial production index rose 0.1%m/m in July, outperforming both our forecast (-1.0%) and the market consensus (-0.7%). This marked the fourth consecutive monthly increase and lifted production to its highest level since December 2023. Growth was broad-based across industries, with machinery production making the largest contribution. Output in the production machinery sector increased 5.1%, supported by robust demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Production of semiconductor equipment rose 11%m/m and 45%y/y, highlighting the continued strength of AI-related investment demand. We also confirmed some strong items relating defense, power related and logistic related sectors (Figure 8). The outlook for August production also remains favourable. After adjusting for typical optimism bias by the METI, production appears on track to increase by around 3.1%. This suggests that the impact of the July 28 Kumamoto earthquake may prove limited. But it is happening inside a system where total energy demand continues to grow, where fossil fuel infrastructure is ageing and underinvested, where geopolitical risk demands redundancy, and where entirely new sources of demand (AI, data centres, electrification) are adding load faster than the grid can absorb it. The net result is that investment is required across resources and infrastructure – traditional and renewable, upstream and downstream, generation and transmission – to maintain a secure, affordable, and resilient energy system. The capital requirements are larger, more diverse, and more sustained than the market is currently pricing. Crucially, the BoJ's adjustments are limited to large-scale institutional changes, such as the "provision of free education." The unadjusted inflation rate for public services has lately been running at around zero. For the past two months, we have been flagging upside risks to our $2.1 trillion forecast for 2026 full-year USD IG gross issuance. While the pace of issuance was clearly robust during 1H2026, we were previously reluctant to raise our forecast ahead of the potential for a seasonal summer lull. That said, with the summer slowdown proving elusive— driven in large part by AI-related supply—and market participants expecting a very busy September, we have decided to raise our full-year gross issuance forecast to $2.3 trillion and also raise our net supply forecast to $1.0 trillion (from $850 billion). The pair rose above 160 early in the week as the USD strengthened following Fed Chair Warsh’s hawkish Jackson Hole speech late last week, but fell from the 160s to the 158s on 2 September and then from the 158s to the 155s on 3 September, its strongest yen level since the intervention at end-July. As for the drivers of JPY appreciation, first, GPIF disclosed on 31 August that its Board of Governors had taken up the “Discussions by the Benchmark Portfolio Review and Related Matters Project Team” at its 21 August meeting. This fueled expectations that GPIF would shift back toward domestic assets, prompting buying of JGBs and the JPY. records.text: M BluePaper 14 The Growth Handoff Canada’s historical growth experience therefore has two layers. The first is the long- running disappearance of MFP growth after 2000. The second is the more recent reliance on rapid labor-input expansion while capital and productivity failed to keep pace. Those two problems require different solutions. Slower labor growth can mechanically reverse some of the recent pressure on capital per hour. It cannot, by itself, restore a durable MFP contribution or raise Canada’s long-run growth rate. The next phase of Canadian growth will consequently look very different from the last. Population and labor-force growth are slowing sharply, and the contribution from hours will be much smaller. A larger share of output growth must come from capital deepening and productivity. The key question is not whether measured productivity will improve. Some rebound is likely as the recent labor-supply surge fades. The more important question is whether that rebound represents a passive reversal of capital dilution or the start of a genuine investment and productivity cycle. USMCA: The Unspoken Risk The principal near-term risk to the productivity-and-investment-driven transition at the center of this Blue Paper is trade. Canada’s existing growth model remains exposed to the US; at the same time, preferential trade access has become less predictable. records.text: ECB Preview—Another Hike Without Guidance The incoming data in recent months have been broadly in line with the ECB staff’s June projections. Growth has again been firmer than expected. GDP surprised to the upside in Q2, printing at around 0.30%qoq (non-annualised) excluding Ireland (Exhibit 1, left). The activity data for Q3 has so far been more mixed as soft data continued to recover from Q2 lows, but hard data showed some sign of softening in July, most notably in Germany (Exhibit 1, right). Our nowcast model currently points to ex-Ireland growth of 0.19% for Q3. Several ECB officials acknowledged the economy’s recent resilience, and both Executive Board member Schnabel and Bank of Ireland Governor Makhlouf hinted at a small upgrade in the projections for growth. We therefore look for the staff to lift Q3 by 0.1pp to 0.3%, which will likely raise the annual averages by 0.1pp each to 0.9% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027 (Exhibit 2). We look for the 2028 figure to remain unchanged at 1.5%, although we see a low bar for it to fall back to 1.4%. records.text: M BluePaper 8 Where Could We Be Wrong? The principal risks are timing and breadth rather than the direction of the initial productivity rebound. Canada can build a larger economy without creating a permanently faster-growing one. • The productivity rebound may remain predominantly arithmetic. Capital per worker could improve because labor growth slows, while private investment remains weak and potential growth stays close to 1.5%. • The infrastructure and resource pipeline may not convert into operating capital on schedule. Permitting delays, construction constraints, cost overruns, and shortages of skilled trades could extend the time between announcements and productive capacity. • The build may remain concentrated in public, regulated, and structures-heavy investment. Canada could add power, transport, and resource capacity without generating sufficient private crowd-in, machinery investment or multifactor- productivity gains in the swing sectors. • Persistent US trade uncertainty could keep hurdle rates elevated and delay the investment response. USMCA preserves valuable access, but a more discretionary and sector-specific trade regime could weaken the durability of that advantage.

records.text: red repo has been an important balance sheet relief mechanism in the past, especially around regulatory snapshot dates, as it allows banks to net down the balance sheet impact of offsetting repo transactions. But running repo through sponsored clearing is not costless, as dealers must bear the associated margin costs. If banks have the leverage capacity to run uncleared activity, it is likely the lower-cost option. That means activity is migrating out of the cleared space not only from a reduction in financing demand but also because of the expanded balance sheet capacity itself. This also suggests an unintended benefit of the scaled-up buyback program, with an effect similar to Treasury potentially investing its excess cash in the repo market. By tempering any sell-off at the long end, Treasury is providing support for spreads. The decline in leverage demand pushes in the same direction, with softer, smoother funding, supporting swap spreads from the funding leg. Together, Treasury should view these as helping reduce its issuance costs. Indeed, swap spreads have benefited from increased leverage capacity in the banking system and a benign funding environment this year. Second-half performance has been notably stronger this year, despite heavy corporate issuance and selling pressure in long-end rates. A TFP contribution of around 0.45 percentage points would be close to the 1981-2000 regime and well below the early postwar contribution. The implication is important: Canada does not need to recreate the 1960s productivity economy to reach 2% growth. But it does need capital deepening near the high end of its historical range and a return to positive MFP growth broadly comparable with the late-20th-century regime. Canada's next acceleration does not depend on an unprecedented investment boom or an implausibly large AI dividend in isolation. Instead, it requires the capital and productivity cycles to become mutually reinforcing. The three routes are accounting illustrations, but K and A are not independent in practice. Canada has a window in which slower population growth can help rebuild capital per worker before labor supply becomes more supportive again. In the 2030s, a still- expanding working-age population and strong human-capital base reinforces those gains through both hours worked and labor composition. Our thesis should become increasingly visible in the composition of growth: financial capital moving into productive assets, infrastructure attracting private investment, and efficiency gains broadening beyond the current technology leaders. The Conversion-Gap Framework Our analysis combines historical growth accounting with proprietary sector-level work. It includes 11 industries accounting for approximately 73% of total-economy gross value added. We use historical capital-intensity contributions, historical and recent MFP, 2026 capex intentions, construction versus machinery-and-equipment spending, sector economic weights, and current AI adoption. We isolate the sectors that determine whether the productivity improvement broadens. 1. How concerned should we be about the decline in the labor force participation n rate this year? Most of the increase in the number of people not in the labor force since January reflects college graduates over the age of 55 retiring from work. While it appears that some of the decline in the labor force participation rate this year is genuine, the fact that it mainly reflects retirement of older, higher-income workers who are potentially well-positioned to do so rather than an increase in discouraged or other marginally attached workers makes the decline somewhat less concerning from a cyclical perspective. records.text: M BluePaper 92 Why Build in Canada? Canada offers many advantages for building data centers — it has plenty of land, water, and clean baseload power (nuclear and hydro). These are essentially the trifecta of natural resources required for a data center, particularly AI training facilities. For inference and colocation, geography matters more too: Latency requirements and network connectivity help dictate site selection. A favorable policy landscape also helps, as discussed in the section Could US Opposition to Data Centers & Sovereign AI Drive Projects North? That said, public opposition to data centers is high in Canada: A recent survey from May found that 68% of Canadians would oppose a large AI data center within a few blocks of where they live, vs. 15% in support. The political backdrop will be important in determining Canada's role in the global data center build. Financing Data Centers Fixed income markets are playing an active role in financing the data center build — and perhaps to an even greater extent than we initially anticipated. While the large hyperscalers do rely on cash from their incumbent businesses to help build & fill their AI data centers, they are increasingly leveraging debt markets in progressively intricate and creative ways to meet their capital needs. Moreover, many other sub-industries rely on debt to complete their role in the AI build, whether it be data center developers issuing ABS to finance their growth or neoclouds issuing chip-backed loans

records.text: Note: the estimates are in terms of the percentage point annual contribution. Why the 2% case is not simply an infrastructure scenario. The capital-build scenario can succeed without producing a broad productivity reset. New utility and transport capacity can raise the level of potential output, improve resilience and support strategic projects. Resource investment can raise exports, profits, fiscal revenue and national income. But Canada's historical experience shows that large capital accumulation in network and resource sectors does not automatically produce positive MFP. From 2000 to 2019, capital intensity was a strong positive contributor in mining, utilities, and transportation, while MFP was negative across all three. The larger macro payoff arises when capital generates effects outside the industry in which it is installed. Power and transport capacity → lower constraints → private investment → scale and technology diffusion → MFP. This is also why trade access is not a separate additive growth contribution. Market access affects the expected return on capital, scale, technology transfer and the allocation of resources. Canada's existing industrial structure remains concentrated in resources and lower-complexity manufacturing, with less capacity in machinery, electronics, and AI-linked production. A benign trade outcome removes a headwind, but stronger capital formation and productive capacity are still required to capture the fastest-growing areas of external demand

Such resilient spreads have supported year-to-date total returns, and have more than offset the negative impact of higher US rates, although these have dragged returns down towards ~1.5% (Exhibit 29). In that sense, the remarkable resilience of spreads so far this year has carried over to total returns. The flip side of the negative impact of higher US rates on returns is that they have supported EM all-in yield levels, like in the US corporate credit space, and those currently stand at attractive levels compared with their-long term history (Exhibit 30). In a resilient US growth environment with lower rates volatility, carry levels are an important dimension of relative performance and their high levels combined with defensive spreads are therefore likely to act as a tailwind for the asset class. More selective in IG, high carry in HY. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Capital Flow Tightening Weighs on Sentiment and Allocation Government capital flow recalibration YTD targeting capital/ wealth flows adds to near-term investor concerns Since March, Chinese authorities have issued a sequence of measures tightening oversight of both listing structures and outbound/offshore wealth flows. For a period of time the market had been debating whether these measures were separate policy tracks (listing governance, unlicensed brokerage enforcement, ODI/national-security review, and tax- enforcement catch-up) rather than a single coordinated capital-control campaign. However, regardless of the individual triggers of these specific measures, their overall direction had gradually led the market to have perceived tham as linked them together. records.text: M BluePaper 80 With respect to natural gas, persistent oversupply has caused Western Canadian (AECO) natural gas prices to trade at stubbornly weak levels. Low producer break-even economics, long resource inventory, and a fragmented upstream industry in the Montney and Duvernay basins have all contributed to supply imbalances. Additionally, Canada’s structural condensate deficit presents another challenge: increasing NGL-rich regional production to supply condensate for oil sands blending also generates associated dry gas, Given that traditional domestic demand growth (residential, commercial, and industrial consumption) is likely to be relatively modest, new LNG export capacity and/or gas-fired power demand associated with data centers are likely necessary to drive higher AECO prices. Beyond 2026, LNG developments remain the primary mechanism for structurally tightening Western Canadian gas fundamentals. Woodfibre LNG is expected in 2027 and Cedar LNG in late 2028, together adding nearly 800 MMcf/d of export capacity. Including LNG Canada Phase 1, Canadian LNG export capacity could reach approximately 2.5 Bcf/d by 2030. Further tightening would depend on LNG Canada Phase 2 and Ksi Lisims reaching FID. Rystad views LNG Canada Phase 2 as technically more advantaged because it is a brownfield development backed by Shell and existing partners, but a weakening global LNG outlook and SHEL’s cautious stance toward additional LNG exposure could delay FID until around 2030. Labor Expansion and a Widening Productivity Shortfall The post-pandemic period added a second, more recent problem to the long-standing MFP weakness. Between 4Q19 and 4Q25, business-sector output grew by approximately 1.6% annually. Total hours rose by 1.3%, while output per hour increased by only 0.3%. Put differently, additional hours accounted for more than 80% of business-sector output growth over this period. That compares with approximately 54% in 2000-19 and around 42-44% in the two earlier historical periods. The official annual decomposition through 2023 tells a similar story from the productivity side. labor productivity increased by approximately 0.3% annually between 2019 and 2023. Positive contributions of roughly 0.3pp each from capital intensity and labor composition were almost exactly offset by a 0.3pp decline in MFP. These figures should be interpreted cautiously. Pandemic closures initially removed many lower-productivity jobs, producing a temporary spike in measured productivity. The return of those workers subsequently reversed much of that increase. Short recent windows therefore contain large cyclical and compositional effects and are less comparable with the cyclically neutral historical periods. Nevertheless, the direction is clear. At the same time, Europe is seeking to expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity through a combination of public funding and private investment. The 2023 European Chips Act and related national initiatives aim to strengthen supply-chain resilience and reduce reliance on overseas manufacturing. However, Europe's limited presence in leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing means the objective of raising its share of global production to 20% by 2030 appears challenging. Artificial intelligence provides an additional structural tailwind. The capital-deepening contribution rises to 1.25pp. That is near the upper end of Canada’s historical experience, but not unprecedented (capital intensity contributed approximately 1.3pp in 1961-81). MFP rises to 0.45pp. This is close to the contribution recorded in 1981- 2000 and well below the early postwar rate. The scenario therefore does not require Canada to recreate the 1960s productivity regime. It requires a combination of capital formation near the high end of the historical range and a return to sustained positive MFP growth. The additional 0.25pp MFP contribution is a broad-conversion assumption rather than a mean-reversion estimate. We assign approximately 0.20pp to wider gains across construction, transportation, manufacturing, and wholesale, and a further 0.05pp to deeper AI diffusion, scale, competition, and improved resource allocation elsewhere in the economy. The magnitude is comparable with the Bank of Canada’s AI upside scenario, but AI is one mechanism within this scenario rather than a separate additive contribution.

Cox Mexico's $2bn dual-tranche issuance for Iberdrola Mexico's 2.6 GW platform further evidences capital flowing toward firm power assets. BoE call unch.: on hold in 2026, near-term risks for a hike We keep our BoE call unchanged, expecting rates to remain on hold through 2026, followed by a 25bp cut in November 2027 to 3.5%. But the move higher in our inflation forecasts due to higher energy prices implies that it remains a close call. So far there has been limited signs of second round effects and passthrough of the energy shock to domestic inflation has been muted, amid a soft labour market. At the same time, the majority of the Committee remains dovish with no rush to act. But the balance of risks still leans towards a hike if evidence of strong second round effects emerges, the risks of which are larger the more prolonged or worse the energy inflation shock is. We think bar for a Sept. hike is very high, but Nov., Dec. and Feb. are live meetings. Speed of adoption vs. labor-market adjustment: a) Transition hinges on speed mismatch: outcomes depend on whether AI diffusion outpaces the labor market’s ability to retrain and rematch workers. b) Fast adoption = transition shock: front-loaded displacement and skill mismatch drive unemployment, disinflation risk, and recession-like dynamics despite similar long-run gains 2. Labor displacement vs. new task creation a) Job impact depends on the balance: AI displaces some tasks but also creates new AI-complementary roles that drive vacancies and labor demand. b) If creation lags displacement: unemployment stays elevated and demand leaks; if it keeps pace, absorption is faster and the transition is smoother. 3. Income loss vs. policy support and indirect feedback effects a) Outcomes depend on buffers: labor income losses vs policy support, wealth effects, and new task creation determine whether AI triggers demand shortfalls or a stable transition. b) With full feedback loops: policy, income gains, and task creation absorb shocks—making unemployment smaller, shorter-lived, and more manageable.

Canada’s 1.5% baseline is already productivity-led, but most of the improvement comes from capital deepening and normalization. Moving toward 2% requires the productivity rebound to broaden from a recovery in capital per worker into sustained active investment and MFP growth. What Would It Take to Reach 2%? The medium-term baseline leaves Canada with potential growth of around 1.5%. The next question is whether that speed limit can move closer to 2%. More important, what kind of growth model would generate the additional 50 basis points? As labor input already contributes very little in the baseline, and the assumed productivity recovery is itself relatively optimistic, this is not a small hurdle. Moving from 1.5% to 2% requires either capital deepening to rise well above its recent and post-2000 rates, MFP to shift into a materially stronger regime, or both. We hold trend labor input and labor composition broadly unchanged in the central exercise. Demographic policy could generate upside to labor supply, while better integration of newcomers could raise labor quality. records.text: day). How energy security is affecting volatility The volatility in both energy security and energy prices is a net positive for the clean technology sector in the US. For commercial and industrial users (including hyperscalers), a lack of trust in the grid's ability to maintain energy creates the need for redundancy, which means additional purchases of our coverage's products. This comes in the form of extra storage and backup units, or perhaps onsite generation to supplement the grid, even if interconnection is secured. Notably, more volatile (and generally higher) energy prices are generally a positive for names in our residential solar space (RUN, SEDG, ENPH), as elevated utility rates and energy bills mean the value proposition of a home solar system increases (and the payback period shortens for consumers). Critically, the increase in utility rates is happening in conjunction with the coming loss of residential solar tax credits, cut short by the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Falling home battery prices and elevated and volatile utility rates will continue to make residential solar an attractive solution. Winners and losers in a fragmented energy world The US has been applying both the "carrot" (tax credits for domestically manufactured clean energy products) and the "stick" (tariffs or outright bans of foreign made competition) in the clean tech sector for some time now, but it has ratcheted up the level in recent years, 3 September 2026 85 Barclay

records.text: rs and industry is therefore not simply replacing one energy source with another. Rather, it is ensuring that sufficient energy is available across multiple sources to meet growing demand while maintaining security of supply and supporting economic growth. This creates an increasingly important role for integrated energy companies. The sector provides oil, gas, LNG, refining, trading and increasingly power solutions. These capabilities position it at the centre of the themes that we believe will shape the next decade: energy security, energy addition, AI-driven electricity demand and the need for large-scale capital deployment. Why our sector matters We expect global energy demand to continue rising through the next decade despite improvements in efficiency and increasing deployment of renewable technologies because of GDP growth, populations getting wealthier, and improving living standards. BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH A compounding problem In addition to higher refinancing costs on the horizon, a more fundamental concern is the feedback loop between interest rates and debt. Ultimately, debt sustainability depends not only on the level of interest rates, but also on how those rates compare with nominal GDP growth. When nominal growth exceed borrowing costs, debt-to-GDP ratios can stabilize over time. However, as the gap between interest rates and nominal growth narrows, higher debt levels become increasingly difficult to sustain. The risk is that the self-reinforcing dynamic between interest costs and deficits can further narrow that gap over time. Meanwhile, there is a feedback loop between higher interest costs and deficits that we must account for. Higher interest costs increase deficits and Treasury borrowing needs. Increased Treasury issuance can put upward pressure on term premiums as investors demand greater compensation to absorb a larger supply of duration. Following this week's developments, an October delay now appears unlikely. Larger-than-expected budget request, but fiscal discipline likely to prevail The FY2027 budget request came in at ¥143tn this week. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 91 Financing AI & Data Centers: Canadian Markets Carolyn Campbell The Canadian Data Center Build The Canadian data center market is today far smaller than in the US, but new capacity additions over the next few years could see it grow by multiple times over. Estimates from S&P 451 Research put the current Canadian data center capacity at 1.8GW, with the majority concentrated in Quebec (585MW) and Ontario (472MW). By comparison, estimates for US data center capacity stand around 55GW, with nearly 9GW in Northern Virginia alone and 7GW in Texas. Over the next several years, many more GW will likely come online, with Alberta a strong leader in new builds. S&P estimates that 2.5GW are planned or under construction, with 1.9GW of those in Alberta (note that S&P tends to have more conservative estimates of planned capacity than some other resources, due to its bottom-up build of assets). Other estimates place proposed capacity much higher: Recent research from York University (and cited here by CBC) projects over 13GW of planned or proposed capacity in Canada, with over 90% of those builds going to Alberta. (Other estimates put the planned capacity even higher, up to 20GW. Like in the US, it is possible that many proposed plans will not come to fruition, with bidders filling queues without concrete plans.) Passive Normalization or Active Capital Deepening? We distinguish between two forms of capital deepening. Passive capital deepening occurs when hours growth falls faster than capital growth. Capital per hour rises, but the economy is not necessarily undertaking more investment. This raises measured productivity while leaving aggregate potential growth relatively subdued. Active capital deepening occurs when the productive capital stock itself accelerates. Firms and governments add machinery, equipment, software, intellectual property, infrastructure, and other productive assets quickly enough to raise capital per worker, even while labor input stabilizes or expands. The Bank’s baseline contains elements of both. Slower population growth produces passive capital deepening, while stronger projected business and government investment provides an active component. The open question is which channel will dominate. The current investment evidence remains mixed. Machinery and equipment — the category most directly associated with productive capital deepening — has remained soft. Business fixed investment weakened after trade-policy uncertainty intensified, while recent strength in aggregate investment has been disproportionately government-led and concentrated in a relatively narrow set of categories. Page 5 Rates Strategy: What a September Hike changes for JGBs A September hike is a curve story, not a level story The bottom line is that a September hike is a curve story, not a level story. The timing of the move is already priced in, as the swap market has fully digested a September hike since the G20 statement, leaving the front end with little further to travel. The live risk, therefore, is not the timing but the terminal rate; if the BoJ signals a faster pace, the market will reprice a higher end-point, leading to a bear-flattening move concentrated in the belly of the curve (+15–25bp in 2y/5y) rather than a parallel shift. This flattening dynamic is reinforced by a firmer yen, which compresses the imported-inflation premium and acts as an anchor on the long end. Consequently, our trade book focuses on the curve: the 5s20s flattener remains the core position, and the 1y1y vs 3y1y steepener is retained to reflect the pace of future hikes. We are withdrawing the September-October forward receive, as its premise is no longer valid, and taking off the standalone 1y1y receive which has hit its stop. The front end already priced September; the terminal rate is what is unpriced The swap curve moved before the house did. This has resulted in a smaller and more episodic CMBS market, but has also reinforced conservative underwriting, stronger lender- borrower relationships, and historically stronger credit performance. Canadian Securitized CRE Market Despite the size of Canada’s commercial mortgage market, securitization has historically played a more limited funding role. According to Intellifi’s 2023 Canadian Commercial Mortgage Survey, the Canadian commercial mortgage market totaled approximately C$449 billion, while nonagency CMBS represented only ~1% of outstanding commercial mortgage debt as of 2022. Despite the size of the underlying CRE debt market, cumulative Canadian CMBS issuance has totaled only C$37.8 billion since the market emerged in the late 1990s, as we noted in our publication titled A Primer on the Canadian CMBS Market from last November. Historical issuance has been concentrated across a handful of major property types, led by retail at C$12.3 billion (32.4%), office at C $7.6 billion (20.0%), and industrial at C$7.3 billion (19.4%), which together account for more than 70% of issuance. Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech gave a hawkish jolt to Fed expectations. Michael Gapen characterized it as "decidedly hawkish" and acknowledged that a September hike is "a very close call." Warsh stated plainly that "progress over the past two years has been modest," that "broad financial conditions" are not restrictive, and that "we have work to do" on inflation — resolving prior ambiguity by confirming the policy rate, not the balance sheet, as the primary tightening tool. Markets responded by pricing a 58% probability of a 25bp September hike and roughly 44bp of total hikes by year-end. Morgan Stanley's base case remains the Fed being on hold — contingent on a benign August CPI print driving core PCE lower.. However, the team is explicit that the hawkish signal from Warsh keeps a hike scenario live. Even if the Fed ultimately holds, the persistent ambiguity around its reaction function is likely to keep rate volatility elevated and market sentiment cautious and choppy heading into the September FOMC and beyond. records.text: European Rates Weekly 03 September 2026 Citi Research 3 Insurance hikes might make a comeback. Energy prices will of course remain volatile. Indeed, some of the increase in European natural gas prices could be speculative or short-term hedging activity. Prices may fall back if Asian demand weakens and allows Europe to rebuild its (currently low) storage levels. Moreover, there are still no clear signs of second round effects. Given this, it will be interesting to hear if the ECB offers any guidance on whether any future hikes (beyond 2.5%) would still have to be ‘robust’ or could be considered as ‘insurance’ hikes. There was a snippet on this in the ECB accounts for July: “While in June the appropriate decision had been to set interest rates in a manner that was robust in all scenarios, in other instances, ‘insurance’ considerations might be more at the forefront, for example to prevent a move towards more adverse scenarios”. Bringing insurance hikes back into the near-term playbook could allow the ECB to hike pre-emptively into restrictive territory – given the risk of second round effects is greater amid wider economic resilience - while also implicitly signaling that it can be reversed should the risk subside. The ECB is unlikely to exceed 3% depo this cycle and might not stay there for long. Market pricing suggests the peak for this cycle could be 3%. records.text: Generation mix shift: Data centre growth has reshaped the utility sector's generation strategy. The need for large amounts of reliable, around-the-clock generation has strengthened the case for gas and is accelerating interest in nuclear. Gas gives utilities a relatively fast and flexible source of firm generation, while nuclear provides high capacity factor, carbon-free power that can support hyperscaler loads. At the same time, renewables remain an important part of utilities' plans, but their intermittency makes them less suited to serving data centres on a standalone basis, though they become more attractive when paired with storage. Load growth: The outlook for utility load growth has changed materially as data centres have shifted the industry from a long period of flat demand to sustained growth. We increasingly now expect 4-5% long-term load growth across the sector, although the magnitude will vary by utility and geography. Importantly, utilities are now planning significantly higher generation, transmission and distribution investments in this higher-demand environment, creating longer- duration capex opportunities. The key debate is no longer whether load will grow, but how much of the announced data centre pipeline will ultimately materialize and when. Higher financing needs: Higher load growth translates into the higher capital requirements and, therefore, greater financing needs. This creates higher equity needs to maintain balance sheet health and credit rating

Together, they form the twin pillars of Japan’s corporate governance framework. TSE market reform comprises listing-system reforms led by the Tokyo Stock Exchange. Through the April 2022 reorganization into the Prime, Standard and Growth markets, tighter continued-listing standards, and the March 2023 request for “management that is conscious of the cost of capital and stock price,” the reforms encourage listed companies to undertake ongoing analysis, disclosure, dialogue with investors, and management improvement. TOPIX reform was advanced alongside the 2022 market restructuring and forms part of the wider TSE market reform agenda. Operationally, however, the TSE oversees the equity markets and continued-listing standards, while JPX Market Innovation & Research, Inc. is responsible for index calculation and constituent- selection rules. Next-generation TOPIX decouples index membership from market segment and introduces periodic rebalancing based on liquidity and free-float market capitalization. records.text: C meeting. Data preview: Inflation to keep Sept hike on track Next week's inflation data could be the decisive factor for a September hike. We expect the report to be firm enough for the FOMC to follow through. Specifically, we forecast core CPI to rise a trend-like 0.22% m/m in August and core PCE to increase 0.24% m/m. If correct, core PCE would be running at a 2.9% annualized pace and the year-over-year rate would edge up to 3.4%, both well above levels consistent with the Fed's 2% target. In our view, that should be enough to convince Chair Warsh that underlying inflation trends have not improved sufficiently and that higher rates are warranted. Data review: Low churn, no cracks The July JOLTS report showed a slight decline in hiring. This is in line with soft summer payroll trends reflected in our Aug NFP forecast, ADP, and Revelio data. Hiring remains subdued, but job growth is still running above breakeven. Encouragingly, layoffs remain low, consistent with benign jobless claims and fewer Challenger job cut announcements. Meanwhile, the vacancies-to-unemployed ratio, a key measure of labor market slack improved in July and has stayed above 1.0 for four consecutive months. Bottom line: despite the soft summer jobs data, labor market conditions remain broadly stable. records.text: Winners and losers in a fragmented energy world Importantly, we do not view this volatility as uniformly negative for European utilities. While volatility can create challenges for energy consumers, many utilities own assets and infrastructure that become more valuable when markets tighten. We see increased volatility creating a clear divergence between companies: utilities with merchant power exposure, trading operations, storage assets and flexible generation fleets are well positioned to benefit, especially as European utilities have virtually no direct exposure to disrupted Qatari LNG volumes. US exposure provides an additional buffer against volatility. We also see a strategic benefit for European utilities with meaningful US operations, where even stronger power demand growth is being driven by electrification and data centres. European utilities with US network and generation exposure benefit from geographic diversification while participating in a market where security-of-supply concerns are already translating into higher investment, capacity additions and earnings growth. In our view, US exposure allows utilities to participate in a more advanced version of the same security-driven investment cycle emerging in Europe, reducing reliance on any single regulatory or commodity market. A mine that remains an isolated export enclave can be economically and strategically valuable without materially raising economy-wide MFP. Manufacturing also has positive MFP shortfall, although recent MFP was only slightly negative. AI adoption, at 13.1% of businesses, remains below the national average and well below the leading service sectors. These interventions matter most when a relatively small change in project economics crowds in substantially more private productive investment than the public sector itself commits. The next test is execution. Announced projects and government commitments are leading indicators, not realized capital formation. The evidence becomes more convincing as projects move through approval and final investment decision into construction and commissioning, and as private investment broadens from infrastructure and resources into machinery, software, intellectual property, and other productivity-enhancing assets. Our base case is that project execution and investment strengthen through the second half of the decade. That timing aligns with the demographic adjustment discussed previously: slower labor growth reduces the capital accumulation required simply to stabilize capital per worker. Stronger investment during that window would allow financial balance-sheet capacity to translate more directly into productive capital deepening. A benign USMCA outcome lowers uncertainty and prevents further capital scrapping or reallocation losses. It can support private investment, scale and technology transfer. But preserving market access does not solve Canada’s product-composition and productive- capacity problems. We have previously written about how Canada remains underrepresented in machinery, electronics, and AI-linked production, while its industrial capital stock remains concentrated in resources and legacy manufacturing. Greater certainty around trade policy therefore raises the probability that the economy moves beyond the arithmetic-rebound scenario. It does not, on its own, produce the broad-reset scenario. The same applies to interprovincial integration. Reducing internal barriers can raise the level of MFP through scale, specialization and better allocation. The growth effect persists only if the larger effective market generates continuing investment, innovation and firm entry. Data center-backed bonds have been favored by insurance portfolios and other yield buyers with long-duration needs (such as pension funds) given the spread pickup and duration of the deals. This could certainly be another advantage for Canada, then: Capital within the Canadian pension system stands just shy of $4 trillion while insurance companies hold another $3 trillion in assets. However, the market depth is not comparable to the US, where the bulk of the financing is taking place and where, even though the market has sold off to digest the quantum of financing, deals are still getting done with reasonable covers. In smaller markets, such as Europe, secured bond deals have been far rarer, and indeed some appear to have struggled given tepid demand, and unsecured issuance has been more one-off than programmatic. Corporate tech issuance in Canada to date has been infrequent, even if impressive in its size. The oil shock fades, while stronger confidence and wealth support consumption and business investment. Demand accelerates GDP growth to 2.9% in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027, with unemployment falling to 3.5% by the end of next year. Stronger demand keeps inflation elevated, with headline inflation reaching 3.7% in 2026 before easing in 2027. The Fed waits to confirm growth is demand-driven, then begins hiking in 4Q26, raising rates by 100bp to 4.50-4.75%. Scenario 2: AI productivity boost with labor displacement (10%). AI has boosted productivity without major labor market disruption so far, but broader adoption could lead to greater layoffs. In this scenario, firms maintain output growth while reducing headcount, pushing unemployment to 4.5% in 2026 and 4.8% in 2027. Weaker employment weighs on consumption, investment, and hiring. The Fed begins cutting rates in early 2027, delivering three cuts to bring the funds rate to 2.875%. Scenario 3: Permanent oil premium (20%). Oil prices stay above $100 through 2027, weighing on consumption while AI-related investment remains strong. GDP growth slows modestly versus the base case, while unemployment holds near 4.2-4.3%.

records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 27 Which Countries Are Most at Risk in Europe Due to Low Storage Levels? Major European gas storage holders diverged in their approach to filling inventories over the summer, and consequently are in different positions heading into winter. Italy has offered financial incentives to inject in Spring 2026, compensating storage bookers for the lack of seasonal storage spread. As a result, uptake on Italian storage capacity was in-line with usual levels and the country now has the highest inventory levels of the big four storage holders in the EU (~80% currently). The Italian government took similar action in 2025, which also helped boost Italian storage last year and prevented Italy from exiting last winter with low inventory levels. At the other end of the spectrum there is the Netherlands. The Netherlands started summer with inventories only ~5% full, due to plans to close two storage sites ahead of the coming winter that resulted in full storage drawdowns. These closures were scrapped in February, leaving a sizeable inventory refill job for summer to bring the empty sites in- line with the Dutch storage targets. To aid in the refill process, state-owned EBN was given financing to ensure pre-winter storage of up to 80 TWh out of total storage of ~115 TWh by 1st November, if market fill is not sufficient. Last summer, EBN only had financing to cover 25 TWh, which contributed to storage falling short of the 80% national target. Consistent

The 1Q26 GDP contraction is what affects our 2026 forecasts the most, 2Q growth is actually in line with our expectations again after the revision to zero. But retail prices are a function of spot, so consumers will get squeezed into September and October. And real yields have risen more in France than on average, too. Focus is now going to shift to 2027 budget negotiations. We stick to our 5.3% and 5.5% deficit projections for this year and next. The risk balance for 2026 is no longer biased to a smaller deficit. Uncertainty over 2027 dynamics is large. We work under the assumption that the government manages to present (and push through) a budget plan with sufficient corrective action to keep the planned deficit unchanged vs 2026 (that would likely require c 60bp of measures). Cyclical weakness is then what drives the widening in our forecast. Post-election policy choices are the big unknown at this stage. September maintenance over the last 5 years has averaged ~110 mcm/d, cutting flows to Europe and the UK by roughly a third during the month. Maintenance levels this September are scheduled to be significantly lower than the last few years, cutting flows by only ~70 mcm/d. We assume realised outages to the EU + UK will be ~90 mcm/d this September, as usually outage levels will be revised upwards through the month as unplanned or extended maintenance works occur. For example, in September 2025 the forecast was 77 mcm/d on Aug 18th, revised up to 92 mcm/d by Sept 4th and realised outages of 105 mcm/ d. If September outages do materialise in line with 2025 levels, that would take our September inventory injection forecast from 5.1 bcm to 4.5 bcm. The existing project portfolio explicitly contains several such enabling assets. The clearest evidence of regime change would therefore be a broadening in the composition of private capex. An initial rise in structures investment should eventually be followed by stronger spending on machinery and equipment, software, intellectual property, and other assets that raise productivity throughout the business sector. At the same time, new infrastructure should make additional projects commercially viable without requiring the same degree of public support. The investment cycle then becomes increasingly self-reinforcing: infrastructure relieves bottlenecks → expected private returns rise → complementary investment is crowded in → capital per worker increases → technology and organizational improvements diffuse → productivity strengthens. That progression provides a practical framework for assessing the thesis over the next several years. First, conversion: More projects should move from announcement and referral to FID and construction, ideally on shorter and more predictable timelines. Second, breadth: Investment should spread beyond megaproject structures into machinery, software and intellectual property. The corollary of subdued rate vol in FX is that longer-dated FX vols that in theory should reflect gyrations in matched maturity forwards/ NDFs have not shown much sign of life either. Our previous studies have shown that a pickup in basis between the real- ized vols of longer vs. shorter-expiry forwards is far better captured in EM than in DM, as segmented and sometimes illiquid longer tenor forwards tend to become a tad unhinged in times of increased rate vol. records.text: M Japan Insight 50 Systematic stock screening based on MBO Score To address these issues, we apply the analysis from our 2025 report to carry out a systematic stock screening. More specifically, our process is as follows. (1) We carry out the same logistic regression as in our 2025 report, but only use MBO samples announced over the 10 calendar years starting from a particular year. (2) We use the generated parameters to calculate a monthly trend score (we deem this the likelihood of MBO announcement, but note that the absolute figure holds little meaning, and should only be used for comparison between stocks) for all stocks within the universe for the following year. Below, we call this the MBO Score. However, we also allow for a one-month lag between the logistic regression and the trend score. (3) We organize stocks in the universe into quantiles based on MBO Score, and estimate future returns. (4) We repeat the above process on a rolling annual basis. By way of example, we use data for MBOs announced between January 2000 and December 2009, and carry out a logistic regression. Using the parameters obtained, we calculate an MBO Score for all stocks in the universe as of end-January 2010. We divide the stocks into quintiles based on MBO Score, and calculate share price returns for each quintile in February 2010. records.text: 4 September 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 with persistently high gas prices, they have injected only limited volumes into storage facilities during the summer months, fearing that future sales during the winter would not generate sufficient returns. In effect, this has become a waiting game. More recently, the Federal Network Agency has subtly adjusted its messaging in its daily gas supply assessments. It now explicitly emphasizes that winter preparedness and the filling of storage facilities are fundamentally the responsibility of gas traders . According to the agency, traders have contractual supply obligations to municipal utilities, energy suppliers, industrial customers and other consumers and must ensure that they are adequately hedged against supply risks. At the same time, the agency has shifted its focus away from achieving a storage level of 70% or 80% at the start of winter and towards meeting the legally stipulated target of 30% by 1 February 2027. So far, however, little has changed in practice. The current pace of injections is insufficient to bring storage levels close to 80% by early November. As a result, political pressure on Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche has built in recent weeks, with growing calls for stronger measures to accelerate the replenishment of gas storage facilities, if necessary through public support. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 03 September 2026 Citi Research 4 The Warsh Shadow Rate. One cross-check of whether the list of indicators Warsh suggested is useful—not just for Warsh but also for the overall committee—is to create the median z-score of his indicators and plot it next to Fed Funds over time. Figure 4 shows this “Warsh shadow rate. ” There are two clear lessons here. First, the current reading is close the historical highs where in the past hiking cycles typically occurred. The exception is in the aftermath of the GFC, where, interestingly, Warsh left the Fed in early 2011, partly because he was less comfortable with the continued easing the Fed leadership engaged in at the time. Second, the indicator often leads 2-year rates considerably, and more so before hiking cycles than before easing cycles. This is partly the case because it includes some market variables. Whenever those improve quickly after a crisis, it is natural that policymakers will not react to strong market indicators that mostly are the result of bouncing back from very weak levels. Weakness in the markets should have smaller lags to policymaking. This pattern may tell us that a Warsh Fed may move more quickly to tightening than past Feds, which focused less on market variables, while easing patterns may change less. Figure 3. Investors must now identify – from the limited pool of remaining stocks – those with a relatively high likelihood of conversion to a wholly owned subsidiary where such expectations have not yet been fully priced into the shares. The criteria for stock selection are based on the characteristics of companies that are to be turned into fully owned subsidiaries. We analyzed the determining factors for an unwinding of parent-subsidiary listings in our report Unlocking Japan: Corporate Governance Reform 2025 (May 16, 2025). We found that companies with low valuations, small market caps, high parent-company ownership ratios, and a significant presence of foreign investors are more likely to be converted into wholly owned subsidiaries via TOBs or exchanges of stock ( Exhibit 43 ). omplex Permitting is often discussed as a single process, but in practice it involves multiple federal, state and local reviews that can add years to project timelines. For large infrastructure projects, we estimate developers may face more than 60 permits and reviews across numerous agencies. Our analysis suggests delays are common. Across 104 energy-related projects in the federal permitting system, nearly one-third of completed milestones have been late. State and local approvals can further extend timelines, while litigation risk remains significant. Almost 30% of large energy projects have been cancelled or paused. Prior permitting reforms have under-delivered Congress has repeatedly attempted to streamline permitting, but progress has been modest. The 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act introduced a two-year deadline for environmental impact statements, yet only 39% have met that target. While several new reform proposals are under discussion, the track record of previous efforts suggests meaningful change may prove difficult to achieve quickly. 3 September 2026 39 Barclays | The global energy race

The historical evidence confirms that capital intensity remained Canada’s main positive productivity driver after 2000, but its contribution was well below what would be required under a capital-only route to 2%. The current pipeline includes large investments in electricity, transportation, resource infrastructure and selected digital assets. Slower labor growth also makes it easier for capital per worker to rise. So the capital-only route could be plausible. But this would require more than execution of a limited set of major projects. It would require capital accumulation to broaden into private machinery, equipment, software and intellectual property, and to remain elevated after the initial infrastructure build has matured. The durability issue is central. If the capital-deepening contribution rises to 1.5pps for several years and subsequently returns to 1.0, Canada would retain a permanently larger capital stock and a higher level of potential output. But its growth rate would fall back toward 1.5%. The capital-only route can build a larger economy. It is less likely, on its own, to create a permanently faster-growing economy. Route 2: MFP does all the work. This, in our view, was the big change in the mid-2000s. Decline rates became an issue and we think they were largely ignored since 2014, as excess OPEC spare capacity, shale’s boom and efficiency upgrades moderated their influence. However, this all changed in 2025. The impact was first highlighted by Halliburton in its 2Q call, when it stated that the “decline curve is still working. ” Then in September 2025, the International Energy Agency (IEA) published its first major update on decline rates in a decade in its The Implications of Oil and Gas field decline rates publication. It noted that it believed that the decline rate for conventional oil had moved up to 5.6% per annum, with gas hitting 6.8% for field post peak. This is a significant move up from the typical 3-4% figure quoted in the 2000s. It noted that 90% of all capex spent since 2019 has been to maintain existing production, and that if all capex were to stop overnight, production would fall by 8% per year on average. The analysis suggested that the fall would total 5.5mn b/d of oil and 270 bcm annually, equivalent to the combined oil production of Norway and Brazil and the whole of Africa’s gas production. M BluePaper 48 Canada’s Relative Demographic Advantage Labor, Talent, and the Missing Capital Canada’s labor outlook splits into two distinct periods. The remainder of the 2020s is an adjustment; the 2030s bring a relative demographic advantage. Post-pandemic growth relied unusually heavily on population, employment and hours worked, while productive investment failed to keep pace. The immigration reset reverses that dynamic: labor-input growth will be unusually weak for several years, but slower workforce growth also creates a window to rebuild capital per worker. That weakness should not be extrapolated into the next decade. Under current long-run demographic assumptions, Canada is not heading toward the persistent labor-supply contraction facing many developed economies. Once the temporary-resident adjustment is complete, population growth returns to a more moderate positive pace, while aging creates only a modest drag on participation. Canada also begins that period with a relatively strong human-capital base. Educational attainment, universities, research quality, and workforce skills compare favorably internationally. The weakness lies further downstream: Canadian firms have invested too little in the machinery, software, intellectual property, infrastructure, and R&D required to turn those capabilities into productivity. Canada has accumulated human capital faster than productive capital. That creates the opportunity at the center of our broader Canadian growth thesis.

The natural hedge is most visible during supply disruptions. In Case study: TotalEnergies and the Middle East escalation, we highlighted that Qatar, Iraq and UAE offshore assets represented c.15% of production but only c.10% of upstream cash flow. Management also indicated that an $8/b increase in Brent would offset the expected 2026 cash-flow contribution from those assets under a $60/b oil price assumption. This illustrates how stronger commodity prices can partially offset operational disruption through a price-versus-volume hedge embedded within integrated portfolios. The sector implication is broader than TotalEnergies. Higher commodity prices, LNG optimisation, trading gains and refining margins can partially offset lost production volumes or regional disruptions, creating a price-versus-volume hedge that is largely unavailable to more concentrated business models. LNG remains a key differentiator. As domestic production declines and import dependency increases, scale, trading capability and supply flexibility become increasingly valuable across the gas value chain. records.text: 000 Growth slowed materially after 1981, but productivity remained an important part of the model. Business-sector output growth declined to approximately 3.1% annually between 1981 and 2000. Hours contributed 1.4pp, while labor productivity still contributed around 1.75pp. All three productivity components weakened. The contribution from capital intensity fell to approximately 0.9pp, labor composition contributed 0.4pp, and MFP slowed to just under 0.5pp. The decline was therefore broad-based rather than the result of one component alone. Even so, the model continued to generate more than half of output growth through productivity. Capital deepening remained meaningful, and MFP still made a positive contribution. Canada was no longer converging rapidly with the United States, but it had not yet moved to a predominantly labor-input-led model. However, reinvested earnings are accounting for a growing portion of outstanding overseas investment, and some of these seem to be held as financial assets. If for some reason corporates adopt a more bearish view on the USDJPY, they could repatriate assets and put in place forex hedges on a larger scale than investors. While we outline below how changing policy may help address the former, it is less clear to us that current policy offers a solution to the latter. We see new LNG additions and higher utilisation rates offsetting ~2 Mt/month of this, however this still leaves a net global LNG deficit of 3.6 Mt/month. This offset from new supply is lower than over the last six months, as new capacity additions slow over Q4 26 and Q1 27. In this scenario, lower LNG imports now have to absorb a 3.6 Mt/month deficit, vs 2.2 Mt/month over the last six months. However, this time around European inventories cannot be a major balancing factor. To prevent inventory levels in Europe from falling below our assumed floor of 15% fill for end-winter and using demand estimates for a normal (not mild) winter, we model LNG imports into our perimeter as having to remain flat YoY on average over Q4 and Q1. Policymakers, having previously seen gas (and intentionally labelled ‘fossil gas’ in 2022 EU Taxonomy documents) now acknowledge “the importance of gas for the European economy” (Feb 2025, Affordable Energy Action Plan). Germany is now leading the charge with two upcoming actions for CCGT (combined-cycle gas turbine) newbuilds. The problem with CCGTs is their economics are driven by (a) gas prices, (b) carbon prices and (c) load factors. Europe can do little to control (a) – it is an energy- importing economy – but looks to be penalising the industry through (b) and (c). If the market is structured so that renewables meet all summer demand requirements and CCGTs are held ‘in-reserve’ to meet the higher winter demand needs, then CCGT load factors will be low, and plant breakeven costs will be high. We estimate that at three-year trailing gas prices of c. $12/MMBtu and $100/t carbon prices then a CCGT operating in the 10-40% load spectrum will drive the long-run marginal cost of supply to $130-200/MWh. Prices drop to perhaps $100-170/MWh at $7.5/MMBtu (the price at which we think US LNG will eventually set European import gas prices at). Combine these prices with the cost of building the renewables capacity, then the outcome looks inflationary. T o contextualise the argument, CCGTs running higher load factors and zero carbon would only need prices in the $70-80/MWh range. Prepared for Cayla Buet

French domestic equities are the cleanest market expression of election risk. n The France Domestic basket (GSXEFRDO) derives half of its revenues from France, versus just 7% for the France International basket (GSXEFRIN), and is concentrated in sectors that are inherently more exposed to sovereign spreads, confidence and domestic policy: Industrials account for 28%, Financials 20%, Real Estate 16% and Consumer Discretionary 16%. This creates a much tighter link between politics, fiscal credibility and equity performance. French small caps, although less liquid, provide another interesting way to express a positive view on the French domestic cycle. Valuations are still vulnerable. We see the largest election risk as further de-rating n rather than a sharp fall in aggregate EPS. The CAC 40 is not obviously cheap. The index has underperformed, but it has also seen earnings revised down. As a result, it still trades around the upper quartile of its historical valuation range. That said, this is not uniquely a French phenomenon: most major equity markets currently trade above their long-term averages. records.text: Market implications The near-term hurdle is high for a move back to meaningfully lower convenience yields in the Euro area, in our view, given ongoing fiscal pressures into an important election year in 2027 and the high bar to pause ECB QT. But we see reasons to expect a stabilisation. In particular, QT reached its full speed in 2025 and its pace is poised to mechanically diminish through time. Besides, while ECB bank lending operations will not affect the balance of supply/demand for collateral directly, they are intended to contain the risk of increasing short-term funding costs and could mitigate the liquidity drain from QT. Finally, although we believe the EU will remain an important issuer in coming years, NGEU-related issuance is coming to an end in 2026. Subsequently, ongoing EU budget negotiations are still fairly open, but annual funding needs should head lower. We expect this to limit incremental bond supply in core/semi-core and contribute to stabilising Bund swap spreads, despite the increasing stock of debt.
