records.text: r quality. But neither is likely to provide the principal route to a durable acceleration. That leaves the incremental hurdle concentrated in two components: larger growth in K or in MFP. The distinction between them matters. Faster capital deepening can materially raise growth during an investment cycle, but its incremental contribution eventually fades if capital accumulation returns to its earlier pace. Sustained MFP growth is more capable of raising the economy’s lasting speed limit, although it is also harder to achieve and measure. The Bank of Canada’s upside scenario analysis raise potential-output growth by approximately 0.5ppover 2027-29: 0.2pp from stronger population growth; 0.2pp from faster or more profitable AI adoption; and 0.1pp from a less damaging tariff outcome. Together, those effects would leave the level of potential output around 1.9% higher by 2030 than in the Bank’s baseline. A favorable population outcome can lift aggregate potential growth without changing the economy’s underlying productivity regime. A better tariff outcome can remove a drag without creating a new domestic growth engine. Our scenario analysis is a more demanding test: what would it take for Canada to generate the additional 50bps primarily through active capital deepening and sustained efficiency gains.

Some argue that the oil price response to the 2026 supply shock has been underwhelming and highlights structural weakness in underlying fundamentals. We would note two things. First, it is important to consider the effect of the supply shock on refined product prices as well, because SPR releases and refining capacity constraints have resulted in significant dislocations. Second, in 2020, global oil demand fell by slightly over 9 mb/d and Dated Brent averaged 33% below the forward-implied 2020 average at the end of 2019. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 13 than in earlier decades. The principal change was that the economy stopped generating meaningful productivity gains beyond those directly attributable to greater capital intensity and improvements in labor composition. Around 70% of the decline in labor-productivity growth in 1981-2000 and 2000-19 can be traced to the deterioration in MFP. The remainder was divided broadly evenly between slower capital-intensity and labor-composition contributions. Prior studies similarly found that falling MFP accounted for roughly 72% of the post-2000 slowdown. This was also the period in which Canada’s productivity performance began to diverge materially from that of the United States. Canadian business-sector productivity advanced at less than 1% annually after 2000, while US productivity continued to grow considerably faster. Canada’s productivity level, which had approached the US level in the early 1980s, had fallen to an estimated 70% of the US level by 2022. The weakness was not primarily the result of workers moving into less productive industries. Most Canadian productivity growth after 2000 continued to occur within industries, while net labor reallocation made only a small positive contribution. The challenge was therefore not simply to move workers from one sector to another. Firms and industries themselves were generating less productivity growth. records.text: oductivity Can Rise Our analysis has so far shown that Canada’s measured productivity is likely to rebound as labor-input growth slows and some of the recent dilution of capital per worker reverses. That rebound does not, by itself, establish a new growth model. A sustained acceleration requires productive capital to grow more quickly and the economy to use capital and labor more efficiently. From a Higher Level to a Higher Speed Limit Our growth framework distinguishes between changes that raise the level of productive capacity and changes that raise its ongoing growth rate. Capital deepening usually produces a transition effect. A rise in investment raises the growth rate of capital stock (g_K is approximately I/K - depreciation), and capital per hour rises when capital grows faster than the labor input. While the capital stock is being built, faster growth of K raises both capital per worker and potential-output growth. Once the investment surge ends and capital growth returns to its earlier rate, the incremental contribution to growth fades. Potential output remains permanently higher because the economy has a larger capital stock, but its growth rate returns toward the previous baseline. In the standard neoclassical growth model, a permanently higher investment rate raises the steady-state levels of capital and output per worker. M Europe Insight 22 Exhibit 35: We currently assume LNG imports into Europe will track 6% higher YoY over winter. However, if the global LNG market is even tighter than our forecast due to a prolonged outage of Qatar's Ras Laffan, Europe cannot let LNG imports fall more than 10% YoY or risk record low inventory levels in a mild winter scenario. In a 'normal' winter scenario, imports will need to average flat YoY to avoid inventories falling below 15%. Contextualising our winter scenarios Over the last five months, we have seen a monthly loss to the market of ~5.7 Mt of Qatar/UAE exports, which has been offset by ~3.6 Mt of additional supply. The net impact to the market has therefore only been ~2.1 Mt of LNG loss per month. This LNG market deficit has been absorbed by lower imports across both Europe and Asia, i.e. demand has only had to absorb 40% of the Middle East supply loss. Our European perimeter has played a significant role, alone compensating for ~20% of the lost supply from Qatar. However, this has not been in the form of demand destruction, as underlying demand in Europe was actually +1% YoY over Apr-Aug. Instead, the 1.1 Mt/month of import reduction into our perimeter has been a direct sacrifice of inventory builds. Consequently, true underlying demand decline can only be attributed to the ex-EU +UK portion – so ~1 Mt/month or equivalent to ~18% of the initial supply loss from the Middle East.

records.text: r quality. But neither is likely to provide the principal route to a durable acceleration. That leaves the incremental hurdle concentrated in two components: larger growth in K or in MFP. The distinction between them matters. Faster capital deepening can materially raise growth during an investment cycle, but its incremental contribution eventually fades if capital accumulation returns to its earlier pace. Sustained MFP growth is more capable of raising the economy’s lasting speed limit, although it is also harder to achieve and measure. The Bank of Canada’s upside scenario analysis raise potential-output growth by approximately 0.5ppover 2027-29: 0.2pp from stronger population growth; 0.2pp from faster or more profitable AI adoption; and 0.1pp from a less damaging tariff outcome. Together, those effects would leave the level of potential output around 1.9% higher by 2030 than in the Bank’s baseline. A favorable population outcome can lift aggregate potential growth without changing the economy’s underlying productivity regime. A better tariff outcome can remove a drag without creating a new domestic growth engine. Our scenario analysis is a more demanding test: what would it take for Canada to generate the additional 50bps primarily through active capital deepening and sustained efficiency gains.

The recent composition of greenfield foreign direct investment suggests that this is already happening selectively in the sectors most closely aligned with Canada’s emerging strategic advantages. Announced inbound greenfield investment totalled roughly US$309 billion over 2015-26, but the composition has shifted materially. The clearest comparison is between 2015-17 and 2023-25. Investment associated with energy transition rose from US$4.6 billion to US$28.6 billion, while investments liked to trade diversification and critical minerals security in a multipolar world, as well as AI-linked investments increased from US$6.0 billion to US$28.2 billion. At the sector level, critical-minerals investment increased from less than US$1 billion to roughly US$15 billion, battery investment went from effectively zero to US$11.5 billion, and AI and data-center investment rose from approximately US$3 billion to US$8.3 billion. The investment mix has therefore shifted toward the resource, power and technology-intensive activities that feature prominently in Canada’s prospective capital cycle.

In our latest gold update, we highlighted the binary risks around Jackson Hole and the fragility of the August rally which was spec/paper-driven with a lack of physical demand follow-through. Indeed, gold prices were hit by the hawkish Warsh speech last Friday, which in our view presented dip-buying opportunities. Key technical support levels to watch include the 100dMA ( ~$4,366/oz) and 50dMA ($4,218/oz), while ~$4k/oz has proved to be a solid support level amid weak July trading (China and UHNW buying helped gold put in the lows, and Treasury purchases of the yen and the US long end drove it up). records.text: US Economics 04 September 2026 Citi Research 2 The fate of the September FOMC meeting lies with August CPI, and we expect our forecast for 0.18%MoM increase and the year-on-year reading falling to 2.3% will be a clear enough slowing in inflation that Fed officials will leave rates unchanged on September 16. Not only would three consecutive months of modest core inflation suggest more of a slowing trend (compared to just one or two months), but the annual pace would reach its lowest reading since core CPI jumped above 2% in April 2021. At 2.3%, core CPI is just 0.1% above its 2019 average. The drop in annual core CPI should also be clear evidence that recent slowing in monthly readings do not just reflect overly-soft seasonal adjustment. After comments from Governor Waller this week, we think the bar for what would be considered “too hot” inflation in August data is somewhat higher. Anything that rounds to a 0.2%MoM increase would likely be soft enough for most officials to want to keep rates on hold as they assess more incoming data. Currently, our 0.184% core CPI forecast and details of PPI suggest a 0.19% increase in core PCE inflation. Both CPI and PCE forecasts will change after the release of PPI data just before August CPI. records.text: M Europe Insight 26 Note, we currently view it as unlikely that European gas prices will return to the €200-300/MWh highs of 2022, in the absence of any further supply shocks. Regasification capacity bottlenecks and large outages in the French nuclear fleet helped push up prices to these record levels back in 2022, and we do not see these factors likely to repeat. However, if there was to be a major US liquefaction plant outage or attack on a key pipeline source of supply in Europe, then this could raise our bull price outlook further. Additionally, if the bull case materialises and Qatar flows have not normalised by end-winter and European gas storage is only ~15% full, this sets up a dynamic more similar to summer 2022 where concerns around re-stocking rise rapidly. This could set the gas market up for a very tight summer next year. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 63 Private Crowd-In Is the Decisive Signal Project execution is necessary, but it is not sufficient to establish a durable change in Canada’s investment regime. The first phase of the cycle is likely to be concentrated in structures — transmission lines, ports, mines, LNG facilities, transportation corridors, and other large infrastructure assets. Those projects directly raise the capital stock and can alleviate important constraints, but the productivity implications become considerably larger if they also change investment incentives elsewhere in the private sector. This is where the distinction between a project cycle and a capital cycle becomes important. A transmission line such as the North Coast Transmission Line adds productive infrastructure directly, but its larger economic value comes if additional electricity capacity raises expected returns on mines, mineral processing, LNG facilities, data centers, and other industrial investments. A new port adds capacity, but its broader payoff comes if lower congestion and improved access to export markets induce manufacturers, logistics firms, and wholesalers to invest themselves. The same principle applies across the MPO pipeline: enabling infrastructure can create a second round of investment considerably larger than the initial asset when it removes a binding constraint on complementary private capital. Impact on Europe - Why is Storage So Low? European buyers have generally taken the approach of "wait and see" when it comes to LNG buying this summer, hoping that by Q3 26 the Ras Laffan facility would have been back in the market. The depressive effect on prices of the return of Qatari LNG would have allowed European gas buyers to accelerate gas for storage purchases at lower prices into late summer, just in time for winter demand. European buyers were able to defer gas purchases this way, as Europe's gas demand is 3x lower in summer than it is over winter, so in summer the marginal molecule of gas is not bought to meet end-customer demand but to refill inventories ahead of winter. The lack of the usual seasonal contango in the front of the TTF curve also disincentivised commercial storage injections, as summer'26 prices have either been pricing at a premium or flat on winter 2026/27 TTF prices. Consequently, storage capacity holders have not been able to capture the usual seasonal spread that incentivises use of storage. records.text: M BluePaper 72 Canadian Oil & Gas Devin McDermott, Justin Latran Improving Outlook for Canadian Oil & Gas Canada produces about 6% of the world's oil and holds ~9% of reserves, the 4th highest globally. Higher oil prices, improving market access (pipeline expansions), and a more constructive policy backdrop all support growth in the years ahead. We forecast annual upstream spending for Canadian oil sands producers rising from US $13.4 billion in 2025 to US$16.2 billion in 2030 supporting, 600-700 kb/d of total growth in the country over the same period (+12%). Canada is a globally significant and strategically important heavy-oil supplier. Canada has risen from roughly the 13th-largest crude oil producer in 2000 to the fourth-largest today, as oil-sands development helped more than double national crude production from approximately 1.7 mb/d (million barrels per day) to more than 5.4 mb/d. Pipeline infrastructure expanded alongside that growth — including additions to Enbridge's Mainline system, the start-up of Keystone in 2010 and the completion of TMX (Trans Mountain expansion) in 2024 — although production periodically grew faster than egress capacity, contributing to export bottlenecks and periodically steep price discounts for Western Canada Select oil relative to over global benchmarks. records.text: Europe Multi-Asset 03 September 2026 Citi Research 48 A combination of the Ukraine war and changing US politics have meant that over the last four years Europe has had to reexamine its defense industrial posture as well as increasing defense spending. Increased threat level and higher NATO commitments: 1)2x: Defense spending roughly doubling over a decade as Europe increases defense spending from ~2% of GDP to 3.5% by 2035 (plus some GDP growth) 2)1.3x: Procurement increasing as proportion of defense spending from ~ 30% of the defense budget to ~40%, which we believe is the upper sustainable level (it is possible to go higher – Poland is currently at about 50%, but we believe this is likely to be temporary and is likely to come down over the longer term) As a result, we expect defense procurement to increase by ~ 2.6x from 2024 to 2035, or about 10% CAGR. The 2024 Draghi report on European competitiveness proposed the ambition to increase the proportion of defense procurement from European countries from 40% to 50% in 2030 to 60% in 2035 3)1.5x: Moving from 40% domestic European supply to 60% by 2035. This 50% uplift increases the addressable market from ~ 2.6x (9% CAGR) to ~4x (14% CAGR). Figure 59. Europe NATO defense spending $bn Figure 60. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 04 September 2026 Weekly view Not exactly a restorative break The summer break is over, but it hasn’t done much to restore our energy levels. That’s not because we spent our publication break on forecast updates. It’s more because energy prices and real yields have risen substantially over the last month, and are still on the move. Natural gas prices are in the vicinity of EUR 70 per MWh at the moment, and our commodities team flag upside risk to their winter forecast of EUR 65, which has already been revised higher. Oil prices at USD 97 at the time of writing are also well above previous assumptions. The energy shock is starting to become more persistent and tightening financial conditions more severe. We don’t think that will make the economy roll over, but it does make improving growth look less likely. Euro area: headlines change, core (narrative) remains the same What does that mean in numbers? For the Euro area, we revised our GDP growth forecast to 0.8% this year (+30bp), 1.1% in 2027 (-20bp) and 1.1% in 2028 (unch). These changes reflect better carryovers from 1H26 and a marginal lowering of the sequential growth path on the back of higher energy prices and real yields. Our inflation forecasts move to 2.9% in 2026, 2.2% in 2027 and stay at 1.8% in 2028, with core at 2.3%, 2.1% and 1.8%, respectively. Most of these capacity additions will be undertaken by Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO, Underweight), which is majority-owned by the government. records.text: We expect the Governing Council to hike the policy rate by 25bp next week, as n widely expected and fully priced. Investor focus will be on the updated staff projections and President Lagarde’s commentary on the policy outlook during the press conference. We look for a small upgrade to the growth projections of 0.1pp in each of 2026 n and 2027, motivated by the economy’s recent resilience. The inflation projections will likely be revised down by 0.1pp in 2026, for both headline and core, on account of weaker data than the staff had been anticipating. But we expect the 2027 projections to rise by 0.4pp to 2.7% for headline and by 0.1pp to 2.6% for core, given the increase in spot and forward energy prices. We look for no changes in 2028, although the bar for core to be revised down 0.1pp to 2.1% is probably quite low. The Council’s description of the economy, the risk assessment (with downside n risks to growth and upside risks to inflation), and the formal policy language are likely to remain broadly the same. We expect President Lagarde to leave options open during the press conference by stressing the Council’s data-dependence. The dovish risks are that she highlights the weaker inflation data or signals a growing hurdle to hike further. The hawkish risks are that she conveys greater concern around the increase in energy prices and the length of the projected inflation overshoot, or implicitly endorses market pricing of almost four hikes. Enabling infrastructure operates through scale: transmission, ports and trade corridors can improve the economics of several complementary private projects simultaneously. The common feature is leverage. Public intervention has the largest macro payoff when a relatively small fiscal exposure resolves a binding constraint and mobilizes substantially more additional private productive investment. The relevant comparison is therefore not public versus private spending, but public support relative to the investment it genuinely crowds in. Major Projects Office: From Approvals to Execution: Lowering the Hurdle Rate on Canada's Capital Build The Major Projects Office provides the clearest test of whether the new policy architecture can translate reform into realized capital formation. The MPO is designed to improve project economics by shortening and coordinating federal reviews, reducing execution uncertainty and moving projects more quickly from referral toward approval, final investment decision and construction. Common denominator is share price undervaluation At the same time, parent-subsidiary listings, activist investment, and MBOs share common features. One of these is low stock valuations. A low valuation for a listed subsidiary reduces the cost for the parent company to buy out minority shareholders, strengthening the economic rationale for making it a wholly owned subsidiary. For shareholder engagement, a substantial gap between the market valuation and the value of a company’s underlying assets or business operations creates greater scope to unlock value through capital policy or business restructuring. For MBOs as well, the lower the share price relative to the value perceived by management, the larger the incentive to take the company private to rectify the undervaluation. As such, a low valuation serves as a catalyst for companies or shareholders to initiate corporate action. That said, a low valuation alone does not guarantee future action. Other factors must also be taken into consideration, such as the shareholder base, the presence of an entity capable of executing such action, and the extent to which these expectations are already priced into the shares. records.text: 2H26 and 2027 outlook: Geopolitical uncertainty to amplify structural refining tightness Refining margins have re-rated sharply as product supply has tightened far more than crude supply. Since March, refinery outages across the Middle East and Russia have removed a significant portion of global product exports, with global refined product exports down c.25% YoY and refinery runs running materially below seasonal norms. This has pushed diesel to the centre of the rally, with middle distillates accounting for more than 40% of the increase in global product prices, while product inventories have continued to draw despite some demand destruction. European benchmark refining margins are currently above $40/bbl versus a mid-cycle average of c.$7/bbl. Low inventories and elevated outage risks are now creating a structural premium in product markets. After several months of depressed refinery runs, diesel and gasoline stocks have fallen to below-normal levels globally, while refinery outages remain well above historical averages. This has resulted in a meaningful risk premium being embedded in refining margins, as markets need higher prices to curb demand, incentivize maximum refinery utilization and prevent inventories from falling to critically low levels. Importantly, refining systems outside the affected regions have limited ability to offset lost supply, as US utilization is already high, Asian refiners face feedstock constraints, and China’s export quotas remain restrictive. records.text: Rotation moderation — remain OW equities for 12m but tactically more defensive 1. The procyclical rotation across assets continued over the summer, supported by the higher nominal growth backdrop. Global equities are only modestly up since our last asset allocation update although there have been material reversals underneath the surface with AI capex beneficiaries selling off and a significant broadening out after the narrow rally in 1H. But equities have still outperformed vs. bonds, which have come under pressure with longer-dated bond yields globally nearing their post GFC highs due to a combination of cyclical support, crowding out from AI debt issuance and fiscal concerns. This resulted in the US treasury announcing interventions in long-dated US treasuries, which weighed on the Dollar and boosted Gold. The higher nominal growth backdrop also weighed on JGBs and the Yen, which earlier triggered an FX intervention from the US treasury and boosted Gold. We remain tactically neutral across assets for 3m (N equities/bonds/credit/commodities/cash) and modestly pro-risk for 12m (OW equities, N bonds/commodities/cash, UW credit). As long as earnings growth remains supportive, we expect equities to outperform credit and bonds over the 12-month horizon. records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 04 September 2026 Citi Research 5 Start of some weaker data After three strong months of job gains, employment fell by 42k in August, helping to reaffirm our view that recently stronger data simply reflect the familiar pattern of volatility rather than a sustained pick-up in demand. This re-weakening in activity precedes any likely impact from tariffs, which could weigh further on employment in goods producing industries over the coming months. records.text: Trade and Inventories: A more durable tariff regime The shift toward Sections 301 and 232 authority has put the tariff regime on more durable statutory footing. The final forced-labor Section 301 action now provides a broad country-level tariff floor, while Section 232 remains the targeted sectoral overlay. We continue to expect the statutory effective tariff rate to converge toward roughly 10% by year-end. The remaining uncertainty is increasingly around implementation, pending Section 232 actions, and country-specific escalation rather than the persistence of the broad tariff floor. On USMCA, recent US-Canada tariff escalation points to heightened tensions as negotiations progress and the deadline is pushed to next July; further tariff actions would shift risks toward a more bilateral or fragmented USMCA.

After a decade in which exploration budgets were systematically reduced in favor of short-cycle shale development, management teams increasingly view exploration as a necessary component of long-term inventory replacement. Investors are beginning to focus less on near-term production growth and more on the quality of companies' 2030+ resource pipeline. As a result, exploration spending is rising from historically depressed levels, and management teams are becoming more willing to publicly defend exploration capital. CVX's commentary around strengthening its exploration capabilities following the HES acquisition is one indication of this shift. The renewed activity across Namibia's Orange Basin, the Eastern Mediterranean, offshore West Africa, and other frontier basins highlights a broader industry realization that future resource growth cannot rely exclusively on existing shale inventories. Among U.S. E&Ps, MUR's Vietnam and Côte d'Ivoire programs represent some of the high- impact exploration stories. Investors are increasingly focused on the Hai Su Vang appraisal program in Vietnam, alongside follow-up activity after recent success offshore Côte d'Ivoire. We expect the ECB to deliver a 25bp rate hike. The communication, we think, once again should point to a meeting by meeting approach, and clear data dependency. We expect only little change to the updated projections, showing broadly unchanged inflation and upward revisions to growth (see our Preview here). On the data side, we start the week with the final reading of euro area 2Q26 GDP. Following a strong revision in Irish data (to 10.2%Q from an initial estimate of 3.9%Q) we think the euro area aggregate numbers could be raised to 0.6%Q from initially 0.4%Q. Throughout the week, we also get more hard data for July. On Monday, we expect Germany's industrial production to show a slight contraction (-0.2%M) reflecting impacts from summer heat (especially low Rhine water levels). And German exports, due on Tuesday, are expected to show again robust growth (1.0%M). Industrial production in France is forecasted at 0.2%M, in line with solid signals from surveys. And in Spain, we expect industrial production to decline again (-0.9%M), reverting closer to historical levels. records.text: M Japan Insight 18 Next-generation TOPIX: From market mirror to mechanism for market discipline TOPIX has long served as a “mirror of the markets,” reflecting the overall price movements of Japanese equities. However, the next-generation TOPIX will shift from a mere reflection of the markets to a more active role in selecting listed companies. In the past, the system in effect ensured automatic inclusion in TOPIX upon listing on the former TSE First Section or Prime Market. In contrast, the next-generation TOPIX will involve a periodic reshuffle based on liquidity criteria, covering all market segments, i.e., Prime, Standard, and Growth. This change is significant in light of the massive volume of passive investment assets linked to TOPIX. We estimate that TOPIX-linked assets stood at ¥155trn at the end of June 2026 ( Exhibit 23 ). Inclusion in the index generates mechanical buying demand from index- linked funds and creates ongoing demand for holding the stock. Conversely, exclusion can trigger selling by passive funds, altering the investor base and liquidity profile. Therefore, inclusion in TOPIX is not merely a matter of index categorization, but a management issue that can influence market valuations, liquidity, and even the capital-raising environment for a company. The next-generation TOPIX is not a system that directly mandates ROE targets or capital policies for companies. Gas traders and suppliers decide how much gas to put into storage based on their supply needs and market prices. The government sets minimum filling requirements; for 1 November, the current rules imply an average target of around 70% across German storage facilities. Commercial market participants remain responsible for procuring and storing the gas. What determines whether companies have an incentive to fill storage? A key factor is the spread between current and expected winter gas prices: companies compare the cost of buying and storing gas today with the expected value of having that gas available later. The first would demonstrate that policy reform is reducing barriers to investment; the second and third would provide stronger evidence that Canada is moving from a collection of major projects toward a genuine private capital cycle. If enabling infrastructure also raises expected private returns and crowds in complementary investment, the payoff extends beyond K. Broader machinery, software, and technology adoption create a pathway from capital deepening to stronger multifactor productivity. At that point, financial balance- sheet capacity begins translating into productive capital and, potentially, a more durable improvement in potential growth.

records.text: Europe Multi-Asset 03 September 2026 Citi Research 30 Chemicals: From structural decline to investable? Sector thoughts: The European chemical industry’s loss of market share to Chinese producers has contributed to significant earnings downgrades for Diversified Chemicals stocks over the past four years, alongside the weak industrial cycle. Historically, sector volumes broadly tracked industrial production, but 2022 marked a clear inflection point. The spike in gas prices following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered an unprecedented destocking cycle from 2H22 to 4Q23, resulting in six consecutive quarters of negative year-on-year volume growth and a cumulative decline of more than 10%. Volumes have yet to recover meaningfully and remain around 10% below 2019 levels. European utilisation remains near the trough recorded during the 2Q20 lockdown, which is particularly important given that Europe accounts for close to 40% of sales of our coverage. While weak demand is an important factor, rising Chinese imports have also contributed. Import volumes are now approximately 80% above 2021 levels, pushing Europe’s net trade balance firmly into deficit. Stronger Q2 volumes, supported by temporary Asian supply disruptions related to the Middle East conflict, demonstrate the potential benefit from reduced import pressure but may prove temporary without more durable policy support. The US and Qatar are the two largest suppliers of LNG, accounting for ~25% and ~19% of global LNG exports in 2025 (~437 mtpa total per WoodMac), respectively. Through a large-scale, multi-phased expansion at North Field, Qatar was previously on track to expand production capacity to ~142 mtpa by decade end, up from ~78 mtpa in 2025. However, in the wake of Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan in March, 2 of Qatar's 14 liquefaction trains will remain offline for 3-5 years (~17% of total capacity), and the aforementioned expansions are likely to face material delays. The initial phase of Qatar's North Field expansion was previously slated to achieve First LNG later this year (North Field East, +32 mtpa), followed by subsequent phases in 2027 (North Field South; +16 mtpa) and 2028 (North Field West; +16 mtpa). Per commentary from Qatari Energy Minister Saad al-Kaabi in March, North Field East could be delayed by over a year, pushing back the timeline for North Field South and West as well. We think these realities pave the way for a protracted LNG supply shock that will likely outlast the conflict and any disruptions to the Strait. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 91 Financing AI & Data Centers: Canadian Markets Carolyn Campbell The Canadian Data Center Build The Canadian data center market is today far smaller than in the US, but new capacity additions over the next few years could see it grow by multiple times over. Estimates from S&P 451 Research put the current Canadian data center capacity at 1.8GW, with the majority concentrated in Quebec (585MW) and Ontario (472MW). By comparison, estimates for US data center capacity stand around 55GW, with nearly 9GW in Northern Virginia alone and 7GW in Texas. Over the next several years, many more GW will likely come online, with Alberta a strong leader in new builds. S&P estimates that 2.5GW are planned or under construction, with 1.9GW of those in Alberta (note that S&P tends to have more conservative estimates of planned capacity than some other resources, due to its bottom-up build of assets). Other estimates place proposed capacity much higher: Recent research from York University (and cited here by CBC) projects over 13GW of planned or proposed capacity in Canada, with over 90% of those builds going to Alberta. (Other estimates put the planned capacity even higher, up to 20GW. Like in the US, it is possible that many proposed plans will not come to fruition, with bidders filling queues without concrete plans.) The market is telling us, in the clearest possible terms, that the downstream infrastructure is insufficient. The same logic applies across the energy value chain. Grid investment needs to grow more than 50% by 2030, from roughly $400 billion annually to over $600 billion, just to meet national climate targets, according to the IEA. More than 2,500 gigawatts of renewable energy, storage, and large-load projects (including data centres) are currently stalled in grid connection queues worldwide. The bottleneck is not generation. It is the wires, transformers, substations, and interconnectors that move electricity from where it is produced to where it is consumed. French nuclear output was the standout weak spot, hit by a combination of river-temperature restrictions, maintenance and jellyfish swarms, that pushed output to the lowest level since August 2023. Solar output faded through the month as the seasonal peak passed and northwestern Europe turned cooler, while wind output over the first half of August was little changed YoY, leaving neither renewable source able to offset the shortfall from nuclear and hydro. Pipeline imports into our perimeter eased 2% MoM in August but remained 10% higher YoY at 356 mcm/d. Norwegian flows were broadly stable at 251 mcm/d (-1% MoM, +1% YoY), as the start-up of Troll's Phase 3 Stage 2 expansion late in the month roughly offset scheduled maintenance across several Norwegian fields, including Åsgard, Troll and Kvitebjørn. Flows from Azerbaijan via Albania and TAP dropped 16% MoM and 12% YoY to 23 mcm/d, as planned maintenance at the Shah Deniz field cut deliveries into Europe. Imports from North Africa also fell, down 7% MoM and 10% YoY to 50 mcm/d, while UK flows eased 8% MoM but remained 43% higher YoY at 46 mcm/d. LNG supply to our perimeter reached a 2Y low in early August, before recovering in the second half of the month. Total LNG imports rose 22% MoM but were still down 6% YoY, at 4.6 Mt, while regasification levels rose 19% MoM to 186 mcm/d, still 10% below year-ago levels.

An analysis of projected exclusion candidates (“del”) by free-float market cap decile since July finds that the highest returns were achieved by the tenth decile (D10), which has the largest free-float market cap and is closest to the criteria for continued inclusion ( Exhibit 34 ). Conversely, the highest returns for stocks slated for continued inclusion (“stay_in”) were in the first decile (D1), which has the smallest free- float market cap and is closest to the exclusion criteria (Exhibit 35 ). Both groups consist of stocks positioned near the TOPIX inclusion/exclusion line. The results suggest that companies may have taken actions that positively impacted their shares at a time when their possible adoption or exclusion from the index was a market focus. Indeed, the number of share buybacks since July by quantile yields is consistent with this notion. Specifically, taking excluded stocks as our universe, we observe that quantiles with larger market caps have a higher volume of share buyback announcements ( Exhibit 36 ). records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 04 September 2026 9 Inflation moves higher due to energy prices We raise our inflation forecast in Q4 2026 to 3.4% (+20bps), with 2026 avg. unchanged at 3.1%. We raise inflation more meaningfully in 2027 to 2.6% (+30bps), as oil and gas prices are higher than our post-peace deal assumptions. We incorporate the announced 4% rise in the October price cap (which takes into account the VAT cut on electricity bills). Moreover, our forecast of higher gas prices in the winter is likely to imply a larger rise in January and April price cap vs. before. The change in our core inflation forecasts is more muted at 2.8% (unch.) in 2026 and 2.3% (+10bps) in 2027. Our 2028 forecast remains unchanged at 2.1% for headline and 2.1% for core with upside risks. Headline inflation is expected to pick up from here, with the peak now expected at 3.5% in Nov. vs 3.3% in Sept/Nov 2026 before. Inflation is expected to stay above 3% until Q2 2027 and reach close to target later in Q4 2027. Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Source: Citi Research, CEA Battery Metals Lithium: We are constructive on lithium in the near term as restocking of battery supply chain ahead of traditional season combined with tight supply is likely to drive prices higher. Our new 0–3-month point price forecasts for lithium carbonate, hydroxide, and spodumene (SC6) is $30k/t, $23k/t, and $3k/t. However, improved supply into next year is likely to keep prices under pressure in 2027. Chinese lithium carbonate prices have largely traded range-bound at US$20,000–22,000/t through most of 3Q26, as uncertainty surrounding the restart of the Jianxiawo (JXW) mine, which accounts for roughly 4–5% of global LCE supply, capped upside despite a fundamentally tight market. Prices have rallied in recent days after Yichun City Council withdrew its environmental impact assessment (EIA) notice for JXW ( Asian Metal, Aug’26), indicating the mine is unlikely to restart in the near term. Strong battery production demand, low visible inventories, and tightening feedstock availability continue to underpin prices. However, we see improved supply into next year combined with a mixed cell outlook to weigh on prices. We mark to market our 3Q’26 forecasts and revise our 4Q’26 and CY’27 forecasts. If it persists for 10 years, the level difference approaches 5%. The durability of the scenario depends on its composition. The extra capital contribution may fade after the build phase. For potential growth to remain near 2%, either capital formation must stay persistently stronger or MFP must continue to rise after the initial diffusion period. This is why construction and the other swing sectors are central. A one-time efficiency improvement raises the level of output. Continued adoption, organizational change, and innovation raise its growth rate. Which Scenario Does the Current Evidence Point To? The current data do not yet support the broad-reset scenario as the baseline. The capital pipeline is large but concentrated. The sectors receiving the most tangible investment have historically generated weak direct MFP, while the current AI impulse remains concentrated in services. Manufacturing intentions are broadly flat. Construction has substantial productivity shortfall but low adoption. Transportation combines a major capital pipeline with a large recent MFP shortfall, making it the clearest early test of whether the capital build can become a productivity cycle. records.text: M Idea 8 Oil Tracker: Elevated Prices, Falling Inventories We continue to track the evolution of petroleum-product inventories, production, trade, and prices. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell further, and the total US crude oil and petroleum-product inventories edged lower. US domestic crude oil production edged up slightly, while net imports of crude oil and petroleum products have moved sideways. Meanwhile, oil prices moved higher. As of August 28, US stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represent the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of crude oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period-end, remained broadly unchanged from a week earlier. The stocks of crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) continued to fall to around 286 million barrels, the lowest level since April 1984. The Energy Department said the SPR's minimum inventory is determined by "cavern mechanics," which, when applied across the full system, translates to a conservative operational minimum of about 70 million barrels. If the SPR continues to decline at roughly its recent pace of 30 million barrels every four weeks, inventories would approach the operational minimum by the end of February 2027. Following the recent re-escalation between the US and Iran, both spot and futures prices have risen, renewing concerns about inflation. The latest spot prices, as of September 1, were $91.48 per barrel

e capital and productivity cycles to become mutually reinforcing. The three routes are accounting illustrations, but K and A are not independent in practice. Higher MFP raises the expected return on investment. Firms are more likely to add capital when technology, market access, scale, or organizational change allow them to use it more profitably. Likewise, new capital can enable MFP. AI adoption requires compute, software, data infrastructure, and skills. Advanced manufacturing requires machinery, power, and logistics. Internal trade reform raises productivity more effectively when firms have the capital to expand and serve a larger market. The 2% scenario is therefore less likely to emerge from a simple addition of separate capital and TFP shocks. It is more likely to emerge from a conversion cycle: Infrastructure and resource capital→lower bottlenecks→private crowd-in→technology and organizational diffusion→higher TFP→higher returns to further capital. That feedback loop is what distinguishes a temporary capital build from a lasting productivity reset.

Two venues, one tape: 13 months of the clearing basis Yen interest rate swaps clear in two places—JSCC onshore and LCH offshore—and the same swap rarely prices identically at both. The JSCC −LCH basis is that gap: the fixed rate of a JSCC-cleared swap minus that of an LCH-cleared swap, in basis points. Over the past 13 months, it has been a long-end phenomenon. A negative basis means the LCH rate trades above JSCC —directionally, relative paying pressure at LCH (offshore accounts) or receiving pressure at JSCC (domestic accounts). records.text: sidiaries becoming wholly owned. Events such as the TSE market reforms have sparked a surge in interest from domestic and international investors. As investors built positions in advance in expectation of future conversion of listed subsidiaries to wholly owned status, the stock prices and valuations of those subsidiaries were driven upward, which may have made it harder to generate excess returns. In fact, the median P/B of listed subsidiaries has climbed greatly since 2021 (Exhibit 42 ). While this likely includes changes in composition with the exit of low-valued listed subsidiaries from the market following the dissolution of parent-subsidiary listings, it is also consistent with the discounting in the markets of expectations of such dissolutions. The rise in AI and semiconductor stocks since last year has contributed to a notable increase in the TOPIX P/B. In other words, it is not that the conversion of listed subsidiaries into wholly owned subsidiaries has ceased in recent years. Rather, it has become difficult to acquire the option value of such a conversion at a low price. The parent-subsidiary listing theme has become overcrowded and obsolete, referring not only to the loss of the catalyst itself but to an increase in the price investors must pay for that catalyst.

In Phase 1 of the review, TOPIX constituents as of April 2022 were retained regardless of their market segment, but stocks that failed to meet the ¥10bn market cap requirement for free-float shares were designated as stocks subject to phased weight reduction. JPX announced a list of 493 stocks subject to phased weight reduction on October 7, 2022. The transition factor for these stocks was lowered in ten phases over quarterly intervals from the end of that month through the end of January 2025. In a re-evaluation in October 2023, 43 stocks that had recovered to meet the criteria were removed from the list, and their transition coefficients were subsequently raised by 0.1 each quarter until returning to level 1. Conversely, stocks that failed to meet the criteria continued to see their weights reduced and were ultimately removed from TOPIX at the end of January 2025. This system serves to mitigate the market impact while providing a grace period for companies to make efforts to lift the market caps of their free-float shares. However, as management itself acts as the buyer, there is a structural conflict of interest with ordinary shareholders. It follows that the growing number of MBOs is expanding opportunities for investment that would generate a premium for shareholders, while MBOs are also governance events that test how the board of directors ensures the fairness of both the offer price and the buyout process. In our 2025 report “Unlocking Japan: Corporate Governance Reform 2025” (the 2025 report), we investigated the factors behind the increase in MBOs in recent years (Exhibit 60 ). To summarize our results, we found that undervalued share prices are a major incentive to MBO activity, which is consistent with the large volume of prior research noting that the resolution of low valuations provides a strong motivation to take a company private. What also came out clearly is that the higher management’s effective ownership ratio (including equity indirectly held through asset management companies), the greater the probability of an MBO taking place. Canada combines hydrocarbons, hydroelectricity, uranium, copper, nickel, lithium, potash and prospective rare-earth resources with developed-market institutions, fiscal capacity and direct access to the US economy. The opportunity is to use resource abundance to attract another layer of productive investment. Power can support data centers, compute infrastructure, mineral processing, and advanced manufacturing. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 7 Strategic Abundance Can Raise the Return on Capital Canada’s resource intensity is often treated as a legacy feature of its old growth model. In a more power-, mineral-, and security-intensive global economy, it can enable the next one. Canada combines hydrocarbons, hydroelectricity, uranium, copper, nickel, lithium, potash and prospective rare-earth resources with developed-market institutions, fiscal capacity and direct access to the US economy. The opportunity is to use resource abundance to attract another layer of productive investment. Power can support data centers, compute infrastructure, mineral processing, and advanced manufacturing. Transport infrastructure can enlarge effective markets. Critical-mineral development can support refining, specialized suppliers, and downstream production. Canada has an opportunity to participate in the global compute cycle. If it can provide reliable power, competitive time-to-power, suitable data governance, and adequate grid capacity, then global capital can finance much of the hardware while the installed infrastructure becomes part of Canada’s productive capital stock. Section 338 tariffs, which unlike prior actions do not exempt USMCA-compliant goods, took effect on August 19 — just after the reference week, so their reach is not yet in this print — with counter-tariffs and further measures scheduled into January 2027. records.text: Cross-Commodity Outlook 03 September 2026 Citi Research 4 Energy – Geopolitics driving a large deficit; structural surplus reappears on SoH reopening Oil We see the current situation (US blockade, sizable Oman SoH flows) as unsustainable, with the Iranian regime saying it will escalate imminently if the US does not return to the MoU. We believe that Iran is incentivized to try to break the blockade sooner rather than later, with its economy suffering from a dramatic decline in its currency and lost oil revenues in recent weeks. On the US side, we believe the situation is unsustainable because eventually higher oil prices are likely to negatively affect equity and/or bond markets, to which we believe the administration is sensitive. The November midterms (three months away), as they come closer, may be a catalyst for President Trump to deal, or soften the blockade at least temporarily; however, we think President Trump will not likely stop his current course due to the midterms alone (given the White House seems unlikely to get major policy changes through the House anyway). As such, our central scenario is a near-term escalation in the Middle East that eventually results in another major attempt at dealmaking, or that other factors change (belligerent leadership changes for example, or regional deals emerge) such that the SoH reopens during 4Q26. M Idea 10 Financial Conditions: Easing Since the July FOMC Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we continue to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions. As of the September 3 market close, financial conditions remained tighter than before the recent escalation in the Middle East, yet meaningfully easier than at the time before the July FOMC meeting. Since the July FOMC meeting, financial conditions have eased by 28bp, primarily driven by positive equity returns and U.S. dollar depreciation. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 26bp rise in the federal funds rate. records.text: Markets care more about the policy mix than the political label. Investor n conversations suggest that a pro-European centrist candidate would be viewed as the most market-friendly outcome, while the far-left is broadly perceived as the least favorable, and Le Pen sits somewhere in between. The main reason is that most major candidates, except for Mélenchon, now acknowledge France’s difficult fiscal position. Moreover, the RN has moderated its platform, dropped its previous anti-euro stance, and increasingly emphasizes deficit reduction. Parliament matters more than the Presidency. The key focus should not be on n who occupies the Élysée Palace, but whether the next President can secure a workable majority in the National Assembly. France is now fragmented across three major political blocs, raising the risk of political gridlock and limiting the scope for fiscal consolidation or structural reform. This matters because France enters the election cycle with public debt approaching 120% of GDP , a fiscal deficit still inconsistent with a rapid stabilization of the debt trajectory, unemployment back above 8%, and a pension system that remains central to the long-term fiscal debate. Debt sustainability arithmetic has also worsened, as higher interest costs are making markets less forgiving of delays in fiscal adjustment. As population growth slows, both effects should partly reverse. Capital accumulation has more time to catch up with the labor force, while workers already in Canada become more attached to the labor market and move into roles that make fuller use of their skills. This creates a plausible multiyear catch-up in the level of productivity. But a closing level gap is not the same as a permanently higher growth rate. Once capital per worker and labor composition have normalized, those transitional supports fade. The Same Productivity Growth Can Support Very Different Economies The Bank’s forecast demonstrates why the productivity number cannot be interpreted in isolation. In both 2026 and 2029, trend labor-productivity growth is estimated at 1.5%. But potential-output growth is only 1.2% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2029. The difference is entirely in labor input. Its contribution is -0.3 percentage points in 2026 and +0.3 percentage points in 2029. The same productivity performance is therefore consistent with a 60-basis-point difference in aggregate potential growth. The comparison between 2025 and 2026 is even more striking. Productivity growth rises from 1.0% to 1.5%, but potential-output growth falls from 2.3% to 1.2%. records.text: ergNEF Perhaps the most significant separator for the clean technology space is speed to power. At a time when US grid interconnection queues can stretch up to five years, and gas turbine waitlists have extended past six years, many of the solutions offered by companies in this sector are able to provide power on relatively accelerated timelines (such as fuel cells manufactured by BE, generators provided by EROC, or solar panels put together by FSLR). Many of the products and services that are offered by the companies in our coverage also work alongside, or in conjunction with, a grid interconnection. Some (BE, EROC) offer solutions that can be used by customers as "bridge power" , providing primary electric capacity while full grid interconnection is on hold. When grid connection is available, the customers can either sell the products, or keep them as backup power sources. This eases the constraints on the grid while also providing users with much needed current power. Lastly, the numerous generative technologies in the space provide a growing list of customers with more variety than ever to meet their needs. Hyperscalers can have a very different set of requirements than traditional commercial and industrial users, and there can be a wide range of priorities even between data centres themselves. Canada is producing more oil, has better access to export markets following TMX, and could add further egress capacity later this decade ( Exhibit 70 and Exhibit 71 ). That provides a floor under CAD, in our view. We would not extrapolate the historical oil-CAD relationship too aggressively, however. Our prior work shows that oil’s explanatory power for USD/CAD weakened after 2015. At comparable real Brent prices, USD/CAD has traded much higher in the post-2015 regime as rates, trade uncertainty, and global risk sentiment became more important drivers. We think 1.36 is attainable, while 1.30 would be a big upside case. Better commodity fundamentals can close part of the current valuation gap, but they cannot close all of it without stronger private-sector investment and lower trade-policy uncertainty.

records.text: M Europe Insight 2 Even a Mild Winter Comes At a Price Ongoing tensions in the Middle East have driven a +75% rally in European gas prices (TTF) over the last two months, as the market re-prices longer expected duration of the conflict into both European and Asian gas prices. Despite being 20% above the curve for winter 2026/27 in our last price deck (here), the TTF forward curve has rapidly converged on our price forecasts over August. The window for the return of Qatar's major Ras Laffan LNG export facility in time for Q4 has now effectively closed. This is an important inflection point for the global gas markets, as it removes the possibility of a last minute loosening of the global LNG market before winter that would have enabled Europe to rapidly increase storage injections and enter winter with healthier inventories. We now only assume Qatar LNG flows to Europe normalising into Q1 27. European gas inventories are important despite their regional nature, as they function as a key balancing mechanism for the global LNG market. Storage levels in Europe influence how much LNG Europe needs to import over the winter, as LNG is really the only flexible source of supply to Europe if storage is insufficient. Since Europe is a major marginal buyer of LNG, high or low storage inventories can materially affect global LNG flows, driving competition with Asia for volumes and pushing up international gas prices. Labor Expansion and a Widening Productivity Shortfall The post-pandemic period added a second, more recent problem to the long-standing MFP weakness. Between 4Q19 and 4Q25, business-sector output grew by approximately 1.6% annually. Total hours rose by 1.3%, while output per hour increased by only 0.3%. Put differently, additional hours accounted for more than 80% of business-sector output growth over this period. That compares with approximately 54% in 2000-19 and around 42-44% in the two earlier historical periods. The official annual decomposition through 2023 tells a similar story from the productivity side. labor productivity increased by approximately 0.3% annually between 2019 and 2023. Positive contributions of roughly 0.3pp each from capital intensity and labor composition were almost exactly offset by a 0.3pp decline in MFP. These figures should be interpreted cautiously. Pandemic closures initially removed many lower-productivity jobs, producing a temporary spike in measured productivity. The return of those workers subsequently reversed much of that increase. Together, EDF and CEZ demonstrate how governments can move along a spectrum of intervention, from project-level ownership and funding support to broader corporate ownership solutions. • TenneT is the clearest grid example. The Dutch model goes beyond traditional project financing, with the Kingdom of the Netherlands providing an institutional state-guarantee to TenneT Netherlands (TENNNL) and supporting funding capacity at the operating-company level. The transaction ultimately resulted in guarantee-eligible bonds being upgraded to AAA/ Aaa, illustrating how state support can be used to protect market access and facilitate large- scale grid investment. While the mechanisms differ, the direction of travel is similar. TenneT protects corporate funding capacity, Sizewell C derisks project delivery, CEZ combines project ownership support with a potential restructuring of strategic assets, while EDF demonstrates full state ownership. Together, these examples suggest that financeability is increasingly becoming a policy objective in its own right, with governments adopting a broader range of tools to support strategic energy infrastructure. Our research finds that humanoids could eventually help offset demographic pressures in ageing economies by substituting for labour in manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and agriculture. In China alone, an upper- bound scenario suggests humanoids could reach the equivalent of 3.8% of labour capacity by 2035, helping offset a significant share of projected workforce declines. The final push came from the day's 10y auction. The reopening of issue No. 383 (JPY 2.6trn planned) kept a bid-to-cover of 3.29x, but the lowest accepted price came in below consensus, and the tail stretched to 12 sen. The average yield was awarded at 2.995% and the highest at 3.011%, the first 3%- handle award since 1996. Cover and tail pointing in opposite directions is the signature of a hesitant book: demand exists at the level, but nobody wanted inventory ahead of the milestone—classic supply-demand behavior just below a round number. Three bearish forces are stacked behind the move. First, expectations of a September FOMC hike that firmed after Jackson Hole, with the US 10y near 4.8% transmitting pressure into JGBs through the evening session. Second, expectations of an additional Bank of Japan hike at the September 17–18 Monetary Policy Meeting. Third, the fiscal premium evoked by FY2027 budget requests that have swelled to roughly JPY 143trn. With monetary and fiscal policy pressing from both sides, the 3% price tag became an actual traded level. The September futures contract opened at 125.90, sold off through the auction result to 125.38, and settled at 125.55 (-42 sen)—the lowest front-contract close since at least 2020. records.text: ephemeral; our baseline remains that strong equity market performance should encourage households to rebalance some gains into cash. We had expected the yield advantage of money funds over deposits to support continued inflows into money funds relative to bank deposits. Instead, flows have largely tilted in favor of deposits despite that spread (Figure 6). We are unsure what is driving the slowdown in money fund growth. The deceleration appears concentrated in retail funds rather than institutional funds, suggesting household behavior may be playing an important role. One possibility is that a more active issuance environment is encouraging investors to deploy cash into risk assets rather than maintain similar money fund balances as a share of wealth. A low household saving rate may also be limiting the pace of new cash accumulation. While corporate cash being redeployed to fund AI-related investment remains a possibility, the concentration of the slowdown in retail funds suggests otherwise. Regardless of the underlying driver, the dynamics suggest cash is moving to a sector or segment that has a higher propensity to place cash in bank deposits than in money funds. All told we think these factors combined still tilt in favor of some funding pressures emerging in Q4. We have been recommending being short October SOFR/FF and continue to recommend that trade (entry: -1.5 bps). 3 September 2026 4 Barclays | US Rates Research

Batch Zero is ERCOT's new system-wide framework, approved by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) in June 2026, for studying and allocating transmission capacity to large load interconnection requests of 75MW or greater, replacing the prior project-by-project review process. The delay of this process is not only a reliability pause but also an affordability safeguard. On August 3, Governor Abbott issued an audit directive, following his earlier June 10 letter instructing the PUCT and ERCOT to structure large load interconnections so that data centre growth lowers, rather than raises, residential bills. The core concern is forecast risk: if ERCOT commits transmission capacity to speculative data centre projects that never materialize, the resulting stranded infrastructure costs could flow through to residential and commercial ratepayers. PUCT Chairman Thomas Gleeson has framed the agency's approach explicitly around ensuring that data centres must fund their own transmission infrastructure while contributing to bill reduction. AI, power demand, and the new electricity economy AI and data centres are a structural, not cyclical, source of new electricity demand, and the US is facing risk of inadequate supply. After two decades of essentially flat capacity growth, the grid now faces simultaneous load from AI data centres, reshoring, and electrification just as coal retirements accelerate. We estimate a supply/demand gap on the order of 50 GW by 2028, as gas turbine deliveries, renewables, and storage fall well short of what’s needed, based on current projections. The bottleneck to the AI trade is no longer chips, it’s electrons: interconnection queues stretch into multi-year delays, firm capacity is scarce, and large-scale grid additions get pushed past 2030. For utilities and power-linked sectors this means sustained load growth, grid expansion, and heavy spending on gas generation, transmission, and firm-capacity solutions. The key question for every sector is whether AI turns power scarcity into an earnings stream or into a funding, affordability, and execution risk. records.text: 8 World Energy Outlook 2025, International Energy Agency Why our sector matters Asia Pacific is the largest consumer of energy globally, accounting for 44% of global demand in 2024 and growing, according to the IEA8 . The agency estimates that Asia's share will reach 46-47% by 2050, keeping the continent as the key driver of global energy demand for the foreseeable future. Within Asia, China will likely remain the largest consumer of energy in Asia in 2050. However, demand growth (8-16%) is expected to lag the broader region's 26-39% estimates. Instead, the IEA expects India and Southeast Asia to be the growth engines in Asia: India's demand is expected to grow 80-106% by 2050, with Southeast Asia's expected to grow 63-80%. The IEA expects China's energy consumption growth to decelerate due to a combination of slower GDP growth expectations, a shift in growth from energy-intensive heavy industries such as steel and cement towards services and high value-added manufacturing, improved energy efficiencies, and a shrinking population. Under the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario, China's energy consumption is expected to peak in 2035 and plateau thereafter. In contrast, energy demand growth in India, which is expected to be the largest globally, will be propelled by rising economic activity. records.text: Japan Macro Watch4 September 2026 ab 2 A September BoJ rate hike looks almost a done deal In our previous note, we maintained a September Bank of Japan rate hike as the baseline scenario while also acknowledging the possibility of a move being delayed until October. Following developments this week, however, the case for postponement has largely disappeared. A more hawkish stance from Fed Chair Warsh has increased both depreciation pressure on the yen and upside inflation risks in Japan. In addition, Treasury Secretary Bessent indicated at the G20 meeting that further rate hikes would be appropriate. Bloomberg's report pointing to a 25bp increase in September further reinforced market expectations. Taken together, a September rate hike now appears to be largely priced in. This week, BoJ Policy Board member Takata maintained his hawkish stance in a public speech, not only reiterating the possibility of rate hikes at each meeting but also refraining from ruling out a 50bp increase. As a result, markets briefly moved toward pricing in a larger hike. However, the subsequent BoJ media leak may have reined in excessive tightening expectations. The next key question is the timing of a second rate hike before year-end. While markets currently assign roughly an 80% probability to another increase this year, our base case remains January. records.text: AI, power demand and the new electricity economy AI represents one of the most significant new sources of electricity demand emerging across the global economy. The growth of data centres is increasing requirements for: • electricity generation; • transmission infrastructure; • firm capacity; • backup power; • gas supply. As a result, AI has the potential to strengthen demand for natural gas, LNG and flexible power generation while increasing investment requirements across electricity systems. Increasingly, AI is becoming a matter of national competitiveness and energy security, with countries seeking to develop their own data-centre and AI capabilities. The recent example of the export ban of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 of Anthropic by the US highlight how important AI sovereignty is becoming. The sovereignty of data is also becoming critical with countries now building data centres. This is creating new centres of energy demand, from Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia in Southeast Asia to Abu Dhabi in the Middle East. The scale of power consumption is significant, with projects such as Stargate UAE 5GW that will consume 3-5% of the domestic ADNOC Gas production. Another important consideration is that data centres are increasingly seeking access to low- carbon but highly reliable power. The remaining is allocated to private IPPs. At the same time, PLN provides subsidized electricity domestically, for which it receives subsidy and compensation payments from the government. Positively, the cadence of compensation payments from the Government to PLN has improved significantly year to date, to a monthly frequency with payout of ~70% of claims, from a prior quarterly frequency. This has smoothed pressure on PLN’s working capital cycle. The PLNIJ ‘36s have widened 29bp since issuance, more than the INDON '36s, which are 15bp wider over the same period. Given the PLNIJ ‘36s relative underperformance, we believe current valuations at an OAS of 150bp and cash price of 94pts provide an attractive entry point and offer exposure into Indonesia’s electrification and energy security theme. The improved compensation cycle will support compression of the bond towards the INDON '36s, in our view. Our estimates show that the probability weighted price for this winter should be around €61/MWh, compared with the prompt month (Oct’26) price of €72.9/MWh and the Nov-Mar strip of €70.9/MWh at the time of writing. records.text: sset ownership has given rise to contrarian narratives. Particularly around "Liberation Day" , the concern about capital flight from the US drove a sharp dollar sell- off. But such narratives keep missing two of the most robust fundamental factors driving returns for capital higher and drawing the flow of capital from around the world to the US: energy security and data sovereignty. As we wrote in The Rise of the Mighty Dollar , the past decade has seen the rise of the US as a major energy exporting destination and as a technology exporting hub, which has underpinned higher neutral rates and currency strength. As we discuss in this note, the rise of AI in a world of geopolitical uncertainties and fragmentation makes these two pillars of USD exceptionalism not only more robust, but also more interlinked. The success of the AI experiment of such scale crucially hinges on energy abundance and security. Increasing demand on energy resources makes energy-supplying nations (eg, in the Middle East, Latin America but notably also the US, per Figure 39) crucial participants in the arena of international politics and boosts volumes and their terms of trade. Even successful conversion, however, will not produce an immediate improvement in every macro indicator. The early stages of a capital build are resource intensive, while much of the resulting output arrives only after projects become operational. Canada also imports a significant share of sophisticated machinery, electrical equipment and technology capital, meaning stronger domestic investment can initially raise imports and weaken the contribution from net trade. Large infrastructure projects can similarly absorb labor and intermediate inputs during construction without immediately increasing the flow of output from the completed asset. The likely sequence is therefore FID → construction → capital-goods imports → installed capital → utilization → productivity. This creates an investment J-curve that will be important when interpreting Canadian data over the next several years. A widening trade deficit driven by imported capital equipment is fundamentally different from one caused by weak exports or stronger consumption imports; similarly, soft measured productivity during a period of intensive construction need not signal that the investment thesis is failing. Here, labor input growth falls close to zero. Capital per worker improves partly because the denominator is growing more slowly, while existing investment and government capital spending provide some support to the capital stock. MFP contributes modestly. AI gains remain concentrated in information, finance and professional services, while adoption in construction, manufacturing, transportation and wholesale remains limited. USTR Greer has already signaled that the US may maintain "separate protocols" with Mexico and Canada that are "tacked on" to the USMCA, reinforcing the risk that any resolution is achieved through non-enforceable side agreements rather than institutionally reinforceable commitments. • Lack of certainty and clarity on the rules poses a structural drag on investment. Extended ambiguity around rules of origin, labor enforcement, energy policy, and sector-specific exemptions raises hurdle rates for new capital deployment. Hence, a gradual erosion of confidence in market access, tariffs, and a discretionary implementation of trade policy keeps some firms in a "wait and see" mode and delays the emergence of new industrial ecosystems, particularly in IT hardware and data centers. We think the USMCA negotiations could involve an opportunity to align the North American bloc strategically and economically against China. The capital-deepening contribution rises to 1.25pp. That is near the upper end of Canada’s historical experience, but not unprecedented (capital intensity contributed approximately 1.3pp in 1961-81). MFP rises to 0.45pp. This is close to the contribution recorded in 1981- 2000 and well below the early postwar rate. The scenario therefore does not require Canada to recreate the 1960s productivity regime. It requires a combination of capital formation near the high end of the historical range and a return to sustained positive MFP growth. The additional 0.25pp MFP contribution is a broad-conversion assumption rather than a mean-reversion estimate. We assign approximately 0.20pp to wider gains across construction, transportation, manufacturing, and wholesale, and a further 0.05pp to deeper AI diffusion, scale, competition, and improved resource allocation elsewhere in the economy. The magnitude is comparable with the Bank of Canada’s AI upside scenario, but AI is one mechanism within this scenario rather than a separate additive contribution.

This is consistent with our 2026 Global Energy Transition Barometer, which finds transition momentum improving across every region covered, with clean-energy supply the strongest and most broadly based tailwind. However, it also identifies rising system friction, with renewable capacity expanding while grid investment lags, clean-generation costs falling while integration costs rise, and electrification advancing without sufficient clean power or system flexibility. The constraint is shifting from whether clean technologies can scale to the ability of the wider energy system to absorb that scale reliably and economically. In the new energy equation, reliability is attracting a premium An increasingly electrified economy raises the premium for clean, firm baseload power. Variable renewables will retain a leading role in new capacity additions, but nuclear, hydro, geothermal, long-duration storage and other forms of flexible low-carbon capacity should be viewed as complements, rather than competing transition narratives. We are particularly constructive on nuclear's strategic role, with its position at the intersection of decarbonisation, energy security and powering AI, informing our view that we are in the midst of a nuclear renaissance (Investing in nuclear: From baseload to breakthroughs). Economics Germany Blog Date 4 September 2026 Gas supply: The tone is shifting The tone of the debate surrounding German gas storage levels is beginning to shift. Calls for government intervention are growing louder. What is behind this change? When the conflict in the Persian Gulf broke out at the end of February, gas prices in Europe surged. At the time, many market observers expected the war to be short-lived and therefore anticipated a rapid decline in gas prices. Moreover, with the heating season in the Northern Hemisphere drawing to a close, there was no immediate concern about gas supply security. Six months later, however, the war in Ira n is still going, with no resolution in sight. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. Gas storage levels in Germany and other European countries are low for this time of year, and the next heating season will begin within a matter of weeks. As a result, gas prices in Europe have increased recently, which is expected to add to inflationary pressures in the coming months and dampen the economic recovery, especially in the energy-intensive industrial sectors. Accounting for these communications, as well as recent comments from other Fed officials, in the following table we provide a simplified view of how we see this “family fight” aligning for the September FOMC meeting. We consider three outcomes for the implied core PCE print for August – what would be expected given PPI and CPI data next week, and divide officials into several camps (1) Strong hold (i.e., would likely dissent to a hike), (2) Lean hold/could hike (i.e., may prefer holding but would not dissent to a hike), (3) Lean hike /could hold (i.e., would prefer this outcome but may not dissent to a hold), and (4) Strong hike (i.e., would likely dissent to a hold). This identification is necessarily uncertain, as many officials have not provided their views recently, le t alone a detailed description of how their preference for the September meeting could respond to outcomes for core PCE. Nonetheless, we think this type of classification is still useful for understanding the Committee’s broad reaction function in response to near-term data. A final caveat: We have left Warsh out of these tables intentionally, as our objective is to indicate where we think the remaining officials align for September.
