records.text: Global Gas and Power Insights 04 September 2026 Citi Research 2 European natural gas prices are high and volatile because of the highly uncertain timelines and outcomes of the Strait of Hormuz transit status and winter weather. These price realizations build on top of low inventories ahead of winter that have made the market jittery. Asian LNG prices have also risen along the way, through the LNG bridge that connects the Asian and European markets. More non-energy specialists have also entered this market, partly due to how natural gas prices can drive inflation, and partly due to how much prices rose in 2022 on similar supply cuts. Amid the uncertainty in weather and the Hormuz reopening scenarios, we estimate a range of price outcomes based on different Strait of Hormuz reopening and winter weather scenarios. Instead of estimating base case prices based on a base case scenario, the new base case price is the probability-weighted average of these scenarios. Note that the winter package of Nov’26 – Mar’27 is relatively flat. Our estimates show that the probability weighted price should be around €61/MWh, compared with the prompt month (Oct’26) price of €72.9/MWh and the Nov-Mar strip of €70.9/MWh at the time of writing. A Different Growth Model for the 2030s The remainder of the 2020s is a transition period: Population growth falls sharply, labor contributes little to potential output, and productivity has to carry more of the expansion. On our normalization path, that leaves potential growth around 1½% for a time. The 2030s can look different because labor input becomes supportive again. If total hours show strong growth in the 2030s, labor-productivity growth closer to 2% would move growth toward 2.5%, representing a materially stronger upside case rather than our central assumption. In either case, productivity — not labor input — would remain the dominant source of growth. The sequencing is favorable. Slower labor growth in the late 2020s creates a window to install infrastructure, machinery, software and compute while the workforce expands slowly. As population growth normalizes in the 2030s, workers would enter an economy with more productive capital available to them. Canada’s demographic advantage is therefore not another immigration boom. It is the ability, under current long-run demographic assumptions, to retain positive labor-force growth while aging subtracts less from labor supply than in many developed-market peers. records.text: Cross-Commodity Outlook 03 September 2026 Citi Research 16 Commodities QIS Strategies The commodities QIS space has seen many new product innovations in recent years. We believe further innovation could be made in the following ways. Term structure / backwardation strategies could benefit from using interest rate adjusted spread signals instead of simple contango/backwardation signals. Rising or falling interest rate environments can obscure the fundamental signal given by curve structure, and adjusting for this may improve returns. Further, removing extreme signals is also likely to improve returns, by avoiding going long super backwardations (which can kill demand and create supply), or super contangos (which can kill supply and create demand), negatively impacting returns. Momentum strategies are highly likely to benefit from a skewness overlay, with skewness essentially providing a broad beta signal (according to recent academic literature) confirming or denying to momentum signal. We are very encouraged by this and view it as potentially a pivotal strategy, where drawdown limits of 5–10% are applied. Our preliminary work suggests the strategy would have worked very well over the past 25 years for BCOM, oil, gold, and copper. Momentum strategies that trim winners too much could perhaps adjust adjusted vol^0.5 instead of just vol, without negatively impacting the Sharpe ratio. Note: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: • Overweight BP (BPLN): BP remains a preferred recovery and deleveraging story within European Energy. Since announcing its strategic reset, management has prioritised balance- sheet repair through lower capex, suspended buybacks, planned disposals and debt reduction. We view recent governance noise as secondary to the improving credit trajectory, with stronger commodity prices and disciplined capital allocation supporting further leverage improvement through 2026-27. In our view, BP offers one of the strongest combinations of improving fundamentals, rating momentum and spread-tightening potential within the sector. • Overweight TotalEnergies (TTEFP): Within our coverage, TotalEnergies remains one of the clearest expressions of the resilience themes discussed above. The group combines a highly diversified earnings base across upstream, LNG, trading and refining with low leverage, strong cash generation and disciplined capital allocation. Recent Middle East disruption has reinforced the value of this integrated model, with stronger commodity prices, LNG and trading performance helping offset operational effects. In our view, TotalEnergies remains well positioned to benefit from commodity volatility while maintaining balance-sheet flexibility and shareholder returns. The acquisition of Germany’s KUKA by China’s Midea in 2016 and the EU vetoing of the Siemens Mobility / Alstom merger in 2019 were unrelated events but drove searching questions on national champions, critical industries, and competition policy within Germany, and in the EU more broadly. In the case of KUKA/Midea, where the Chinese appliance manufacturer bought a controlling stake in the German industrial robot supplier, there were fears about losing technology to China, with the German government initially trying to curb Midea’s stake. Ultimately the deal progressed however, with the Economics Minister commenting at the time that “the ministry can only launch a formal inquiry against the sale if crucial German interests such as telecommunications or water and power safety are affected" (DW, 17th August 2016) In the case of Siemens Mobility/Alstom, the 2019 veto by the European Commission brought to a head the perception that EU competition law was ripe for change in light of national champions being built elsewhere, especially China. The French and German governments pushed for a change to antitrust policy following the ruling, in order to promote national champions. Workers, Less Productivity — How Canada Generated Growth Canada’s growth model has changed substantially over the past six decades. In the earlier part of the period, growth reflected a combination of a rapidly expanding labor force, rising capital intensity and meaningful gains in the efficiency with which labor and capital were used. Over time, each of those productivity channels weakened. By the most recent period, aggregate output was being sustained primarily through additional workers and hours, while output per hour was barely rising. We use a standard growth-accounting framework to trace that transition. At the first level, real output can be expressed as the product of total hours worked and output per hour. This decomposition distinguishes growth generated by using more labor from growth generated by producing more in each hour worked. Labor-productivity growth can then be decomposed into three components: capital-intensity contribution, labor-composition contribution, and multifactor-productivity growth.

records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 04 September 2026 3 Paradoxically, the policymaker arguing against forward guidance ended up giving more of it, while the policymaker who openly described the conditional nature of his reaction function gave markets less information about the actual path of rates. The lesson: more transparency means less commitment The hiking analogy captures the distinction neatly. Warsh effectively hinted that the Fed might have waited too long, so be prepared for the Kohn trail. Waller effectively hinted that here is the trail map, if the terrain stays benign, take Bernanke trail, if it deteriorates, take Kohn trail. The first tells market which trail is becoming more likely. The second tells markets how the Fed will choose between them. The communication lesson is evident: the more clearly the Fed explains the rule governing the choice between the slow pre-emptive hike and the delayed aggressive hike, the less it needs to guide markets about which trail it will actually take.

What is approaching maturity is the investment landscape surrounding shareholder engagement. Here, we use the word maturity to refer to changes including 1) broader horizons among activist investors when choosing targets; 2) reduced potential for releasing value owing to a decline in the number of undervalued stocks and simple expansion in shareholder returns; and 3) the pricing in of ownership disclosures over a short period. This means it is now harder to come by easy wins, whether for the activist investors themselves or for the investors who make trades based on ownership disclosures. Data from IR Japan Holdings shows that the number of activist funds participating in Japan and the number of companies that have received shareholder proposals from activist investors has risen from eight funds and four companies in 2014 to 74 funds and 69 companies by 2025 ( Exhibit 49 ). records.text: oductivity Can Rise Our analysis has so far shown that Canada’s measured productivity is likely to rebound as labor-input growth slows and some of the recent dilution of capital per worker reverses. That rebound does not, by itself, establish a new growth model. A sustained acceleration requires productive capital to grow more quickly and the economy to use capital and labor more efficiently. From a Higher Level to a Higher Speed Limit Our growth framework distinguishes between changes that raise the level of productive capacity and changes that raise its ongoing growth rate. Capital deepening usually produces a transition effect. A rise in investment raises the growth rate of capital stock (g_K is approximately I/K - depreciation), and capital per hour rises when capital grows faster than the labor input. While the capital stock is being built, faster growth of K raises both capital per worker and potential-output growth. Once the investment surge ends and capital growth returns to its earlier rate, the incremental contribution to growth fades. Potential output remains permanently higher because the economy has a larger capital stock, but its growth rate returns toward the previous baseline. In the standard neoclassical growth model, a permanently higher investment rate raises the steady-state levels of capital and output per worker. records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 29 The Capital Build Can Raise Capacity; Conversion Determines the Speed Limit Canada’s current investment pipeline can raise the level of potential output even if it does not produce a permanent productivity acceleration. New power, transport, resource and digital infrastructure would expand productive capacity and leave the economy with a permanently larger capital stock. But a one-time build does not permanently raise the growth rate. Once the investment surge matures, the contribution from capital accumulation falls unless private investment remains persistently stronger. A lasting growth acceleration requires the capital build to generate one of two outcomes: 1. Persistent active capital deepening: Capital services continue growing faster than labor input after the initial projects are completed. 2. Sustained MFP diffusion: Infrastructure, technology, and market integration produce continuing efficiency gains in manufacturing, construction, transportation, wholesale, and other swing sectors. Our sector analysis suggests that neither outcome follows automatically from the current capex pipeline. The pipeline is large, but concentrated in structures — and engineering- heavy sectors with historically weak direct MFP conversion. Observable technology adoption is strongest in service sectors with smaller tangible-capital requirements. The opportunity lies in connecting the two. If there was one single indicator that gained prominence in the speech that the market had not focused on previously, it likely was the breadth of inflationary pressures (Figure 3). In particular, Warsh suggested that the breadth could be measuring underlying inflation, and the fact that it is still elevated and not falling likely means the latest, more benign CPIs have to be taken with a grain of salt. Interestingly, on our z-score table, the breadth measure does not appear to be overly hot, at least relative to other indicators in the mix. But maybe more importantly, it does not seem to be leading, but seems to be a lagging indicator, at least at inflation peaks. This makes the focus somewhat curious, but when the Fed Chair speaks, we listen, and we therefore include the breadth measure in our indicators to watch. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

From 2022 to 2025, US investors sold down their holdings of European-only equity funds by c30% of AUM, while European funds also broadly saw outflows. The same can be said for other international investors’ allocations into European equities. However, since 2025, European equity funds have seen sizable inflows from global investors. So-called “Global” equity funds—which maintain a geographically diversified equity portfolio and now hold similarly sized pool of European equities as Europe-only funds— have also seen consistent inflows. We think this trend can continue, both on a tactical and more strategic horizon. Beyond this, we find that European households also have capacity to increase equity allocations. According to national accounts, European households only hold c20% of their savings in equities, compared to c40% allocations from the US. Notably, German pension reforms (FT, 31 August 2026) are likely to boost inflows into equities, in line broader efforts from Brussels (FT, 30 September 2025)to channel European savings into the stock market. records.text: M BluePaper 22 Our new sector-level work suggests that these two improvements are unlikely to originate in the same parts of the economy. The sectors with the largest forward capital- spending pipelines are utilities, transportation and resources. The sectors with the strongest observable technology adoption and recent multifactor-productivity performance are information, finance, and other knowledge-intensive services. This creates what we call Canada’s conversion gap: Capital is building where direct TFP performance has historically been weak, while digital adoption is strongest in sectors with comparatively modest tangible-capital pipelines. The macro payoff therefore depends on what happens between those two groups. Power, transportation, resource, and digital infrastructure can raise the stock of productive capital. But they generate a broader productivity reset only if they lower economy-wide costs, crowd in private machinery and intangible investment, expand market scale, and allow technology to diffuse into larger, lower-readiness industries. What Is New in Our Framework? We construct a framework to map different sectoral dimensions into a conversion gap framework. We use historical capital-intensity contributions, historical and recent MFP, 2026 capex intentions, construction versus machinery-and-equipment spending, sector economic weights, and current AI adoption. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 04 September 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen Global Economist BofAS claudio.irigoyen@bofa.com Antonio Gabriel Global Economist BofAS antonio.gabriel@bofa.com Is this a Kohn day or a Bernanke day? Chairman Warsh started his Jackson Hole speech comparing his hiking experiences with former Vice Chair Don Kohn and former Chair Ben Bernanke, contrasting the brisk style of Kohn vs the more leisurely style of Bernanke. And then he asked "Is this a Kohn Day or a Bernanke Day?". After listening to his relatively hawkish speech and, moreover, after listening to Waller's relatively dovish speech, it is becoming evident that Chair Warsh was trying to tell us more than an innocent joke with that analogy. The Bernanke trail is the slow, pre-emptive route: start hiking earlier, move gradually, and reduce the risk that inflation or financial conditions get far enough out of line to require a more painful tightening later. The Kohn trail is the alternative: wait longer but if the inflation outlook deteriorates, be prepared to hike faster and more aggressively. The question is then not really whether to hike, but whether to hike slowly and pre- emptively today or risk having to hike much faster tomorrow. Forward Misguidance This framing helps explain why Warsh's Jackson Hole speech was so forceful. A net MFP contribution of 0.7pp would therefore be well above the 1981-2000 rate, below the early postwar regime, and almost 0.8pp above the post-2000 experience. This route would require broad gains from technology, scale, competition, organizational change, and resource allocation. AI adoption would need to extend materially beyond the current leaders in information, finance, and professional services. It would also require stronger productivity in industries where recent performance has been weakest: construction, manufacturing, transportation, wholesale trade, and parts of the resource economy. The Bank of Canada's AI baseline provides only part of the required impulse. Its central estimate is that AI adds ~0.2pp annually to MFP for 10 years. The upside scenario adds another 0.2pp, bringing the potential AI contribution to around 0.4pp annually. Even with that upside, AI alone would not close the full 50bp gap unless its effects were materially larger than the Bank assumes. The remaining contribution would need to come from other sources of MFP: internal-market integration, trade-related scale and technology transfer, improved permitting and project execution, stronger competition, better infrastructure utilization, or wider organizational diffusion. Since constituent stocks are selected based on their relative ranking by free-float market cap, their ranking will decline if their competition is growing even if their free-market cap remains flat. While TOPIX inclusion or exclusion is not management’s ultimate goal, it is an issue that cannot be ignored. Portfolio management and investment advice The BEA plans to move away from directly using a portfolio management and advice PPI- based deflator and instead infer prices by dividing nominal spending by a quantity measure derived from employment and hours worked in the industry. In practical terms, prices will no longer be directly observed. They will instead be backed out of nominal consumption and a measure of "quantities" consumed. It is not fully clear how the BEA will construct the quantity measure or whether it will incorporate a productivity adjustment. Assuming the quantity index is approximated by the product of total employment and average hours worked in the sector without productivity increases, we estimate that the 12-month inflation rate for this category will be revised lower (see Exhibit 7 ). Legal services The legal-services revision appears to be the most straightforward, but also the least consequential for core PCE inflation. After replacing CPI legal services with its PPI counterpart on an ad hoc basis in January and March of this year, the BEA has decided to use a PPI measure on a permanent basis. It is not fully clear which legal-services PPI indexes the BEA will ultimately use. However, judging from the numbers published in January and March, we think the aggregate PPI for legal services provides a reasonable approximation.

The productivity payoff from power, transport and resource infrastructure does not need to appear mainly in the measured MFP of utilities, transportation or mining. It may appear in: lower electricity constraints for manufacturing and data centers; shorter shipping times and lower inventories; increased feasibility of mineral processing; larger effective domestic markets; or higher private investment in downstream sectors. BoC estimates that labor-composition effects accounted for a meaningful part of the recent shortfall in output per trend hour relative to its pre-pandemic path. As newcomer inflows slow and workers already in Canada become more established in the labor market, part of that shortfall should close. There is considerable uncertainty around this component. Our 0.2pp contribution is therefore a deliberately modest assumption: It allows for partial normalization without treating the recent composition gap as certain to close fully. MFP improves but remains narrow. We assign the remaining 0.2pp to trend MFP. The BoC assumes that AI raises MFP by approximately 2% cumulatively over 10 years, equivalent to around 0.2pp annually. Its calibration is based on the share of the economy exposed to AI, the proportion of tasks for which adoption is profitable and the expected labor-cost savings from adoption. But in our view, the 0.2pp per year AI assumption should not simply be added to a normal historical MFP trend. Underlying Canadian MFP performance remains weak, while tariffs and trade-related reallocation create efficiency losses. The literature tells us that services and digitalization are likely to generate much of the MFP improvement, while infrastructure and resources are likely to attract much of the capital. Our analysis shows that the sectors building Canada’s new capital stock are not the ones generating the most visible technology diffusion. Thus, we shift the focus from which sector has the highest capex or MFP to which investments generate productivity gains elsewhere in the economy. This is the conversion gap. The capital builders create capacity. The digital leaders generate a growing share of current efficiency gains. The swing sectors determine whether those gains spread across the physical economy. Redirecting European demand The Industrial Accelerator Act is the most advanced proposal. Presented by the Commission in March 2026, it aims to create demand for European-made and low- carbon products, accelerate industrial investment and ensure that large foreign investments generate tangible value within the EU. The proposal would apply Made-in-EU and low-carbon requirements to public procurement and public- support schemes in selected sectors. Its initial scope includes Steel, Cement, Aluminium, Autos and net-zero technologies, while establishing a framework that could be extended to other energy-intensive industries, including Chemicals. The commercial significance could be substantial even without restricting imports. Products failing the relevant origin, content or carbon criteria could remain available in Europe but lose access to public procurement, subsidies, auctions, corporate fleet incentives or other supported demand. Public procurement in the EU accounts for over €2 trillion annually, while corporate fleets account for ~60% of EU auto sales. The IAA would therefore provide demand-side protection rather than a conventional tariff. The central political dispute concerns which non-EU products should receive equivalent treatment. In recent years, Mandom and Pacific Industries had offer prices that were lifted, respectively, around 60% and 50% above the initial offer in circumstances featuring activist involvement, competing bids, and market prices that were above the tender offer price. Toyota Industries also saw its price raised several times before reaching a tender agreement. The Commission’s initial approach allowed broad recognition of products from countries covered by EU trade, customs-union or procurement commitments. France has advocated a narrower interpretation, while Germany, the Nordics and export-oriented member states have historically favoured greater openness to allies. The latest Council compromise reportedly introduces the concept of “partner origin, ” with eligibility determined according to the EU’s actual trade and procurement commitments for a particular product. Member states would also have a formal role in considering reciprocity, dependency and security-of-supply concerns. This may result in a more legally robust but product-specific framework rather than one uniform list of trusted countries. This distinction matters for Morocco and Turkey. Both countries are important production locations for European companies but are also attracting Chinese investment intended partly to serve the European market. Broadly recognising their production as equivalent to European output could protect existing European supply chains while also allowing Chinese-owned facilities to qualify for public support. Excluding them could strengthen European localisation but penalise European OEMs and suppliers with established production there. Historically, Italian BTPs have traded at higher yields than Italian covered bonds, reflecting their lower ratings and higher beta to sovereign risk. In France, by contrast, covered bonds traditionally traded at higher yields than OATs, but this relationship has reversed in recent years. As concerns around France's fiscal trajectory, political uncertainty and potential sovereign downgrades have increased, investors have increasingly favoured French covered bonds, whose rating buffers provide insulation from sovereign downgrade risk. As a result, covered bonds trading through OATs has become the new normal. Meanwhile, in Italy, investors seeking exposure to the improving macro, fiscal and rating story have increasingly favoured BTPs, which offer greater upside to sovereign spread compression and potential rating upgrades. Consequently, Italian covered bonds have lagged the sovereign rally despite retaining robust credit fundamentals. While sugar and robusta coffee have consistently exhibited the greatest production sensitivity to El Niño-related weather disruptions, the largest rallies have occurred when adverse weather coincided with already depleted inventories. Cocoa's exceptional 2023/24 rally illustrates this dynamic clearly, as severe West African crop losses were amplified by a roughly 30% collapse in inventories, triggering an unprecedented price response. Looking at the current cycle, sugar and robusta coffee appear most vulnerable, combining elevated weather exposure with relatively thin inventory cushions, while cocoa enters this El Niño event with a more comfortable stock position than in 2023/24. Overall, history suggests that investors should focus less on headline weather forecasts and more on whether inventory buffers are sufficient to absorb potential production shortfalls, as this has proven to be the key driver of price volatility across the soft commodities complex. As a result, Western Canadian Select (WCS) crude tends to trade at a large discount to other global price benchmarks like WTI (West Texas Intermediate). Source: RBN Energy. Pipeline capacity has historically been a key constraint on growth. Over 80% of Canadian oil production and 97% of reserves are in Alberta. Much of this is tied to the oil sands, which produce bitumen (heavy oil). While there is some local refining capacity, most of this oil is either upgraded to a lighter crude or blended with condensate for pipeline transportation to other regions. Since Canadian oil production far exceeds domestic refinery demand, the sector is structurally export-oriented. Pipeline capacity to move this oil to demand centers has been a key limiter of growth over the past decade. In 2024, the Trans Mountain pipeline improved the egress situation and opened a new end market — the Pacific Coast. With more pipe expansions on the horizon, Western Canada is well positioned for further growth.

The balanced route assigns half of the incremental 50bpto capital deepening and half to MFP. Capital deepening rises from 1.0 to 1.25pp, while TFP rises from 0.2 to 0.45pp. So, K=0.25pp and A=0.25pp. Using a 35% capital share, the required increase in capital-per-hour growth is: g(K/H)= 0.25/0.35 ≈0.71pp. A capital-intensity contribution of 1.25pp would be near the upper end of Canada’s historical experience, but not materially above the 1961-81 rate. A TFP contribution of around 0.45 percentage points would be close to the 1981-2000 regime and well below the early postwar contribution. The implication is important: Canada does not need to recreate the 1960s productivity economy to reach 2% growth. But it does need capital deepening near the high end of its historical range and a return to positive MFP growth broadly comparable with the late-20th-century regime. Canada's next acceleration does not depend on an unprecedented investment boom or an implausibly large AI dividend in isolation. Instead, it requires the capital and productivity cycles to become mutually reinforcing. The three routes are accounting illustrations, but K and A are not independent in practice. Accordingly, we lower our 2027 NYMEX gas price forecast to $2.80/mmBtu (vs $3.50 previously), below forwards at $3.30. Even under our lower 2027 Henry Hub price forecast, our estimated end-Oct27 storage level still approaches the max observed level of just over 4000 Bcf, suggesting that risks to our 2027 price forecast are skewed to the downside. Hence, we recommend that US gas producers hedge their 2027 exposure, including the 2027-28 winter, which looks significantly softer than this year’s upcoming winter, while still pricing almost $0.60/mmBtu higher. We don’t yet recommend an outright short 2027 position to investors given winter weather uncertainty ahead, and we might wait for a better entry point for such a trading recommendation. M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 5 Exhibit 6: Only two Qatar LNG cargos are confirmed to have exited the Gulf in August Exhibit 7: The volume of LNG sat on tankers inside the Gulf is currently ~2.2 Mt But Other Supply Side Solvers Have Helped Alleviate Market Tension A combination of new project start ups and higher run rates at existing LNG facilities has offset ~60% of the lost supply from the Middle East over March-August. This has helped the global LNG market avoid >$25/mmbtu prices over summer, unlike in 2022, despite the initial volume loss from the Middle East being on a similar scale to the loss of Russian pipeline gas to Europe. Projects that started up last year and have continued to ramp through summer include Plaquemines in the US, LNG Canada and Tortue FLNG in Senegal/Mauritania. Supply is also being supported by new projects coming online through this year, including Golden Pass and Corpus Christi Trains 5–7 in the US, Congo FLNG and, most recently, Energia Costa Azul in Mexico. At the same time, exports have increased from a number of existing suppliers, notably Nigeria on better feedgas availability, Russia through higher Arctic LNG 2 volumes, as well as Norway, Angola and Oman. The global average utilization rate (ex Qatar and UAE) was 96% in July, above the 90% rate seen last year and 5-year average of 83%.

records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 47 What the calibration does — and does not — establish. The calibration is a scenario analysis, not a causal model. It does not assume that: all announced capex is completed; every dollar of investment provides the same capital-service flow; MFP gaps automatically close; AI-adoption rates translate directly into productivity; infrastructure spillovers can be observed immediately in the receiving sector. Our purpose is narrower. We use the scenarios to identify the scale and breadth of sector improvement consistent with each aggregate potential-growth outcome. The current capital pipeline can plausibly move Canada from a 1.5% economy toward a 1.7% economy. Reaching 2% requires the capital build to broaden into private machinery and intangible investment and to generate roughly 25bp of additional MFP across the swing sectors.

records.text: oured concentrated production (OPEC, Russia), long global supply chains (LNG tankers, oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz), and minimal investment in redundancy. It was efficient. It was also fragile. The system that is emerging is different. Countries are building strategic reserves, contracting for long-term LNG supply, investing in domestic production capacity, and – critically – diversifying not just their energy sources, but also their energy suppliers. This is not cost-optimised. It is resilience-optimised. And resilience requires capital. More LNG regasification terminals. More pipeline interconnectors. More strategic storage. More refining capacity distributed across regions, rather than concentrated in the lowest-cost locations. Global refining is a case in point. Permanent plant closures and war- related damage have cut global refinery output by an estimated 4.5 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026. Crack spreads – the margin between crude oil and refined products – have reached record levels, with the US 3-2-1 crack spread hitting $64 per barrel and global refining margins touching $59. These are not normal numbers. They reflect a structural shortage of refining capacity that years of underinvestment and geopolitical disruption have created. Even if both the Ukraine and Iran conflicts were to end tomorrow, it would take years to rebuild the refining capacity that has been lost. records.text: M BluePaper 20 of projects. Capital services must continue to grow fast enough to offset depreciation and remain ahead of labor-input growth. MFP can generate a level or a growth effect. A one-time improvement in A — for example, the removal of an internal trade barrier — raises the amount of output that can be generated from the existing capital and labor stock. Potential growth rises while the economy moves to the more efficient level of production. Once that adjustment has occurred, growth returns toward its earlier rate, leaving a permanently higher level of potential output. A sustained increase in the growth rate of A is different. If TFP continues to grow more quickly each year, potential- output growth also remains persistently higher. The gap between the new path and the old path widens over time rather than stabilizing at a fixed level. AI illustrates the point particularly well. The Bank of Canada assumes that AI contributes about 0.2 percentage points annually to TFP for 10 years, producing a cumulative TFP-level gain of approximately 2%. If that contribution ends once diffusion matures, growth returns toward baseline after 10 years while the 2% level gain remains. If AI capabilities and adoption continue advancing, the growth contribution can persist for longer. The distinction can be illustrated using the capital-intensity benchmarks discussed above. records.text: 2 September 2026 Japan Rates Strategy Page 4 Deutsche Securities Inc. Policy pricing and volatility—The case for selling rallies The swap market has all but priced in a 25bp hike at the September 17–18 meeting. Meeting-dated OIS for the next MPM sits at 1.209%, +21bp over the current 1.00% policy rate (over 80% priced), and the cumulative path eight meetings out reaches +88bp—a policy rate approaching 2% is entering the price. The near meeting can hardly surprise; the distribution of uncertainty sits with the far meetings, which is exactly what the volatility term structure shows next. In swaptions, 3m10y vol has reached 66.9bp/yr, the 98th percentile since 2020, and is closing in on the year's high (74.7bp). The composition matters: 20-day realized vol is only 41.7bp, so implied carries a fat +25bp event premium. The term structure adds the second message: 1y10y at 74.0bp trades 7.1bp above 3m10y, at the top of the range since 2024 (-18.3 to +8.7bp). records.text: Workers, Less Productivity — How Canada Generated Growth Canada’s growth model has changed substantially over the past six decades. In the earlier part of the period, growth reflected a combination of a rapidly expanding labor force, rising capital intensity and meaningful gains in the efficiency with which labor and capital were used. Over time, each of those productivity channels weakened. By the most recent period, aggregate output was being sustained primarily through additional workers and hours, while output per hour was barely rising. We use a standard growth-accounting framework to trace that transition. At the first level, real output can be expressed as the product of total hours worked and output per hour. This decomposition distinguishes growth generated by using more labor from growth generated by producing more in each hour worked. Labor-productivity growth can then be decomposed into three components: capital-intensity contribution, labor-composition contribution, and multifactor-productivity growth.

records.text: M BluePaper 48 Canada’s Relative Demographic Advantage Labor, Talent, and the Missing Capital Canada’s labor outlook splits into two distinct periods. The remainder of the 2020s is an adjustment; the 2030s bring a relative demographic advantage. Post-pandemic growth relied unusually heavily on population, employment and hours worked, while productive investment failed to keep pace. The immigration reset reverses that dynamic: labor-input growth will be unusually weak for several years, but slower workforce growth also creates a window to rebuild capital per worker. That weakness should not be extrapolated into the next decade. Under current long-run demographic assumptions, Canada is not heading toward the persistent labor-supply contraction facing many developed economies. Once the temporary-resident adjustment is complete, population growth returns to a more moderate positive pace, while aging creates only a modest drag on participation. Canada also begins that period with a relatively strong human-capital base. Educational attainment, universities, research quality, and workforce skills compare favorably internationally. The weakness lies further downstream: Canadian firms have invested too little in the machinery, software, intellectual property, infrastructure, and R&D required to turn those capabilities into productivity. Canada has accumulated human capital faster than productive capital. That creates the opportunity at the center of our broader Canadian growth thesis.

records.text: M BluePaper Morgan Stanley Research 5 Executive Summary Overview In this report, we offer an alternative to the current Canada narrative and a framework for a new growth path. The prevailing view of Canada's economy is well established: weak productivity, falling GDP per capita, excessive reliance on immigration and labor supply, and chronic underinvestment, compounded by growing uncertainty around access to the US market. We argue that Canada is entering a new growth phase. Bolstered by supportive government policy, it is moving beyond the post-commodity boom adjustment and a post-pandemic expansion that was driven by rapid labor-force expansion. We chart a course to sustained acceleration in potential growth, anchored in higher productivity, capital deepening, and efficiency gains. Our model suggests that the current investment pipeline can raise productive capacity and plausibly move potential growth from around 1.5% toward 1.7%. Reaching 2% requires the capital build to spread into private machinery and intangible investment and to produce sustained multifactor- productivity (MFP) gains in the industries that build, move, and manufacture across the economy. We envision a two-stage process. In the late 2020s, the growth comes from capital deepening and multifactor productivity (MFP), not labor input (from K and A, not L). Canada has a window in which slower population growth can help rebuild capital per worker before labor supply becomes more supportive again. In the 2030s

records.text: al agenda depends on its ability to deliver projects. Raising construction productivity lowers the effective cost of building capital throughout the economy. Manufacturing and wholesale perform a similar conversion role. Their adoption rates remain below the leading services sectors, but machinery investment, supply-chain integration and scale could allow them to translate infrastructure and technology into broader output gains. Transportation straddles the categories. It is already one of the largest capital builders, but also has substantial productivity shortfall and wide economy-level spillovers. It is therefore the clearest empirical test of whether the current K cycle can become an A cycle. A Sector Framework for K and MFP For each industry in the economy, labor productivity growth can be expressed as a sum of the industry-specific growth of capital per hour multiplied by the share of capital in the industry, the growth of labor composition times the share of labor input, and the growth of industry-specific MFP. Our sector exercise focuses on two components: (1) Active capital deepening: faster growth in productive capital per hour because capital accumulation accelerates, rather than simply because hours growth slows. (2) MFP growth: additional output generated through technology, organization, scale, competition, infrastructure and more efficient allocation of capital and labor. The result is a growing race for capital across resources, infrastructure, and power systems – a race that the current level of investment is not winning. Not only has the energy transition not stopped, but the next phase will require significantly more investment across a far broader set of assets than the market currently appreciates. That includes not only renewables and electrification, but also oil and gas exploration, LNG export capacity, power transmission and storage networks, refining resilience, energy services, and other critical infrastructure that keeps the system functioning while it transforms. The implications for equity, credit, and commodity markets are substantial. The sector-by-sector analysis that follows in subsequent sections, written by our analysts across the energy complex, identifies which parts of the value chain are best positioned to attract this capital and generate returns from it. records.text: M Japan Insight 2 Executive summary Exhibit 1 provides the roadmap for this report: governance reform has simultaneously reshaped corporate behavior and the opportunity set for investors. Governance reform has encouraged improvements in ROE and shareholder payouts, reductions in cross- shareholdings, business restructuring and take-private transactions, contributing to a broader re-rating of Japanese equities. At the same time, as these catalysts have become more widely recognized and more rapidly priced into shares, we believe the “easy alpha” once obtainable from straightforward signals has diminished. As some of the alpha embedded in individual companies migrates into broadly defined “Japan equity beta,” this report analyzes four themes separately in search of the next sources of alpha. Under next-generation TOPIX, we screen for prospective additions and stocks near the inclusion/exclusion threshold; within parent/subsidiary listings, inexpensive listed subsidiaries; within shareholder engagement, candidates with low valuations, strong cash balances and high foreign ownership; and within MBOs, stocks ranking highly on our MBO Score. Immigration: From Growth Engine to Reset Canada’s post-pandemic expansion was exceptionally labor intensive. Between 2019 and 2025, Canada’s population increased by almost 11%, equivalent to roughly 1.7% annually, the fastest pace among the major developed economies in our comparison. records.text: M BluePaper 92 Why Build in Canada? Canada offers many advantages for building data centers — it has plenty of land, water, and clean baseload power (nuclear and hydro). These are essentially the trifecta of natural resources required for a data center, particularly AI training facilities. For inference and colocation, geography matters more too: Latency requirements and network connectivity help dictate site selection. A favorable policy landscape also helps, as discussed in the section Could US Opposition to Data Centers & Sovereign AI Drive Projects North? That said, public opposition to data centers is high in Canada: A recent survey from May found that 68% of Canadians would oppose a large AI data center within a few blocks of where they live, vs. 15% in support. The political backdrop will be important in determining Canada's role in the global data center build. Financing Data Centers Fixed income markets are playing an active role in financing the data center build — and perhaps to an even greater extent than we initially anticipated. While the large hyperscalers do rely on cash from their incumbent businesses to help build & fill their AI data centers, they are increasingly leveraging debt markets in progressively intricate and creative ways to meet their capital needs. Moreover, many other sub-industries rely on debt to complete their role in the AI build, whether it be data center developers issuing ABS to finance their growth or neoclouds issuing chip-backed loans

Energy security and the return of capital How energy security is changing capital allocation We believe European utility capital allocation has undergone a notable shift away from a singular focus on decarbonisation and towards a broader energy-security agenda. Within Europe’s energy trilemma, security of supply and affordability have risen sharply in importance following recent supply disruptions and grid availability shortcomings. As a result, capital has been directed towards regulated networks, flexible generation, batteries, inertia-providing assets and life extensions for existing nuclear capacity, rather than purely maximising renewable deployment. We see this as a structural reallocation of value towards assets that support system reliability and resilience, with integrated utilities emerging as the primary beneficiaries given their exposure to networks, dispatchable generation and balancing services. Tight reserve margins across several European markets, long lead times for new thermal capacity, and concerns about system stability have been reinforcing investment in assets that guarantee reliability of supply. Latin America is one of the few regions globally where both oil and gas production can still grow materially through 2030–35, making it a direct beneficiary of the "energy addition" thesis. Argentine Vaca Muerta producers — Vista Energy, YPF, Tecpetrol, Pluspetrol — operate with lifting costs of c.$4–5/boe and can sustain profitable operations even at $60/bbl crude, well below the breakeven of most conventional global peers. The contrast with Brazil and Colombia's junior and mid-cap producers is instructive: both groups are far more sensitive to crude price downside given higher-cost conventional operations. Brazil's independents (Prio, Brava Energia/Ecopetrol, Vast Infraestrutura) hit record output levels in 2025 but remain burdened by high leverage after aggressive M&A — Brava was at 2.3x L TM in Q3 25 on reported numbers, rising to 3.5x excluding oil inventories. Colombian juniors such as Gran Tierra Energy or GeoPark may carry lower absolute leverage, but their conventional cost structures and heavy-crude exposure make them acutely vulnerable to oil price declines — particularly from increased global supply — with companies such as Gran Tierra explicitly relying on oil prices to manage financial pressures in 2026. The assumption that energy could be sourced from the cheapest global supplier, transported through open sea lanes, and priced in transparent commodity markets has been challenged in ways that are not reversible. Europe's forced pivot away from Russian pipeline gas replacing it with LNG from the United States, Qatar, and a patchwork of alternative suppliers – was the most dramatic example, but it is not the only one. Asia's LNG importers scrambled to diversify supply chains after the Iran conflict threatened critical transit routes. Countries across the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America are positioning themselves as alternative suppliers and competing to attract international energy capital. The result is a global energy system that is less integrated, more regionalised, and more expensive to operate, requiring significantly more redundant infrastructure than the pre-2022 model assumed. Energy security is reshaping capital allocation The geopolitical dimension deserves particular emphasis because it changes the investment calculus in ways that standard energy models do not capture. When energy security is taken for granted, as it largely was in the two decades before 2022, capital allocation optimises for cost. The cheapest source of supply wins. That logic favoured concentrated production (OPEC, Russia), long global supply chains (LNG tankers, oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz), and minimal investment in redundancy. It was efficient. The challenge is no longer simply replacing one source of energy with another, but expanding the entire energy system to support a more digital, electrified and resilient economy. For Europe, this is increasingly an issue of both economic growth and security. The Russia- Ukraine war exposed the vulnerabilities created by years of underinvestment and dependence on external suppliers, while more recent tensions in the Middle East have reinforced the value of a secure and reliable energy supply chain. Energy security has therefore shifted from a policy objective to an economic imperative and is increasingly becoming a core pillar of strategic autonomy. At the same time, the investment case extends well beyond geopolitics. AI-related power demand, electrification, industrial reshoring and decarbonisation are creating multiple structural drivers of energy investment. Consistent with this backdrop, our economists expect a multi-year investment cycle to remain firmly in place, forecasting average annual investment growth of more than 6% in the US and 4.5-5% in Europe and the UK (see Supersize me: The coming investment cycle, 26 Mar). To try and model the effect of weather on European gas demand, and by extension inventories, we have run sensitivity analysis between gas demand and weather. Weather affects gas demand through both the heating and power components and we attempt to capture both of these in this analysis. In this scenario modelling, warm/cold weather is defined as ±1 standard deviation in heating/cooling degree days relative to trailing history e.g. a warm scenario combines 1 std lower HDDs with 1 std higher CDDs. We derive these sensitivities from regressions of gas demand on HDDs and CDDs by country. Similarly, for the power component, we approximate renewables generation as the weather influence and test the sensitivity of gas demand to swings in renewable power generation. This analysis implies a peak-winter gas demand sensitivity of ~80 mcm/d for each ±1°C deviation from normal temperatures across our European perimeter, equivalent to an ~8–9% swing in demand. Our base case demand assumption is for a mild winter with weaker than average renewables generation. Warmer than average winter temperatures under El Nino support a 4.5% reduction in gas demand YoY, as previously discussed. records.text: US gas markets have been oversupplied for most of the last 18 years, since shale n significantly boosted low-cost production. More often than not, this oversupply has pressured US gas prices lower to compete with coal for power generation share, managing gas storage away from congestion. The few exceptions to that pattern included the occasional exceptionally cold winter event, like the 2013-14 polar vortex, or freeze-off-driven damage to production, like in 1H2022. With US demand for natural gas now rising at a faster pace than previously, n driven by higher LNG exports and power demand, and approaching the pace of US supply growth, we believe a tightening or loosening of the balance going forward will be largely driven by the mismatched timing of US supply and demand growth, creating a “push and pull” on prices, likely in a $2.50-$5.00/mmBtu range. This year’s US gas supply growth is on track to match demand growth at just over n 4 Bcf/d, leaving the 2026 balance comfortable, while far from congested. However, we revise our expected 2027 Permian gas production higher by 2 Bcf/d — 2026 base effect and an assumption of a faster forward ramp — taking our estimated 2027 US supply growth more than 2 Bcf/d above our estimated 3.8 Bcf/d US gas demand growth under current forward prices. We estimate that this oversupply would lead to storage congestion next year and, accordingly, we lower our 2027 NYMEX gas price forecast to $2.80/mmBtu (vs $3.50 previously), below forwards at $3.3

Europe's ability to navigate the coming winter without significant gas supply stress has become increasingly dependent on mild winter weather, as record low inventory levels reduce the system’s buffer. If the weather turns out mild to warm and Qatar returns in Q4 then Europe may still exit winter with inventories >30% full. In that scenario, we likely see downside to the current forward curve into Q1 27. However, this benign outcome has two disrupters - 1) Qatar exports remain severely disrupted for several more months and 2) winter weather is not as mild as expected. Given risk of either of these events occurring is still substantial, we still see the risk profile around TTF skewed to the upside and bake risk premium into our price forecasts. A Strong El Niño Winter Could be Europe's 'Get Out of Jail Free' Card The NOAA currently forecasts a 95% chance of a record El Niño event expected to peak in 4Q 26 and persist into 1Q 27. A strong El Niño event has the ability to influence not only gas market supply and demand, but also oil, coal and a range of metals commodities (see: metal&ROCK: Metals in the Eye of El Niño). records.text: Banks remain the highest-beta exposure to French political risk. Together with n the France Domestic basket (GSXEFRDO), French banks are the most direct equity proxy for sovereign spreads and fiscal credibility. Wider OAT-Bund spreads raise funding concerns, increase the cost of equity, pressure valuation multiples and revive concerns around regulation, taxation and financial-policy intervention. The link is reinforced by banks’ holdings of French sovereign debt, which tie balance-sheet risk directly to spread dynamics. French banks trade on roughly 8x forward earnings and at a c.25% discount to their European peers. Across sectors, it is one of the largest valuation discounts, suggesting a meaningful amount of risk is already reflected. That said, it is difficult to ignore the sector’s strong performance: French banks are up roughly 140% since January 2022, comfortably ahead of the STOXX 600 (+50%), the S&P 500 (+70%) and even the Magnificent 7 (+110%), albeit well behind the c.300% rally in European banks. French banks remain cheap, but they are no longer as cheap as they once were, and positioning has become increasingly constructive. As the 2027 election cycle approaches, we would not be surprised to see a period of consolidation or modest profit-taking until there is greater clarity on the political and fiscal outlook. records.text: M Japan Insight 30 Parent-subsidiary listings: Beginning of the end as an investment theme Parent-subsidiary listings are a key topic for corporate governance in Japanese equity markets. As an investment theme, though, we are already arguably facing the beginning of the end. That is, it is a self-consuming theme in that the pool of investment targets itself inevitably shrinks as the practice is unwound. The TSE has long maintained that while it does not prohibit the listing of firms that have a parent company, it does not consider such a structure to be a desirable capital policy (“TSE’s Views Regarding the Listing of Companies Having Parent Companies,” 2007). Debate regarding parent-subsidiary listings reignited around 2019 due to concerns that such arrangements could compromise the interests of minority shareholders (“Study Group to review Minority Shareholder Protection and other Framework of Quasi- Controlled Listed Companies”). Market and corporate governance reforms implemented by the TSE in the 2020s heightened the pressure on companies to justify maintaining their listed status and strengthen their protection of minority shareholders. The number of listed subsidiaries has been in steady decline, a trend that has accelerated in recent years ( Exhibit 38 ). Even narrowing the focus solely to TOPIX stocks, which generally boast relatively high liquidity, only around 60 stocks remain. records.text: distinction can be illustrated using the capital-intensity benchmarks discussed above. Canada’s official capital-intensity contribution was around 0.3pp annually in the recent weak period and around 0.8pp over 2000-19. If active capital deepening raises the contribution from 0.3 to 0.8 percentage points for five years, potential- output growth would be approximately 0.5 percentage points stronger during that period. The cumulative level effect would be approximately: 0.5pp×5=2.5%. Potential output would therefore be around 2.5% higher after five years than under the weak-capital baseline. If the capital-intensity contribution then falls back to 0.3 percentage points, growth returns to baseline, but the 2.5% level difference remains. We checked the data and don’t find evidence of Rhine water effects on aggregate manufacturing data, though select sectors (pharma, chemicals and refineries) show tentative signs of impact (see note: Europe Economic Weekly: Summer break, not summer calm 14 August 2026). The impact on refineries may be the most important given the ongoing energy crisis and the widening in gasoil crack spreads. But, in that respect, it is also worth noting that Rhine levels have increased close to the critical thresholds again over the last 10 days (and headlines have vanished simultaneously). Politics, meanwhile, need watching. Short term, the Saxony-Anhalt state election this Sunday (6 Sep) is likely to make headlines as far right Alternative fuer Deutschland (AfD) is polling close to an absolute majority. An AfD-governed state could have deep institutional consequences, but we don’t think that is the most relevant market aspect. We had previously argued that the July reform package deal provided credible glue for the federal ruling coalition over potentially very controversial state elections in the fall (Mecklenburg Vorpommern and Berlin also vote on 20 Sep). records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 04 September 2026 5 worse than Medicare, Defense Spending and even Social Security, which have been more stable. Higher rates will exacerbate this trend The current level of interest rates is likely to exacerbate these trends as Treasury refinances maturing debt at higher borrowing costs. The average interest rate on outstanding marketable Treasury debt remains well below prevailing market yields, at roughly 3.4%. Looking specifically at coupon-bearing securities, current market rates imply that debt rolled over in coming years will be refinanced at interest rates approximately 1.4 percentage points higher, on average, than those on the securities being retired (Exhibit 2). The Treasury's increased reliance on bills also leaves borrowing costs more sensitive to near-term monetary policy. Nearly $7 trillion of Treasury bills are currently outstanding, the vast majority of which mature within one year (Exhibit 3). Assuming the Fed hikes rates by 75bp this year as we expect, annual interest costs on outstanding T-bills could increase by roughly $50bn or ~15bp of GDP. records.text: Monetary policy: Inflation in the spotlight We expect evidence of disinflation to keep the Fed on hold in 2026. Our forecast has inflation falling enough to justify 50bp of cuts in 2027. How far disinflation goes remains an open question. The Middle East conflict and AI demand-side price pressures could mean less inflation that we expect (or firming in inflation), leading the Fed to hike rates. An “oil risk premium” alternative scenario seems like the most pressing risk, but markets see greater risk of an “animal spirits” outcome.

Note: The split of trend labor productivity into capital deepening, labor composition and MFP is our calibration; it is not published by the Bank of Canada. The estimates are in terms of the percentage point annual contribution. These routes produce the same headline growth rate, but they have very different implications for durability, investment, sector performance and the level of potential output. Route 1: Capital deepening does all the work. The first route raises the capital-deepening contribution from 1.0 to 1.5pp. Using an illustrative capital share of 35%: g(K/ H)=0.50/0.35≈1.43pp. Capital per hour would therefore need to grow around 1.4pp faster than in the baseline. That is a demanding result. The capital-intensity contribution averaged approximately: 1.3pp in 1961-81, 0.8-0.9pp in 1981-2000, ~0.8pp in 2000-19, and ~0.3pp in 2019-23. A contribution of 1.5pp would therefore exceed any of the longer, cyclically neutral historical regimes in our decomposition. The historical evidence confirms that capital intensity remained Canada’s main positive productivity driver after 2000

More broadly, we have found that debt growth matters most at the extremes. IG Energy currently trades at its richest level versus IG Industrials in more than a decade, with the spread ratio sitting just below 1.0x (Figure 139). records.text: Inflation momentum based on market prices declined in Q2 and was followed by a decline in macro data, but it has rebounded more recently (Exhibit 3). In fact inflation has broadly come down across G10 economies, generally surprising to the downside with core inflation continuing to trend down. Pockets of overheating remain limited and inflation expectations do not appear at risk of unanchoring. That said, with a continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the risk of more inflation volatility linked to energy prices remains elevated in the near term, due to both potential upside risk in refined products and higher TTF gas prices for Europe – this makes further ECB hikes beyond September more likely, also considering evidence of stronger fiscal spending in Germany. In addition, our economists now expect a hike from the BOJ in September (followed by another hike in January 2027). The global cyclical backdrop has been resilient to the energy shock with PMIs picking up YTD (Exhibit 4). Global manufacturing PMIs increased most in Germany and Japan, likely supported by fiscal policy – services PMIs, especially in Europe have somewhat lagged, possibly due to the drag from energy costs. In China the divergence between strong exports (driving large currency account surpluses) and weak domestic activity has continued. In 2H, rising geopolitical uncertainty and risk could create more headwinds for the cyclical picture with upcoming US midterm elections, elevated US/Canada trade tensions,

volume, although the balance will vary by product and producer. Third, greater price and demand visibility can improve investment incentives. More durable regional economics can support maintenance, modernisation and selective capacity investment. This does not eliminate Europe’s energy, carbon or regulatory disadvantages, but it could reduce the risk that low-priced imports undermine the return on domestic investment. Fourth, the valuation effect can exceed the immediate change in earnings estimates. ArcelorMittal and the broader European Steel sector have re-rated by more than the associated increase in forward EBITDA expectations. This is consistent with investors assigning higher multiples where policy improves the perceived durability and quality of earnings. The re-rating should not be attributed to protection alone, but it demonstrates that policy can influence valuation as well as near-term forecasts. Steel is not a universal template. Much of the EU’s rationale for intervention also applies to Autos, Chemicals and Machinery. records.text: M BluePaper 72 Canadian Oil & Gas Devin McDermott, Justin Latran Improving Outlook for Canadian Oil & Gas Canada produces about 6% of the world's oil and holds ~9% of reserves, the 4th highest globally. Higher oil prices, improving market access (pipeline expansions), and a more constructive policy backdrop all support growth in the years ahead. We forecast annual upstream spending for Canadian oil sands producers rising from US $13.4 billion in 2025 to US$16.2 billion in 2030 supporting, 600-700 kb/d of total growth in the country over the same period (+12%). Canada is a globally significant and strategically important heavy-oil supplier. Canada has risen from roughly the 13th-largest crude oil producer in 2000 to the fourth-largest today, as oil-sands development helped more than double national crude production from approximately 1.7 mb/d (million barrels per day) to more than 5.4 mb/d. Pipeline infrastructure expanded alongside that growth — including additions to Enbridge's Mainline system, the start-up of Keystone in 2010 and the completion of TMX (Trans Mountain expansion) in 2024 — although production periodically grew faster than egress capacity, contributing to export bottlenecks and periodically steep price discounts for Western Canada Select oil relative to over global benchmarks.
